[{:db/id 17592186120091 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "319007b2-b622-521a-9fbd-6b55411ba8fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186244758} {:answer/id #uuid "77d27a23-474c-5fd8-b89a-b5cf94e06791" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "u\sqrt{1+4v}" :db/id 17592186245376} {:answer/id #uuid "93b89d68-2ae3-5725-a00d-dea53dab7aaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{{v}^{2}-{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186245602} {:answer/id #uuid "a4251703-6830-575d-b816-b1664fbed324" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186245780} {:answer/id #uuid "ffcccb75-fd9a-544a-9328-801afbd6a123" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{v}^{2}\sqrt{1+4{u}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186246547}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186244758} :answer-field/id #uuid "8bbe3440-ff66-5a42-bcf4-05a3f9473d00" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186246790}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a126827b-bc56-516e-a030-80e53d51bfcf" :question/math-academy-id "q-109941" :question/problem "$${∬}_{D}\boxed{\phantom{AAAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A,\,D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\}$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface $\mathbf{r}(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}u-{v}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}{v}^{2}⟩$ for $0\le u\le 2$ and $0\le v\le 2.$ What is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-{v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\hspace{0.222em}1,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-{v}^{2}),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}-2v,\hspace{0.222em}2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 2u & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2v & 2v\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2v & 2v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}2u & 1 \\ 0 & -2v\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨2v,\hspace{0.222em}-4uv,\hspace{0.222em}-4uv⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨2v,\hspace{0.222em}-4uv,\hspace{0.222em}-4uv⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(2v)^{2}+(-4uv)^{2}+(-4uv)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+32{u}^{2}{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}(1+8{u}^{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}}\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}} \\  & =2v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\sqrt{{v}^{2}}=v$ since $v\ge 0$ on $D.$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{\color{blue}2v\sqrt{1+8{u}^{2}}}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120109 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8311c425-96db-50b4-bda2-7afc21298e5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,5)" :db/id 17592186261013} {:answer/id #uuid "970d51ce-6cc7-567e-b921-0a5f575739b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(10,-7)" :db/id 17592186261184} {:answer/id #uuid "aed5ed6e-37c8-5e3c-ae55-c95e30ce3202" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(6,-7)" :db/id 17592186261416} {:answer/id #uuid "bc52c38c-023f-560d-827e-ce988bae6a2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,2)" :db/id 17592186261533} {:answer/id #uuid "c912ae60-77c2-546c-be59-6f64006178e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(3,2)" :db/id 17592186261652}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186261533} :answer-field/id #uuid "0c61931c-b6de-57e6-b862-b7df723296cc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262146}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "22d6e6f4-daf0-5645-a375-f0c335545e70" :question/math-academy-id "q-126902" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2{t}^{2}-t,5-3{t}^{2}⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨-1,2⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-3{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨4t-1,-6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨-1\,,\,2⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨-1,2⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨-1,2⟩ \\ ⟨4t-1,-6t⟩ & =c⟨-1,2⟩ \\ ⟨4t-1,-6t⟩ & =⟨-c,2c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4t-1 &=-c \\ -6t &=2c\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=-4t+1.$ Substituting $c=-4t+1$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6t & =2(-4t+1) \\ -6t & =-8t+2 \\ 2t & =2 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨-1,2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨2(1)^{2}-1,5-3(1)^{2}⟩=⟨1,2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨-1,2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,2).$"} {:db/id 17592186120141 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bb782c95-7af3-526a-9bb9-7b058730fb65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.97986" :db/id 17592186117053} {:answer/id #uuid "d1b8e582-6c54-5345-b578-61913b7c90ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.76327" :db/id 17592186117054} {:answer/id #uuid "e250d959-170b-52d9-b20a-5923502520d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5" :db/id 17592186117055} {:answer/id #uuid "1c1e023d-bb14-56f4-9b27-bbc37573d64c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.95431" :db/id 17592186117056} {:answer/id #uuid "46811194-b144-5843-b5c6-57be7b71a456" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.03210" :db/id 17592186117057}] :answer-field/id #uuid "b4caec8d-32d0-5130-bea1-50ad06c9cca1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186117052}] :question/id #uuid "82df7b11-5afb-5bc3-ba85-98c15caddadf" :question/math-academy-id "q-144139" :question/problem "Evaluate $\cos (\frac{11π}{3}^{∘})$ using a calculator. > A graphing calculator is required to answer this question." :question/requires-calculator true} {:db/id 17592186120156 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d37b0ad3-d75a-5e9c-b32f-03d04a5aa5da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186367916} {:answer/id #uuid "07857a98-a240-5250-8ec4-acfbd5c7ae04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186367917} {:answer/id #uuid "65ee85e5-b512-5d13-8b8c-1dd0de294bb8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/id 17592186367918} {:answer/id #uuid "00ecb62a-ae5e-5aed-867f-320853bd4196" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186367919} {:answer/id #uuid "ea1b9131-e15e-5c67-8056-20b52038f360" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186367920}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186367916} :answer-field/id #uuid "8cbcea62-bc50-5399-998e-516065a90ade" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186367915}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7f0173d8-1b20-5423-8c43-633f5b8b0c9b" :question/math-academy-id "q-165243" :question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,2t⟩,$  use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature of this curve as a function of $t.$ 

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)=8(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j+\,k).$*" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(2)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{\sin }^{2}⁡2t+4{\cos }^{2}⁡2t+4} \\  & =\sqrt{4({\sin }^{2}⁡2t+{\cos }^{2}⁡2t)+4} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are told that

$$
{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)=8(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j+\,k),
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =8\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =8\sqrt{{\sin }^{2}⁡2t+{\cos }^{2}⁡2t+1} \\  & =8\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{{(2\sqrt{2})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{16\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120164 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9455b7e1-8e45-5b8d-8930-b09294afde81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{sin}t" :db/id 17592186289026} {:answer/id #uuid "39d23c9a-dade-5d1b-902c-eabbc6bdf7de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sin t" :db/id 17592186442571}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442571} :answer-field/id #uuid "b860cd5e-c7b3-588c-8a3f-8511ad544821" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186290133}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "bbe7871a-ccc9-5a95-8370-21299423ec38" :question/math-academy-id "q-222851" :question/problem "Given  the curve $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,4t⟩$, find the principal normal vector $N(t)$ at an arbitrary point on the curve.

$N(t)=⟨\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$
{{field-1}}$,0\,⟩$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the unit tangent vector $T(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({\sin }^{2}⁡t+{\cos }^{2}⁡t)+16} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{4}{5}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{4}{5}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}({\cos }^{2}⁡t+{\sin }^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{-\frac{3}{5}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩}{\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)}=⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120195 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2104e133-914f-5ccf-9abb-bb338526ec6d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{18}" :db/id 17592186300116} {:answer/id #uuid "2e7b2fae-8ac3-57a0-bffe-05751f19e1e4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{54}{7}" :db/id 17592186300187} {:answer/id #uuid "9e343b3d-6257-5d65-9a7e-1c0b02359997" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9}{5}" :db/id 17592186300760} {:answer/id #uuid "a782896a-abec-59e4-9290-6a432fe3815a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{9}" :db/id 17592186300805} {:answer/id #uuid "bebe977a-dc05-5a44-8579-fd4c6afc897a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{18}{7}" :db/id 17592186300914}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186300914} :answer-field/id #uuid "38691da1-c3cd-5bcd-bc71-b36d06760bd6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186301409}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e944b722-89ed-5df5-8b31-cb3570eaaf1f" :question/math-academy-id "q-32595" :question/problem "If $x=2\sqrt{y}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{y}},$ find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at the point $(5,9).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(2\sqrt{y}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{y}}) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{y})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\right) \\  & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{1/2})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{-1/2}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}-3\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-3/2}) \\  & ={y}^{-1/2}+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{-3/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}+\frac{3}{2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}+\frac{3}{2y\sqrt{y}} \\  & =\frac{2y+3}{2y\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{2y\sqrt{y}}{2y+3}.
$$

Finally, substituting the point $(5,9),$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(5,9)} & =\frac{2(9)\sqrt{9}}{2(9)+3}=\frac{18}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120196 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16d73b7d-9403-55ab-b551-e19830698e26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\frac{x}{12}+\frac{9}{4}" :db/id 17592186300052} {:answer/id #uuid "6a33eeae-06c8-52d2-b05c-f45a9e998a06" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\frac{x}{12}+\frac{7}{2}" :db/id 17592186300498} {:answer/id #uuid "9e0ef0fa-a60f-528b-b723-df752ee1c670" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\frac{x}{12}+\frac{7}{4}" :db/id 17592186300758} {:answer/id #uuid "b2d76d1c-be51-51c6-8cde-9ba71e9a668a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=9x+3" :db/id 17592186300855} {:answer/id #uuid "b6e2c41b-b138-5e44-b020-de7bc94b2004" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=12x-27" :db/id 17592186300874}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186300052} :answer-field/id #uuid "2a3602d1-8784-558b-8e8c-d79f5c14e514" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186301360}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c7ef2446-7ddb-53cb-83cf-b4fed6b4ea6f" :question/math-academy-id "q-32596" :question/problem "Given a curve $x=\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2},$ what is the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point $(9,3)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we differentiate $x(y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3{y}^{2}-2y \\  & =2{y}^{2}-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, taking the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y},$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}\right)}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2{y}^{2}-2y}.
$$

The slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $(9,3)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{(x,y)=(9,3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{2(3)^{2}-2(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point-slope formula for a tangent line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =\frac{1}{12}(x-9) \\ y & =\frac{x}{12}-\frac{3}{4}+3 \\ y & =\frac{x}{12}+\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t}-1\,,{e}^{-2t}⟩ & =⟨0,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}-1 &=0 \\ {e}^{-2t} &=1\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}-1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-2t})⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-2{e}^{-2t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},\,-2{e}^{0}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point  $P(0,1)$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨0\,,\,1⟩+u⟨1\,,\,-2⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120216 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b73b04b7-7f81-5da6-b3eb-9ceb86cb6994" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0, 1, 2)$ "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2{t}^{2}\,,\,{e}^{t}\,,\,2{e}^{t}⟩$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel." :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨4t,\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩ & =c\,⟨4t,\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩ \\ ⟨2{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{t}⟩ & =⟨4ct,\,c{e}^{t},\,2c{e}^{t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2} &=4ct \\ {e}^{t} &=c{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t} &=2c{e}^{t}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second and third equations, we obtain that $c=1.$ Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2} & =1\cdot 4t \\ {t}^{2} & =2t \\ {t}^{2}-2t & =0 \\ t(t-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=0$ and $2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨2(0)^{2},\,{e}^{0},\,2{e}^{0}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩ \\ r(2) & =⟨2(2)^{2},\,{e}^{2},\,2{e}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨8,\,{e}^{2},\,2{e}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(0,1,2)$ and $(8,{e}^{2},2{e}^{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186120242 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b3ad161-64a2-5b71-ad24-c120e8ec6285" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}\,i-\frac{4}{5}\,k" :db/id 17592186398741} {:answer/id #uuid "9b7e3c75-5535-5316-bea0-bf6c928449b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}\,j-\frac{3}{5}\,k" :db/id 17592186398742} {:answer/id #uuid "6a162c78-4b2f-5cb3-bbfc-9d6ac2a6eb14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j" :db/id 17592186398743} {:answer/id #uuid "d2f7e9c3-d0a4-5c14-ad36-84ce7ce201f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{4}{5}\,i-\frac{3}{5}\,j" :db/id 17592186398744} {:answer/id #uuid "cbf33e14-d217-5957-83e1-d43d4854445a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k" :db/id 17592186398745}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186398745} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ffbf219-9fc7-55d4-a011-546b8183375e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186398740}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fee02912-87a3-5a99-92ba-f8ae9f270c88" :question/math-academy-id "q-33233" :question/problem "The equations of a curve $r(t)$ and its corresponding unit tangent vector $T(t)$ at an arbitrary point are given below. Find the principal normal vector to that curve at the point $P(0,3,4).$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k,\,t\in [0,2\pi ) \\ T(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k,\,t\in [0,2\pi )\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(0,3,4)$ on the given curve. We know that:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,3,4⟩ \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k & =0\text{ }i+3\text{ }j+4\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components of $i$, $j$, and $k$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{cos}⁡t &=0 \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t &=3 \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t &=4\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(0,3,4)$ is at the tip of the vector $r\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right).$ 

Now, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k \\ {T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,k \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)‖ & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+{\left(-\frac{3}{5}\right)}^{2}+{\left(-\frac{4}{5}\right)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}+\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,3,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)}{‖{T}^{′}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)‖}=\frac{-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k}{1}=-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where at $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)\cdot N\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right) & =(-i)\cdot (-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}(i\cdot j)+\frac{4}{5}(i\cdot k) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120252 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2e221a65-a44e-5346-8777-5df15d203193" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\left\langle \frac{2}{3},-\frac{1}{3},-\frac{2}{3}\right\rangle " :db/id 17592186117674} {:answer/id #uuid "3d439e47-3587-59b8-90e6-26a8e6ad90ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3},-\frac{1}{3}⟩" :db/id 17592186442572} {:answer/id #uuid "524146c4-7e77-5f6d-af6c-ffd660ac28d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{2}{3},-\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}⟩" :db/id 17592186442577} {:answer/id #uuid "b1c1d1e6-bb07-517c-8756-922d8ba89e65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}⟩" :db/id 17592186442592} {:answer/id #uuid "fbaf0be8-2245-53a4-8fe1-5686e5bfe610" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\frac{2}{3},-\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3}⟩" :db/id 17592186442600}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186442577} :answer-field/id #uuid "4aee8c82-8119-5217-bc70-4d42d2a818f7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186117671}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2f555a45-5f75-599a-8fee-db06b9f6384d" :question/math-academy-id "q-33493" :question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}⟨-2,\,2t,\,{t}^{2}⟩.
$$

 
Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=2.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}⟨-2,\,2t,\,{t}^{2}⟩) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}\right)⟨-2,\,2t,\,{t}^{2}⟩+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =-\frac{2t}{({t}^{2}+2)^{2}}⟨-2,\,2t,\,{t}^{2}⟩+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}⟨0,\,2,\,2t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{({t}^{2}+2)^{2}}[-2t⟨-2,\,2t,\,{t}^{2}⟩+({t}^{2}+2)⟨0,\,2,\,2t⟩] \\  & =\frac{1}{({t}^{2}+2)^{2}}⟨4t,\,-2{t}^{2}+4,\,4t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{((2)^{2}+2)^{2}}⟨4(2),\,-2(2)^{2}+4,\,4(2)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{36}⟨8,-4,8⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{9}⟨2,-1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(2)‖ & =\frac{1}{9}‖⟨2,-1,2⟩‖ \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(2)$ and obtain the principal normal vector to the curve at the point where $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(2) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(2)}{‖{T}^{′}(2)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{9}⟨2,-1,2⟩}{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}=⟨\frac{2}{3},-\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$P(x(t),y(t),z(t))$ is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(2,0,5)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2,0,5⟩ \\ ⟨t+1,\,8\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,2{t}^{2}+3⟩ & =⟨2,0,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}t+1 &=2 \\ 8\operatorname{ln}⁡t &=0 \\ 2{t}^{2}+3 &=5.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the first equality, $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,0,5)$ is at the tip of $r(1).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,\frac{8}{t},\,4t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1,\,\frac{8}{1},\,4(1)⟩=⟨1,8,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{8}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+64+16} \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${r}^{′}(1)$ and obtain the unit tangent vector to the given curve at $P(2,0,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(1)}{‖{r}^{′}(1)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}⟨1,8,4⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{9},\frac{8}{9},\frac{4}{9}⟩\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120270 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "69b74c9f-1ac7-5a46-a1ba-f698684da9b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+\sqrt{3}z+1=0" :db/id 17592186485942} {:answer/id #uuid "69efef97-f312-5209-9f6a-670aa33a1ef7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}x-z-\sqrt{3}=0" :db/id 17592186485943} {:answer/id #uuid "ee6844a6-528c-589f-8c8f-0e27539f7d38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-z+1=0" :db/id 17592186486197} {:answer/id #uuid "f230ed97-e97b-5244-a435-92e949f80f8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-z+\sqrt{3}=0" :db/id 17592186486204} {:answer/id #uuid "f8b4d79d-0b34-5b15-9b62-727ead6d0a6b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+\sqrt{3}z-\sqrt{3}=0" :db/id 17592186486214}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485943} :answer-field/id #uuid "b1e11bc9-cec7-5abb-9e74-1d0988c65cb7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186117759}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3005bcca-c33e-585c-8e84-018875446bff" :question/math-academy-id "q-33665" :question/problem "Find a Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0,$ given that

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=0$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,j+\sqrt{3}\,k)=\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,k \\ N(0) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,j=j.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=0$ is

$$
p=r(0)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡0+(0)\operatorname{sin}⁡0)\,i+(\operatorname{sin}⁡0-(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0)\,j+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(0)^{2}\,k=⟨1,0,0⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(0)$ and the principal normal $N(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\times N(0) & =(\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,k)\times j \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ \frac{1}{2} & 0 & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=2\cdot (T(0)\times N(0))=-\sqrt{3}\,i+k=⟨-\sqrt{3},0,1⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨-\sqrt{3},0,1⟩ & =⟨1,0,0⟩\cdot ⟨-\sqrt{3},0,1⟩ \\ -\sqrt{3}\cdot x+0\cdot y+1\cdot z & =-\sqrt{3} \\ \sqrt{3}x-z-\sqrt{3} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120272 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fc3dbeb4-85f0-5977-97bc-032932c84bc6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}2t+9{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}3t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186391649} {:answer/id #uuid "769deadf-6f4e-5979-ab29-41e31ac33156" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}2t+9{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}3t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186391650} {:answer/id #uuid "8acb4dd0-ab7b-50a4-bed8-752a2b64b388" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}2t+9{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}3t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186391651} {:answer/id #uuid "4b968ecc-eb2e-5899-bdd8-779a4c1f182d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{2{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}2t+3{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}3t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186391652} {:answer/id #uuid "0ec6159d-f7de-5b2f-b124-7ba4b0ab6ebc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{2{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}2t+9{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}3t}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t" :db/id 17592186391653}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186391651} :answer-field/id #uuid "438187f3-2ea9-5adc-8e76-df9ae09801fc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186391648}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "994d254c-8dfb-50db-8abf-3c167a677836" :question/math-academy-id "q-33728" :question/problem "![](images/d1/d162245ac19c3ef9ae63d602fb4e188ddfd241a1a604304f6c272c3902ce1e93.png)

Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $\mathbf{g}(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}2t,\hspace{0.222em}\operatorname{cos}3t⟩$ from $t=0$ to $t=\pi ?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find ${\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{g}}^{'}(t)‖:$

$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ are

$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{3}$ is

$$
p=r\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}),\,4\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{3})⟩=⟨-1,\frac{4\pi }{3},0⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)$ and the principal normal $N\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\times N\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,3⟩\times ⟨1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 4 & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\left[\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,k\text{ }\right] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,j-4\,k) \\  & =⟨0,\frac{3}{5},-\frac{4}{5}⟩\end{aligned}

$$

from $t=1$ to $t=3.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find ${\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)$ and $‖{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)‖:$

\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t+t\operatorname{sin}t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t-t\operatorname{cos}t),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}t+(\operatorname{sin}t+t\operatorname{cos}t),\hspace{0.222em}\operatorname{cos}t-(\operatorname{cos}t-t\operatorname{sin}t),\hspace{0.222em}\sqrt{3}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t\operatorname{cos}t,\hspace{0.167em}t\operatorname{sin}t,\hspace{0.167em}\sqrt{3}t⟩ \\ ‖{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(t\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}+(t\operatorname{sin}t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t+{\operatorname{sin}}^{2}t)+3{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}} \\  & =2t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t>0$ for $t\in [1,3].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{3}‖{\mathbf{f}}^{'}(t)‖\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}2t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =9-1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(1,0,0)$ is $p=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

To find the equation of the osculating plane, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to it. To do that, we find the cross product of the unit tangent $T(1)$ and the principal normal $N(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1)\times N(1) & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\,i+\,j))\times k \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left[\text{ }\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\,i-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\,j+\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix}\,k\text{ }\right] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=\sqrt{2}\cdot (T(1)\times N(1))=i-j=⟨1,-1,0⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a general point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,0⟩ & =⟨1,0,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,0⟩ \\ 1\cdot x+(-1)\cdot y+0\cdot z & =1 \\ x-y-1 & =0.\end{aligned}

tangent to the given curve as a function of the parameter $t.$ Since we are given the curve $r(t)$ parametrized by the parameter $t$ (not the arc length $s$), we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the corresponding unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

$r(t)=⟨t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi .$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨2,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨2,\,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =-2\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2}{{2}^{3}}=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120305 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "87f8fd91-1f28-5015-8ff3-d0b2082bef4a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}" :db/id 17592186117970} {:answer/id #uuid "914487bc-36a9-59b4-b8af-f5eb56218162" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{5}" :db/id 17592186117971} {:answer/id #uuid "11300089-4bdb-5b31-83da-8d7c4fa157c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{25}" :db/id 17592186117972} {:answer/id #uuid "231e3368-2ef5-597d-b3f5-65e238df3219" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{9}" :db/id 17592186117973} {:answer/id #uuid "6db9076c-e9d2-5c8a-a0f1-03aa0f346943" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{25}" :db/id 17592186117974}] :answer-field/id #uuid "779d705d-5df8-51c8-9de4-e7bd9e9ac3be" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186117969}] :question/id #uuid "6bfabb63-8d04-5b0d-ad72-c2353e9edf10" :question/math-academy-id "q-34209" :question/problem "Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(t)$ given that its derivative $r^{′}(t)$ and the derivative of the corresponding unit tangent $T^{′}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,i+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since the curve $r(s)$ and its unit tangent vector $T(s)$ are both parametrized by arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$

$$

We differentiate $T(s)$ with respect to $s$ and calculate its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right))i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right))k \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,i+\frac{3}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,j-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,k \\  & =-\frac{4}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,i+\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,j-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,j-5\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\,k] \\ ‖{T}^{′}(s)‖ & =\frac{1}{10}\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right))^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right))^{2}+(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\sqrt{16{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)+9{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)+25{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\sqrt{25({\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)+{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right))} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\sqrt{25} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

Therefore, the radius of curvature is

$$
R(s)=\frac{1}{‖{T}^{′}(s)‖}=\frac{1}{\,\frac{1}{2}\,}=2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120326 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9cb19795-d34e-5eab-996c-a0750fdc83c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}" :db/id 17592186118096} {:answer/id #uuid "a4164bd7-cfc7-5984-a022-a3657f7c7aba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{10}}{3}" :db/id 17592186118097} {:answer/id #uuid "d1087dd0-88f5-570e-9a06-92ad31fd2f0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{10}{3}" :db/id 17592186118098} {:answer/id #uuid "f392ca45-fded-5387-970f-6c0e65df7b09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{10}" :db/id 17592186118099} {:answer/id #uuid "418dcfbf-c00e-53c1-9492-73920469e660" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{10}" :db/id 17592186118100}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186118099} :answer-field/id #uuid "a7bbcb5c-6f44-588f-a8d6-899a42547484" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186118095}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4aa7d1da-7858-5140-849b-d462fe65d915" :question/math-academy-id "q-34355" :question/problem "Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by its arc length $s$, where

$$
r(s)=⟨\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}},\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right),\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right)⟩,\,0\le s<2\sqrt{10}\,\pi .
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $T(s)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the arc length $s.$ Since we are given the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖=‖{r}^{″}(s)‖
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(s)$ and ${r}^{″}(s)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}},\,-3\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right),\,3\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨1,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right),\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right)⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(s) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(1),\,-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}),\,3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}})⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨0,\,-3\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right),\,-3\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right)⟩ \\  & =\frac{3}{10}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(s) & =‖{r}^{″}(s)‖ \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right))}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}\sqrt{0+{\cos }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right)+{\sin }^{2}⁡\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{10}}\right)} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120331 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a5f1f0b-4308-5c1d-8f16-4ed19660a555" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6e^{-2t}+5e^{-5t}" :db/id 17592186498861}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186498861} :answer-field/id #uuid "a369d386-1789-55a9-90f7-852ad4fcce9a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186118125}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a7545e66-503e-5c9b-bd20-0b973a3cc598" :question/math-academy-id "q-343826" :question/problem "The charge $q(t)$ on the capacitor, in coulombs, in a series RCL circuit at time $t$ seconds is

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above, rounded to two decimal places.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $50\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $105\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $\frac{1}{180}\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $15\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=105\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=105I=105\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{(1/180)}=180q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=15\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=15\,\frac{dI}{dt}=15\,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dq}{dt}\right)=15\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
50\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=105\,\frac{dq}{dt}+180q+15\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+12q=\frac{10}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+12{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-3t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+7(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\, &  \\ +12(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{10}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ (-21\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(3\alpha +21\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =\frac{10}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-21\alpha +3\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ 3\alpha +21\beta &=\frac{10}{3}\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{1}{45},$ $\beta =\frac{7}{45}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{45}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{45}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{45}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{45}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Differentiating this expression for $q(t),$ we obtain the following expression for $I$ in amperes:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}(A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{45}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{45}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =-4A{e}^{-4t}-3B{e}^{-3t}-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{15}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=-4A{e}^{-4t}-3B{e}^{-3t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function $$
\displaystyle {I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{15}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)
$$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{15}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{1}{15}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{7}{15}\right)}^{2}}≈0.47,
$$

rounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186120347 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04645806-e767-51f6-b56b-a967a3dc35eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{25}" :db/id 17592186317584} {:answer/id #uuid "16fca06f-ad2b-5ab8-8589-6844750db1b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{9}" :db/id 17592186317638} {:answer/id #uuid "815819ce-d705-5379-ba5c-0d922afcf192" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}" :db/id 17592186318002} {:answer/id #uuid "8bad3fd1-ca56-5eea-b1ef-c4edb5db52bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{27}" :db/id 17592186318034} {:answer/id #uuid "8f73c15c-c406-513b-871a-da9696850ca1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}" :db/id 17592186318054}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186317584} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6368194-6360-5320-9e2f-ba4aa8d2e3e8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186318908}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "08113b99-b301-5e33-b007-837ba481f7b5" :question/math-academy-id "q-34549" :question/problem "Find the curvature of the curve $y=2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)$ at $x=2.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(x)$ of a plane curve $y=y(x)$ is given by

$$
κ(x)=\frac{|{y}^{″}(x)|}{(1+[{y}^{′}(x)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${y}^{′}(x)$ and ${y}^{″}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{2}{x-1},\, & {y}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{2}{(x-1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(x) & =\frac{|-\frac{2}{(x-1)^{2}}|}{{[1+{\left(\frac{2}{x-1}\right)}^{2}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(x-1)^{2}{[1+\frac{4}{(x-1)^{2}}]}^{3/2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $x=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(2) & =\frac{2}{(2-1)^{2}{[1+\frac{4}{(2-1)^{2}}]}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{5}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120354 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1d5732a0-d981-581b-bed3-e658d886cdb8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(-1,0)$ and the radius is $1$" :db/id 17592186317661} {:answer/id #uuid "3aad45a8-b349-54d3-9a1d-d7e6a55c1789" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(-1,0)$ and the radius is $\pi $" :db/id 17592186317754} {:answer/id #uuid "591f3088-c0f6-5f09-8428-ea4ebf479939" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(-1,-\pi )$ and the radius is $\pi $" :db/id 17592186317867} {:answer/id #uuid "8dadc1f8-5608-58e2-86fe-62d6e0a688ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(-1,-2\pi )$ and the radius is $\pi $" :db/id 17592186318044} {:answer/id #uuid "efcd825d-266c-5ffd-a9e5-69b4061e3d7d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(-1,-2\pi )$ and the radius is $1$" :db/id 17592186318366}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186317754} :answer-field/id #uuid "0d7a6c3a-6be8-5e35-9a64-ce8b55e5a19a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186318452}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2b843aaf-f0c5-5942-abb0-c6ab73ca4229" :question/math-academy-id "q-34624" :question/problem "Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(-1,-\pi )$ where $t=\pi $, given that $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖=\pi ,$ and the unit tangent vector $T(t)$ to the curve is

$$
T(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(\pi )=⟨-1,-\pi ⟩$,  since the point $P(-1,-\pi )$ is at the tip of $r(\pi ).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(\pi )$ and $‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨0,1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖}{‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖}=\frac{\pi }{1}=\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=\pi $ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\pi ) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\pi )}{‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖}=⟨0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi )+R(\pi )N(\pi ) & =⟨-1,-\pi ⟩+\pi ⟨0,1⟩=⟨-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120356 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "808c3d96-e051-54b7-abc8-f503d0f4399f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "T(s)=\frac{1}{2}\,i-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,j-\frac{1}{2}\,k" :db/id 17592186485095} {:answer/id #uuid "8516513a-8c46-5d5b-9c96-4f7574d94c8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "T(s)=\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k" :db/id 17592186485105} {:answer/id #uuid "c575acd8-bd34-5084-ac96-b6d573032127" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "T(s)=\frac{s}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}s}{2}\,j-\frac{s}{2}\,k" :db/id 17592186485240} {:answer/id #uuid "cbc40c26-154e-540c-b167-bab2ca6ddfbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "T(s)=\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j-\frac{1}{2}\,k" :db/id 17592186485252} {:answer/id #uuid "e226f754-b94d-52bf-a072-a6d3d6155d75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "T(s)=\,i+\sqrt{3}\,j-\,k" :db/id 17592186485295}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186485252} :answer-field/id #uuid "b10f0145-3d4d-5529-9dac-9ea4a90d8cc8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186118250}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "dcc2eb2b-f195-52bb-b223-b20a6a536e9f" :question/math-academy-id "q-34666" :question/problem "Given the curve  $r(t)=(t+2)\,i+(\sqrt{2}t-2)\,j-t\,k,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=2t$, find the corresponding unit tangent $T(s),$ parametrized by $s.$" :question/worked-solution "First, since $s=2t$, we have that $t=\frac{s}{2}.$

Therefore, the vector function $R(s)$ that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r\left(\frac{s}{2}\right) \\  & =(\frac{s}{2}+2)i+(\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{s}{2}-2)j-\frac{s}{2}\,k \\  & =\left(\frac{s+4}{2}\right)i+\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}s-4}{2}\right)j-\frac{s}{2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, since the curve is parametrized by its arc length $s$, the unit tangent can be found as

$$
T(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s).
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}\left(\frac{s+4}{2}\right)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}s-4}{2}\right)j-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j-\frac{1}{2}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120378 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e0f45a25-d89b-59f0-b682-db08e3a291b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2t" :db/id 17592186118383} {:answer/id #uuid "22675a90-fa26-5949-99d4-00a707c43f1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2t" :db/id 17592186118384} {:answer/id #uuid "60a61f4d-5225-5ced-b103-7eed0fc7995e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2t^{3}" :db/id 17592186118385} {:answer/id #uuid "731cfafb-70d2-5614-931b-2a4a624d35c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2t^{4}" :db/id 17592186118386} {:answer/id #uuid "77255aa5-7297-55a9-a839-1a127b5cc520" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2t^{2}" :db/id 17592186118387}] :answer-field/id #uuid "2c07beb7-9735-587b-a811-fcc882587c58" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186118382}] :question/id #uuid "0ddd6b57-2b12-5cd0-94b6-d136a7530311" :question/math-academy-id "q-35199" :question/problem "The signed curvature of the plane curve $r(t) = ⟨\frac{1}{t}, t⟩$ is given by

What is the missing part of the expression?"} {:db/id 17592186120381 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17384576-28e7-52ca-be84-31346c0aaf88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186319459} {:answer/id #uuid "1bfcc0b5-84e0-5cad-a8ce-afa104f12d09" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e" :db/id 17592186319473} {:answer/id #uuid "5a0ae87f-252a-521a-9e75-ecf415890513" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186319657} {:answer/id #uuid "89f86e8b-6020-5cff-b701-c78c7706ee0a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186319803} {:answer/id #uuid "9de1f880-12ef-5e2a-9bf6-9e617eaeec22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186319864}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186319473} :answer-field/id #uuid "e84c516c-97ad-5af5-bb55-47c5df3bdfaf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186320643}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7abe7733-3947-526c-99df-24f7379a5dbd" :question/math-academy-id "q-35234" :question/problem "Find the radius of the osculating circle at the point where $t=\pi $ for the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t},\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}⟩.$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given only the curve $r(t)$, we will use the cross product formula to find the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t})⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,\,-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{0},\,-{e}^{-1}\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+0}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{″}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\cos }^{2}⁡t,\,-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\sin }^{2}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨-{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{\cos }^{2}⁡\pi ,\,-{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }{\sin }^{2}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨0+1,{e}^{-1}+0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\frac{1}{e}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩\times ⟨1,\,\frac{1}{e},\,0⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1/e & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1/e\end{vmatrix}\,k \\  & =-\frac{1}{e}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =\frac{1}{e}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖}=\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{e}\right)}=e.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120494 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b00855ab-cf4f-598c-98e3-70f570e975f1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186119079} {:answer/id #uuid "de4ddacb-de2e-506b-9cd6-ca31cbd7387e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186119080} {:answer/id #uuid "4ec4d528-3865-566e-b0f2-7928ad804460" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186119081} {:answer/id #uuid "71eb4d9d-bf87-5ee1-bab6-0262a42b7b26" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186119082} {:answer/id #uuid "73cab0bc-9afb-5a1a-827a-444f5929111e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186119083}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186119080} :answer-field/id #uuid "058516c5-41da-5120-8490-39e6081e2067" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186119078}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ff2e0fe9-5f3d-51ba-a9a0-292022683d43" :question/math-academy-id "q-64584" :question/problem "Consider the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by arc length $s.$ Find the curvature at the point where $s=\frac{3\pi }{2}$ if the unit tangent vector of the curve is given by

$$
T(s)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{s}{3},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{s}{3},\,0⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given that the curve $r(s)$ and its unit tangent vector $T(s)$ are both parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖
$$

Now, we differentiate $T(s)$ with respect to $s$ and evaluate it at $s=\frac{3\pi }{2}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{s}{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{s}{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{s}{3},\,-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{s}{3},\,0⟩ \\ {T}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) & =⟨-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}),\,-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{3\pi }{2}),\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right),\,-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right),\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{3},\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the curvature:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right) & =‖{T}^{′}\left(\frac{3\pi }{2}\right)‖=\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120495 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d0c9c1f0-df55-556e-833a-7fb64732dde4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186119085} {:answer/id #uuid "f30dc2a4-65fc-5750-b501-c7c5b426ccda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186119086} {:answer/id #uuid "092a0aaf-082d-545c-9806-110ce43d35b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186119087} {:answer/id #uuid "3ef17328-d207-5798-8681-f24753e09c81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186119088} {:answer/id #uuid "62750844-6757-5328-89ca-54678ebfa45e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186119089}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186119087} :answer-field/id #uuid "4ccd57a8-0a01-50d0-ac4b-6f5f8f6b6e44" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186119084}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4163ce17-8c2e-5e7a-b5d2-d7191ad32de0" :question/math-academy-id "q-64700" :question/problem "Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by its arc length $s$, where

$$
r(s)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡s,\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s,\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s⟩,\,0\le s<2\pi .
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $T(s)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the arc length $s.$ Since we are given the curve $r(s)$ parametrized by the arc length $s$, we will use the following formula for the curvature:

$$
κ(s)=‖{T}^{′}(s)‖=‖{r}^{″}(s)‖
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(s)$ and ${r}^{″}(s)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡s),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡s,\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡s,\,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡s⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(s) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡s),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡s),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡s)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡s,\,-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s,\,-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the curvature is  

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(s) & =‖{r}^{″}(s)‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡s)}^{2}+{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s)}^{2}+{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡s)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{\cos }^{2}⁡s+\frac{1}{2}{\sin }^{2}⁡s+\frac{1}{2}{\sin }^{2}⁡s} \\  & =\sqrt{{\cos }^{2}⁡s+{\sin }^{2}⁡s} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120497 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "82fe3e9a-c737-563c-8a64-414cab503d5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩=⟨2t,\,2t,\,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4{t}^{2}+4} \\  & =\sqrt{4(2{t}^{2}+1)} \\  & =2\sqrt{2{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)⟩=⟨2,\,2,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2t,2t,2⟩\times ⟨2,2,0⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2t & 2t & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2t & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}2t & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}2t & 2t \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =-4i+4j+(4t-4t)k \\  & =-4\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{32} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{{[2\sqrt{2{t}^{2}+1}]}^{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2(2{t}^{2}+1)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120498 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0159ae1f-8d8b-505c-91bb-33e3cb94ce88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,-1)$ and the radius is $\frac{1}{2}$" :db/id 17592186119104} {:answer/id #uuid "18864349-f844-598b-8bd8-2499081b262c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(1,0)$ and the radius is $\sqrt{2}$" :db/id 17592186444662} {:answer/id #uuid "26713c2f-51c0-5113-aace-e97dae2a9d84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(1,1)$ and the radius is $2$" :db/id 17592186444664} {:answer/id #uuid "c21a2526-c8f2-5cf5-8dba-ef6702413f42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,2)$ and the radius is $1$" :db/id 17592186444681} {:answer/id #uuid "d94db2da-7382-5233-8016-048bd89a7acd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The center is $(0,1)$ and the radius is $1$" :db/id 17592186444684}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444681} :answer-field/id #uuid "02dc88d7-02c9-503f-943d-b4979f80536a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186119102}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "69b5cf6a-1be8-58cf-9f82-85a803f2002d" :question/math-academy-id "q-64839" :question/problem "Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,1)$ where $t=0$, given that $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖=1,$ and the unit tangent vector to the curve is

$$
T(t)=⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}},\,\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}⟩\,.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(0)=⟨0,1⟩,$ since the point $P(0,1)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$, ${T}^{′}(0)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(0)‖$: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}\right),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{t}{\sqrt{({t}^{2}+1)^{3}}},\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{({t}^{2}+1)^{3}}}⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =⟨-\frac{0}{\sqrt{({0}^{2}+1)^{3}}},\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{({0}^{2}+1)^{3}}}⟩=⟨0,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{1}{1}=1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=0$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=⟨0,1⟩\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0,1⟩+1⟨0,1⟩=⟨0,2⟩\,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120511 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8cdd6dd8-590b-5f34-9327-62411a358180" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y = x + \frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186119181} {:answer/id #uuid "929921e9-a3cc-57e2-b83a-5409ded96489" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y = x - $$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{t}\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}\,,\,\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨0\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨0\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$

$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{e}^{0}\,,\,\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}}⟩=⟨1\,,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(1,1).$"} {:db/id 17592186120527 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "75e5fa3c-091c-520e-8479-d218155399c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14" :db/id 17592186343254} {:answer/id #uuid "8b51d751-2961-50bb-98bc-c99dea65a8e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186343452} {:answer/id #uuid "8baa903e-69cf-5fab-bf1d-52f2ba066f34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186343455} {:answer/id #uuid "c0402a4e-bae1-581e-b109-bffe3d5de024" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "21" :db/id 17592186343924} {:answer/id #uuid "deebeadd-1734-5b4a-bc84-8d64bed65493" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186344193}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343455} :answer-field/id #uuid "e0be3d9a-49eb-5fc8-91bf-4c96b81633a1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344886}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d67d847a-8cc9-599e-9782-16c3ef20921d" :question/math-academy-id "q-77065" :question/problem "![](images/b6/b614e2c3e6abf0d7ddb8399aa7ea78b7a0e618a965ee7b5481edf08310a45031.png)

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} &={b}_{1}-2{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} &={b}_{1}+{b}_{2}.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. Multiplying the second equation by $2$ and adding the equations, we get 

$$
{c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}=3{b}_{1}\,⟹\,{b}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{c}_{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{1}=(\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{c}_{2})-2{b}_{2}\,⟹\,{b}_{2}=-\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}{c}_{2}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2{b}_{1}-3{b}_{2} \\  & =2(\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{c}_{2})-3(-\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}{c}_{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{4}{3}{c}_{2}+{c}_{1}-{c}_{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}{c}_{1}+\frac{1}{3}{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}.$"} {:db/id 17592186120553 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3625fe28-3df8-54e5-bd47-d40fc48b3509" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0214" :db/id 17592186355155} {:answer/id #uuid "4e9610de-c23c-543d-89e5-b6447e707976" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0342" :db/id 17592186355365} {:answer/id #uuid "7dcd36dd-d107-52c1-b130-8a48abc341a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0283" :db/id 17592186355776} {:answer/id #uuid "e6c58b2a-e877-50ec-9cb9-ad5e383a1924" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0386" :db/id 17592186356682} {:answer/id #uuid "edb40588-8324-5df8-977d-4bcc71504351" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.0546" :db/id 17592186356735}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186355776} :answer-field/id #uuid "f4c752ee-6e7b-56cb-905a-7817149765da" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186357344}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "5a6c56ff-5e80-58cf-bba5-4120eb643ddb" :question/math-academy-id "q-94319" :question/problem "The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.
