" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Given a normal random variable $X∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),$ we have

$$
P(a<X<b)=P(\frac{a-\mu }{\sigma }<Z<\frac{b-\mu }{\sigma })
$$

where $Z∼N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu =2$ and $\sigma =\sqrt{25}=5.$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.65<X<-0.25) & =P(\frac{-0.65-2}{5}<Z<\frac{-0.25-2}{5}) \\  & =P(-0.53<Z<-0.45)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](images/3d/3d73cc4661eb9f68f636803918b3e55942e6538e4e70d13277d125386dad257e.png)

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.53<Z<-0.45) & =P(Z<-0.45)-P(Z\le -0.53) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.45)-P(Z\le -0.53) \\  & =Φ(-0.45)-Φ(-0.53)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.53) & =0.2981 \\ Φ(-0.45) & =0.3264\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.53<Z<-0.45) & =Φ(-0.45)-Φ(-0.53) \\  & =0.3264-0.2981 \\  & =0.0283.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
P(-0.65<X<-0.25)=0.0283.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120995 :tutorial/content "Since the integration of vector functions is done component-by-component, the properties of integrals of vector functions are immediately inherited from those of the integrals of real-valued functions. 

Suppose that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are vector-valued functions that are continuous on a closed interval $[a,b],$ and $\alpha$ is a scalar. 
Then, the *vector addition and scalar multiplication rules* are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}(f(t)+g(t))\text{d}t={\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\,+\,{\int }_{a}^{b}g(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{vector addition rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}\alpha \,f(t)\,\text{d}t=\alpha \,{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{scalar constant multiple rule}\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, if $\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle t, \: \cos t\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf g(t) = \left\langle -t^2, \: \sin t \right\rangle,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int [f(t)+2g(t)]\text{d}t & =\int f(t)\,\text{d}t+2\int g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t+2\int ⟨-{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩+⟨2\int -{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\,2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩+⟨-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{3},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{2}-4{t}^{3}}{6},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $C_1, \, C_2, \, C_3, \, C_4$ are arbitrary real constants and ${\mathbf C} = \langle C_1+C_3, C_2+C_4 \rangle$ is a constant vector." :tutorial/id #uuid "b3d07bd2-8d66-5645-a140-c638f5e9f002" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2342 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186120996 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve $C$ that's defined parametrically by 
$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle t, \: t^3 +1 \right\rangle, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

The point $P$ corresponding to $t=1$ on the curve has coordinates $(1,2).$ We know that a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is given by $\mathbf f'(1),$ as shown below.

![](images/2b/2b4f4dad09042b761fe950c694c8cf645501106cd1d1d9c0f7a78967b224951c.png)

We compute $\mathbf f'(t)$ as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\mathbf{f}}^{\prime } ( t ) & \displaystyle  = \langle  {\displaystyle \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} t}} ( t ) , \hspace{0.222em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} t}} ( {t}^{3} ) \rangle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \langle  1 , 3 {t}^{2} \rangle  ,\end{array}
$$

Substituting $t=1$ into the above gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P:$

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\mathbf{f}}^{\prime } ( 1 ) & \displaystyle  = \langle  1 , \hspace{0.222em} 3 ( 1 {)}^{2} \rangle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \langle  1 , 3 \rangle  ,\end{array}
$$

As we'll see, it's more helpful to work with unit vectors. Notice that $\mathbf f'(1)$ is not a unit vector because

$$
\begin{array}{cc}\Vert  {\mathbf{f}}^{\prime } ( 1 ) \Vert  &  = \sqrt{{1}^{2} + {3}^{2}} \\  &  = \sqrt{10} .\end{array}
$$

However, we can create a unit vector, which we'll call $\mathbf{T} ( 1 ) ,$ by dividing $\mathbf f'(1)$ by its magnitude:

$$
\begin{array}{cc}\mathbf{T} ( 1 ) &  = \frac{{\mathbf{f}}^{\prime } ( 1 )}{\Vert  {\mathbf{f}}^{\prime } ( 1 ) \Vert } \\  &  = \frac{\langle  1 , 3 \rangle }{\sqrt{10}} \\  &  = \langle  \frac{\sqrt{10}}{10} , \frac{3 \sqrt{10}}{10} \rangle  .\end{array}
$$

In general, for a vector valued function $\mathbf f(t),$ the **unit tangent vector** $\mathbf T(t)$ to the curve traced by $\mathbf f$ can be computed using the following formula:
$$
\mathbf{T} ( t ) = \frac{{\mathbf{f}}^{\prime } ( t )}{\Vert  {\mathbf{f}}^{\prime } ( t ) \Vert }
$$

**Note:** When we take a vector $\mathbf v$ and create a unit vector that's parallel to it, we say that we have **normalized** the vector $\mathbf v.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "de55871f-089d-5982-98d6-3ea78f7e3b5d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2364 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186121002 :tutorial/content "The **curvature** of a curve measures how much the curve "bends" at a given point. It can also be thought of as a measure of how much the curve deviates from being a straight line. Curvature is denoted by the Greek letter $\kappa$ (pronounced "kappa"). 

If $\kappa=0$ at some point on a curve, then that curve looks like a straight line in some neighborhood of the point.

If the curve $\mathbf{r}(s)$ is parametrized by the arc length $s,$ then the curvature $\kappa$ is the magnitude of the change of direction of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T$ per unit of arc length. That is,

$$
\kappa(s) = \left\| \dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf T}{\textrm{d}s}  \right\|= \| \mathbf T'(s) \|.
$$

Note that $|| \mathbf v ||$ denotes the magnitude of the vector $\mathbf v.$

For example, suppose we are given the curve 

$$
\mathbf r(s)= \left\langle \sin\left(\dfrac s2\right), \: \dfrac{\sqrt{3}s}{2}, \: -\cos\left(\dfrac s2\right)\right\rangle
$$

 
which is parametrized by arc length $s.$ Let's find the curvature of  $\mathbf r(s)$  at the point where $s={\pi}.$

First, we find the unit tangent vector:

$$
\mathbf T(s) =\dfrac 12 \left\langle \cos\left( \dfrac s2\right), \: \sqrt{3}, \: \sin \left(\dfrac s2\right)\right\rangle
$$

 

Next, we differentiate $\mathbf{T}(s)$ and evaluate its absolute value at $s=\pi\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(s) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\sqrt{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right),\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{4}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right),\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the curvature by taking the magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖=\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Note:** To calculate $\kappa,$ the function $\mathbf{r}(s)$ should be at least twice differentiable with respect to $s.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "d74577d5-5fe6-5544-bd86-b20fee42defa" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2402 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186121009 :tutorial/content "The center of the osculating circle for a curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at a point where $t=t_0$ is located at the tip of the vector 

$$
\mathbf r(t_0)+R(t_0) \mathbf N(t_0)
$$

where $\mathbf N(t)$ denotes the principal normal vector to the curve.

For example, the curve $C$ parameterized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \bigg\langle t+1, 2- \dfrac{t^2}{2} \bigg\rangle
$$

has the normal vector

$$
\mathbf{N}(t) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+t^2}} \langle -t, \: -1 \rangle ,
$$

and the radius of curvature at the point $P(1,2)$ where $t=0$ is $R(0)=1.$

So, the center of the osculating circle is at the tip of the vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0+1,\,2-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}⟩+1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}}}⟨0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2⟩+⟨0,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the center of the osculating circle at the point where $t=0$ is located at $\left(1, 1 \right),$ as shown below.

![](images/d8/d8cd8407e6398b3409e7f575e152976669393914e2e5d7335121287276af6e41.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "5a31a99b-6c09-5d1c-ad68-7b5f38c17efb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2489 :tutorial/title "The Center of the Osculating Circle"} {:db/id 17592186121010 :tutorial/content "If a curve has a curvature of zero at some point, the radius of curvature at that point is defined to be infinite.

It follows from the definition that a straight line has zero curvature at all of its points. Conversely, if a curve has zero curvature at any point, it must be contained on a straight line.

Suppose now that we want to find the radius of curvature for the curve 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle t^2, \: 1 - t^2, \: 1+ t^2 \right\rangle
$$

at an arbitrary point where $t> 0.$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and its magnitude $\| \mathbf r'(t) \|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,-2t,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the last step, we used the fact that $\sqrt{t^2}=t$ since $t>0.$

Next, we find the unit tangent and its derivative for $t>0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}t}\cdot ⟨2t,\,-2t,\,2t⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨1,-1,1⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(t) & =⟨0,0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}t}{0}=\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, despite its "parabolic" appearance, the given curve is contained on a straight line!

**Note:** Often, the unit tangent vector of a curve $\mathbf T(t)$ may look a bit complicated. In such cases, the following formula involving a cross product may be useful. It says that the radius of curvature of a twice-differentiable curve $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by 

$$
R(t)=  \dfrac{1}{\kappa(t)} =\frac{{{{\left\| {\mathbf r'\left( t \right)} \right\|}^3}}}{{\left\| {\mathbf r'\left( t \right) \times \mathbf r''\left( t \right)} \right\|}}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "590485ba-30a6-549b-a4cf-d6641c92a033" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2490 :tutorial/title "Infinite Radius of Curvature"} {:db/id 17592186121047 :tutorial/content "To demonstrate using Cramer's rule on a $3 \times 3$ system, consider the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+z &=9 \\ 2y+3z &=7 \\ -8x+y+6z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+1z &=9 \\ 0x+2y+3z &=7 \\ -8x+1y+6z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start finding the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ -8 & 1 & 6\end{vmatrix} & =4\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{vmatrix}+1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4(12-3)-2(0+24)+(0+16) \\  & =36-48+16 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $D_x,$ $D_y,$ and $D_z.$

- To find $D_x,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *first* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x}=\begin{vmatrix}9 & 2 & 1 \\ 7 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 6\end{vmatrix} & =9\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{vmatrix}+1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}7 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =9(12-3)-2(42-0)+(7-0) \\  & =81-84+7 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

- To find $D_y,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *second* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{y}=\begin{vmatrix}4 & 9 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3 \\ -8 & 0 & 6\end{vmatrix} & =4\cdot \begin{vmatrix}7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{vmatrix}-9\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{vmatrix}+1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -8 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4(42)-9(0+24)+(0+56) \\  & =168-216+56 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

- To find $D_z,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *third* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{z}=\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 7 \\ -8 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & =4\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 7 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -8 & 0\end{vmatrix}+9\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4(-7)-2(0+56)+9(0+16) \\  & =-28-112+144 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to the system is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩ & =⟨\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},\frac{{D}_{y}}{D},\frac{{D}_{z}}{D}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4}{4},\frac{8}{4},\frac{4}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9d916943-4be4-554c-a4f5-51aef55e8254" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3241 :tutorial/title "A Demonstration of Cramer's Rule on a 3x3 Linear System"} {:db/id 17592186121078 :tutorial/content "To compute a probability involving a normally distributed variable $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),$ it is convenient to transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}
$$

So, we have

$$
P(X <  x) = P \left( Z <  \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right)
$$

where $Z \sim N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable.

For example, suppose we have a random variable $X \sim N(1,2^2)$ and we want to compute $P(X \leq 1.4)$ using the following $z$-table:

<tr> <th data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8">$\, 0.2 \,$</th><td data-cell-align="center">$\, 0.5793 \,$</td><td data-cell-align="center">$\, 0.5832 \,$</td><td data-cell-align="center">$\, 0.5871 \,$</td></tr>

The $z$-table above shows the cumulative probabilities for a normal random variable $Z \sim N(0,1).$ In order to use the table to compute $P(X \leq 1.4),$ we must first transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 1.4) & =P(Z\le \frac{1.4-1}{2}) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.2)\end{aligned}
$$

According to the table, we have

$$
P(Z \leq 0.2) = 0.5793 .
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X \leq 1.4) = 0.5793.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "425f33ad-bd05-5384-94cf-ea650aca5146" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4919 :tutorial/title "Transforming a Normal Random Variable into a Standard Normal Random Variable"} {:db/id 17592186121083 :tutorial/content "If a surface is parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

where $(u,v) \in D\subseteq \mathbb R^2,$ then the **fundamental vector product** of the surface is defined as

$$
\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v = 
\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂u} \\ \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.
$$

In particular, if the fundamental vector product of a surface is nonzero at a point $(x_0, y_0),$ then it defines a normal vector to the surface at this point.

Let's find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function 

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle \sqrt{2}\cos{u}, \: \sqrt{2}\sin{u}, \: v \big\rangle.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u,\hspace{0.222em}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u,\hspace{0.222em}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f1b86df9-267c-5991-bc04-39d7b75cdf3a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5332 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186121099 :tutorial/content "To derive a formula for a conical frustum's volume, we first extend the frustum to form a complete cone.

![](images/dc/dccb56262085d93198e45754f7e4ae7e1c106ec21dfd41733aefe86151c37d41.png)

Our frustum is the object that remains when we remove the smaller cone (on top) from the larger cone.

To calculate the volume of the frustum, we subtract the volume of the smaller cone from the volume of the larger cone. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{L} &= V_{big} - V_{small} \\
&= \frac{1}{3}πR^{2}(h + h^{′}) - \frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h^{′} \\
&= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + R^{2}h^{′} - r^{2}h^{′}) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + h^{′}(R^{2} - r^{2}))
\end{aligned}
$$

Now consider the right triangle made by the complete cone, shown below.

![](images/2a/2a1f0ca0e176fee61a5978971aaae76d8cac39de418a3616dece128b83bb7673.png)

Notice that $\triangle OPT$ and $\triangle OQS$ are similar by the AA criterion. So, we have

$$
\dfrac{h'}{r} = \dfrac{h+h'}{R}
$$

which can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}
h^{′}R &= (h + h^{′})r \\
h^{′}R &= hr + h^{′}r \\
h^{′}R - h^{′}r &= hr \\
h^{′}(R - r) &= hr \\
h^{′} &= \frac{hr}{R - r}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of our frustum is

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{L} &= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + h^{′}(R^{2} - r^{2})) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + \frac{hr}{R - r}(R^{2} - r^{2})) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + \frac{hr}{R - r}(R - r)(R + r)) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + hr(R + r)) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}πh(R^{2} + rR + r^{2}) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}πh(R^{2} + r^{2} + Rr)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "465e78d4-42d3-5dea-b275-0e17a5cda255" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5632 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Volume Formula"} {:db/id 17592186121134 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to calculate the arc length of the curve $C$ given by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(t)= \left\langle \dfrac{t^3}{3}, \: \dfrac{t^2}{2}\right\rangle, \qquad    t \in [0,1].
$$

 

The length of this curve is given by

$$
L= \int_{0}^{1} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t.
$$

To compute $\| \mathbf r'(t) \|,$ we take the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ and compute its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}\right),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}t⟩, \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{({t}^{2})^{2}+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of the curve $C$ is given by the integral

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{2}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}|t|\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this integral using substitution. Let $u = t^2+1,$ then $\textrm d u = 2 t\,\textrm d t.$ Therefore, our integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2\sqrt{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "615541cf-962a-50be-88eb-1d0b64de5509" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7824 :tutorial/title "A Concrete Example"} {:db/id 17592186121138 :tutorial/content "Recall that if the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ is parametrized by a general parameter $t,$ then the curvature of $\mathbf{r}$ is given by

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|},
$$

where $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}$ is the unit tangent vector to the curve. 

Here, $\mathbf r'(t)$ is a vector function and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|$ is a scalar function.
So, we differentiate $\mathbf T(t)$ by using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(T) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}\left(\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\right) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{′}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}\left(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\right)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}({r}^{′}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}\left(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\right)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{″}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the cross product of a vector with itself equals $\mathbf{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\times {T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\times (\frac{∂}{∂t}\left(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\right)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{″}(t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,({r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the magnitude of both sides and use the fact that $\mathbf T$ is a unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖T(t)\times {T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ ‖T(t)‖\cdot ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ 1\cdot ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|} = \dfrac{\left\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \right\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f59936dc-ef8e-53d7-be8e-244d577dd658" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7885 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Cross Product Formula"} {:db/id 17592186121148 :tutorial/content "The **principal normal vector** to a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is a unit vector that 

- is perpendicular to the unit tangent vector, and

- points in the direction that the curve is bending.

In general, if the unit tangent vector is given by $\mathbf T(t),$ then the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|},
$$

where it is assumed that $\|\mathbf T'(t)\|\neq 0.$

To demonstrate, suppose that the curve $C$ is parametrized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle 2\cos t, \: 2\sin t \right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0, \pi].
$$

We will compute the principal normal vector at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

First, using the formula for the unit tangent, $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf f'(t)}{||\mathbf f'(t)||},$ we find that the general unit tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf T(t)= \left\langle {-\sin t}, \cos t\right\rangle.
$$

Now, when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ we have the point $P(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).$ The unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and the principal normal vector $\mathbf{N}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ at this point are shown below:

![](images/d0/d0a30a44bb825a8a12ca54153b6223b9bf0c2b754245b21650a5664db5e1647e.png)

To calculate the principal normal vector, we start by calculating the derivative of the unit tangent function. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general principal normal vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{||{T}^{′}(t)||} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{{\cos }^{2}⁡t+{\sin }^{2}⁡t}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $\mathbf N\left(\dfrac\pi 4\right),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}N\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, it's easy to check that $\mathbf T'(t)$ and $\mathbf N'(t)$ are perpendicular for all $t$ by computing the dot product and showing that we get zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\cdot N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "03709847-4a63-5975-b20a-1d6693ceadb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9376 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:answer/id #uuid "ab35114f-7f90-51a7-96c4-0853516af332" :answer/type "38d9418f-2ba6-5c46-984d-5eabfe8939dd" :question/math-academy-id "e-16544" :question/problem "Solve the recurrence relation
$$
\displaystyle a_n = a_{n-1} + 6\cdot 7^n, \qquad a_1=8, \quad n \geq 2.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The solution of a linear recurrence relation

$$
a_n = a_{n-1} + g(n)
$$

with linear coefficient $1$ is given by

$$
a_n = a_1 + \sum_{k=2}^n g(k)
$$

Therefore, the solution of the recurrence relation is

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {a}_{n} & \displaystyle  = {a}_{1} + \sum _{k = 2}^{n} g ( k ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 8 + \sum _{k = 2}^{n} ( 6 \cdot  {7}^{k} ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 8 + 6 \sum _{k = 2}^{n} {7}^{k} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 8 + 6 [ ( \sum _{k = 1}^{n} {7}^{k} ) - {7}^{1} ] \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 8 + 6 ( {\displaystyle \frac{7 ( {7}^{n} - 1 )}{7 - 1}} - 7 ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 8 + 7 ( {7}^{n} - 1 ) - 42 \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \bbox[3pt,gainsboro]{ {\color{blue}7 \cdot  {7}^{n} - 41}} .\end{array}}
$$

Note that we made use of the following result:

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^n r^k = \dfrac{r(r^n-1)}{r-1}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124243 :question/id #uuid "75c0deaf-38a7-5a81-afac-cae2978d52b4" :question/math-academy-id "e-3070" :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,1)$ lies on $C,$ and that $$
\displaystyle f_x =  \dfrac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{4} \sin{\left(2 x + \dfrac{\pi y}{4} \right)},
$$ find a tangent vector to $C$ at $P.$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x(0,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0)+\frac{\pi (1)}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-1 & =\frac{\pi }{4}x \\ z & =\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(0,1,1)$ has the equation $y=1.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y &=1 \\ z &=\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

To find a tangent vector, we can find a normal vector to each plane and compute their cross product.

- For the plane $y = 1,$ we write $0x + 1y + 0z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle.$

- For the plane $z = \dfrac{\pi}{4} x +1,$ we write $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} x + 0y + 1z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2 = \left\langle -\dfrac{\pi}4,0,1 \right\rangle.$

Computing the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨-\frac{\pi }{4},0,1⟩ \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\pi /4 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we've found a tangent vector, and this could be our final answer. However, just to make our answer a little nicer, we can multiply the vector by $4$ to yield a simpler, parallel vector:

$$\begin{aligned}4\cdot (\mathbf{i}+\frac{\pi }{4}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}) &=4\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\pi \hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}\end{aligned}$$"} {:db/id 17592186124251 :question/id #uuid "67e9bcb5-4bf2-56b8-8d82-95355841eaaa" :question/math-academy-id "e-3150" :question/problem "Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y) g(x,y)$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =xy,\hspace{1em} &  & \mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=y\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j}, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\sqrt{xy},\hspace{1em} &  & \mathrm{∇}g(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }\mathbf{j}. &  & \end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by

$$
\nabla [fg] = g \, \nabla\! f  + f \, \nabla\! g.
$$

Using the product rule shown above, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)+f(x,y)\mathrm{∇}g(x,y) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j})+xy(\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2x}\text{ }\mathbf{i}+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2y}\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\sqrt{xy}(y\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j})+\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{xy}}{2}(y\text{ }\mathbf{i}+x\text{ }\mathbf{j}).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124262 :question/id #uuid "bf35c502-5a22-5953-9158-b2464d28c09f" :question/math-academy-id "e-3377" :question/problem "Find the directional derivative of the function $g(x, y) =3x^2+4xy$ at the point $A(0,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(1,4).$" :question/worked-solution "The directional derivative $g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b)$ of a function $g(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v$ is given by

$$
g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b) = \nabla g(a,b)\cdot\mathbf u
$$

where $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨1,4⟩-⟨0,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3⟩ \\ \mathbf{u} & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}⟨1,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $\nabla g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+4xy),\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+4xy)⟩ \\  & =⟨6x+4y,\,4x⟩ \\ ∇g(0,1) & =⟨6\cdot 0+4\cdot 1,\,4\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{\mathbf{u}}^{'}(0,1) & =\mathrm{∇}g(0,1)\cdot \mathbf{u} \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}},\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{10} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124264 :question/id #uuid "1eea4610-508a-5437-802e-9d009b777e82" :question/math-academy-id "e-3382" :question/problem "Consider the function $g (x, y) = \ln \left(\sqrt {xy^3}\right).$ What is the rate of change of $g$ at the point $\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $\nabla g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $$
\displaystyle \left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)\!\mathbin{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x{y}^{3}})),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{2\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}},\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}\cdot \frac{3x{y}^{2}}{2\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2x},\,\frac{3}{2y}⟩ \\ ∇g(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}) & =⟨\frac{1}{2\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)},\frac{3}{2\cdot \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)$ in the direction of $$
\displaystyle \nabla g\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)
$$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇g(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2})‖ & =‖⟨1,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124266 :question/id #uuid "3ab5ece1-03aa-5fb0-9952-b858b6ca67b4" :question/math-academy-id "e-3433" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0, 4).$" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $$
\displaystyle f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16} - 1,
$$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,4).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)j \\  & =\frac{2x}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{8}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{(4)}{8}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j \\  & =⟨0,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{x-{x}_{0}}=\frac{{v}_{y}}{{v}_{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{y}(x-{x}_{0}) & ={v}_{x}(y-{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(x-0) & =0(y-4) \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the equation of the normal line to the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1$ at the point $(0,4)$ is $x=0.$"} {:db/id 17592186124268 :question/id #uuid "db58088e-59e0-5ca4-82a2-991bb6a4e7be" :question/math-academy-id "e-3435" :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z = \ln (x^2 - xy)$ at the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right).$" :question/worked-solution "To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z) = \ln (x^2 - xy) - z,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2){:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)k \\  & =\left(\frac{2x-y}{{x}^{2}-xy}\right)\text{ }i+\left(\frac{1}{y-x}\right)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =\left(\frac{2\cdot 2-1}{{2}^{2}-2\cdot 1}\right)\text{ }i+\left(\frac{1}{1-2}\right)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{3}{2}i-\,j-k \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf v = \langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $$
\displaystyle \nabla f(2,1,\ln 2)= \left\langle  \dfrac {3} {2}, -1, -1\right  \rangle,
$$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-1} \\ \frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124273 :question/id #uuid "96b34678-8282-5691-8a4b-83a28e504727" :question/math-academy-id "e-3609" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \lim_ {x\to (\pi/4)} 2\sec \left(2x\right).
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's attempt to evaluate the limit by direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{x \to  (π/4)}2\sec (2x) &= 2\sec (2 \cdot \left(\frac{π}{4}\right)) \\
&= 2\sec \left(\frac{π}{2}\right) \\
&= (2)/(\cos \left(\frac{π}{2}\right)) \\
&= \frac{2}{0}
\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of

$$
y = 2\sec\left(2x\right)
$$

![](images/24/2456c4bd5a25316fff60b7cc4de8a5562ac8f3a6144b1d45c042c26319eb7901.png)

As $x$ approaches

$$
\dfrac\pi {4}
$$

from the left, the values of $y=2\sec(2x)$ are positive and grow without bound. Therefore

$$
\lim_ {x \to (\pi/4)^-} 2\sec(2x) = \infty
$$

Similarly, as $x$ approaches

$$
\dfrac\pi {4}
$$

from the right, the values of

$$
y=2\sec (2x)
$$

are negative and decrease without bound. Therefore

$$
\lim_ {x \to (\pi/4)^+} 2\sec (2x) = -\infty
$$

Therefore, since the two limits are not equal, we conclude that

$$
\lim_ {x \to (\pi/4)} 2\sec (2x) = \text{DNE}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124275 :question/id #uuid "0a271825-7ad1-5262-9b81-f03ecc8955d6" :question/math-academy-id "e-3612" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \lim_ {x \to \pi/3} \cot \left(3x\right).
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's attempt to evaluate the limit by direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{x \to  π/3}\cot (3x) &= \cot (3 \cdot \frac{π}{3}) \\
&= \cot (π) \\
&= (\cos (π))/(\sin (π)) \\
&= \frac{-1}{0}
\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of

$$
y = \cot\left(3x\right)
$$

![](images/57/5711d4f447378c9e60c204b7e17d0f941ec87853507ce055f671df7af18371b0.png)

As $x$ approaches

$$
\dfrac\pi 3
$$

from the left, the values of $y=\cot(3x)$ are negative and decrease without bound. Therefore

$$
\lim_ {x \to (\pi/3)^-} \cot(3x) = -\infty
$$

As $x$ approaches

$$
\dfrac\pi 3
$$

from the right, the values of $y=\cot(3x)$ are positive and increase without bound. Therefore

$$
\lim_ {x \to (\pi/3)^+} \cot(3x) = +\infty
$$

Since the left and right-sided limits are not equal, we get

$$
\lim_ {x \to \pi/3} \cot \left(3x\right) = \textrm{DNE}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124278 :question/id #uuid "f44b6ea6-694c-5f54-94ee-4c4a699bf4eb" :question/math-academy-id "e-3696" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=x^2-y^2-z$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf r (t) = \left \langle \sin t, \cos t, t  \right \rangle$ at the point $t=\dfrac \pi 4.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf r (t)$ is given by $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] .$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x = \sin t, y=\cos t,$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf r(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}t,-2\operatorname{cos}t,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}t,-\operatorname{sin}t,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}t,-2\operatorname{cos}t,-1⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}t,-\operatorname{sin}t,1⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t-2\operatorname{cos}t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}t)-1\cdot 1 \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t+2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t-1 \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))] & =4\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-1 \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124392 :question/id #uuid "0fc616fa-c901-53ff-acab-cdada6bb5ce2" :question/math-academy-id "e-80" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle \lim_{x\rightarrow \infty} \dfrac{3x^4+9x}{6x^4-x^3}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x^4.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{3{x}^{4}+9x}{6{x}^{4}-{x}^{3}} & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{3{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{9x}{{x}^{4}})}{(\frac{6{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{(3+\frac{9}{{x}^{3}})}{(6-\frac{1}{x})} \\  & =\frac{3+0}{6-0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124394 :question/id #uuid "b648ed80-e2e1-57c4-bd37-147d92315e90" :question/math-academy-id "e-81" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \lim_{x\rightarrow -\infty} \dfrac{4-5x-2x^3}{x^2+3}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x^2.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to -\infty }\frac{4-5x-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}+3} & =\lim_{x\to -\infty }\frac{(\frac{-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{5x}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{4}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to -\infty }\frac{(-2x-\frac{5}{x}+\frac{4}{{x}^{2}})}{(1+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to -\infty }\left(\frac{-2x+0+0}{1+0}\right) \\  & =\lim_{x\to -\infty }(-2x) \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124395 :question/id #uuid "c3798fe4-058f-5970-a903-65c654abb788" :question/math-academy-id "e-82" :question/problem "What is the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ with $f(x)=\dfrac{2x^3+1}{x^3-15x}?$" :question/worked-solution "The horizontal asymptote is $$
\displaystyle y=\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x).
$$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x^3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }f(x) & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{2{x}^{3}+1}{{x}^{3}-15x} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{15x}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{(2+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}{(1-\frac{15}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{2+0}{1-0} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote is $y=2.$"} {:db/id 17592186124408 :question/id #uuid "32a8e4bb-4191-55a8-883b-baa36f67b061" :question/math-academy-id "e-83" :question/problem "Find the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=\dfrac{x^5-10}{x^3-8x^2}.$" :question/worked-solution "The horizontal asymptote is $$
\displaystyle y=\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x).
$$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x^3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }f(x) & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{5}-10}{{x}^{3}-8{x}^{2}} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{x}^{5}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{10}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{8{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{({x}^{2}-\frac{10}{{x}^{3}})}{(1-\frac{8}{x})} \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }\left(\frac{{x}^{2}-0}{1-0}\right) \\  & =\lim_{x\to \infty }{x}^{2} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not come out to a finite number. Therefore, there is no horizontal asymptote."} {:db/id 17592186124760 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "30cbc511-46f2-57a7-a1e6-5b9df41e93f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+1)" :db/id 17592186362597} {:answer/id #uuid "67e259c2-66b9-50e9-b578-1c42714caf20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,\frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186362598} {:answer/id #uuid "c6bb899f-cddb-5bbd-8b15-deb369bf541e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\sqrt{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186362599} {:answer/id #uuid "e33d1235-04f0-5510-b143-ff55309b0743" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{3}{2},\frac{7}{4})" :db/id 17592186362600} {:answer/id #uuid "32a85622-d88c-5334-b282-e0da8268939c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,\sqrt{2}+1)" :db/id 17592186362601}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186362597} :answer-field/id #uuid "b819c7c7-4de5-5d16-a83f-aab407f3ff76" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362596}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "24eb3f60-8596-5c16-bdd4-fd742e474035" :question/math-academy-id "q-106084" :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y)=2{x}^{3}-y$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,2⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{3}-y$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,2⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,2⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ (2(2)^{3}-2)-(2(0)^{3}-1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨6{x}^{2},-1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨6{c}_{1}^{2},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =⟨6{c}_{1}^{2},-1⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =12{c}_{1}^{2}-1 \\ 16 & =12{c}_{1}^{2} \\ {c}_{1}^{2} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ {c}_{1} & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}<0<2,$ it's clear that $-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ corresponds to the $x$-coordinate of a point that does not lie on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ Therefore, we can ignore it. Thus, ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}$ to find ${c}_{2}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{2-1} & =\frac{x-0}{2-0} \\ y-1 & =\frac{x}{2} \\ y & =\frac{x}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},$ we obtain that $$
\displaystyle {c}_{2}=\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+1=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+1.
$$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $$
\displaystyle (\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+1).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124761 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "07f8a323-c0be-535b-948e-c78114672e3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{3})$ and $(1,1,1)$" :db/id 17592186564953} {:answer/id #uuid "50cf239c-b6f5-566d-958b-b55860061ad8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,0,0)$ and $(\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3})$" :db/id 17592186565053} {:answer/id #uuid "c298df37-cd11-54c8-a6ae-8244b42ec27a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and $(1,1,1)$" :db/id 17592186565233} {:answer/id #uuid "c92734c5-3437-5572-a60d-19e95c9b9d36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and $(\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3})$" :db/id 17592186565242} {:answer/id #uuid "e1cfcf18-3023-5d0a-9e55-6fde879778df" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$(0,0,0)$ and $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$" :db/id 17592186565272}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186565053} :answer-field/id #uuid "568fe48b-b287-53d7-8a0d-1c40859c56fb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186121163}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "7a75a7fb-927d-5de3-ad94-97e90ac6e83d" :question/math-academy-id "q-106583" :question/problem "Find the points that satisfy the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)={x}^{3}-yz$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨1,1,1⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{3}-yz$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨1,1,1⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1)-f(0,0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,1,1⟩-⟨0,0,0⟩) \\ 0-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ 0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨3{x}^{2},-z,-y⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨3{c}_{1}^{2},-{c}_{3},-{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ 0 & =⟨3{c}_{1}^{2},-{c}_{3},-{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ 0 & =3{c}_{1}^{2}-{c}_{3}-{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-0}{1} \\ x & =y=z\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t,\,y=t,\,z=t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t,\,{c}_{2}=t,\,{c}_{3}=t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $3{c}_{1}^{2}-{c}_{3}-{c}_{2}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}-t-t & =0 \\ 3{t}^{2}-2t & =0 \\ t(3t-2) & =0 \\ t & =0,\,\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem.

- For $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & ={c}_{2}={c}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the first point $C$ are $(0,0,0).$

- For $t=\frac{2}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & ={c}_{2}={c}_{2}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the second point $C$ are $(\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$"} {:db/id 17592186124767 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "q-106806" :question/problem "Let $S$ be the set of all $2\times 2$ real matrices with determinant $1.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of our statements in turn.

- Statement “For any $A\in S,$ we have $1\cdot A=A.$” is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A=({a}_{ij})\in S,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, we have

$$
1\cdot {a}_{ij}={a}_{ij},
$$

and hence,

$$
1\cdot A=A.
$$

- Statements “For any $A\in S$ and $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we have $(\alpha +\beta )A=\alpha A+\beta A.$” is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A=({a}_{ij})\in S,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, for any $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
(\alpha +\beta ){a}_{ij}=\alpha {a}_{ij}+\beta {a}_{ij},
$$

and hence,

$$
(\alpha +\beta )A=\alpha A+\beta A.
$$

- Statement “There is a matrix $A\in S$ such that $\frac{1}{2}(2A)\ne A.$” is false. For a matrix in $A\in S,$ we have that

$$
\frac{1}{2}(2A)=(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2)A=1\cdot A=A
$$

since the scalar multiplication of matrices is associative.

Therefore, the correct answer is “For any $A\in S,$ we have $1\cdot A=A.$”; “For any $A\in S$ and $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we have $(\alpha +\beta )A=\alpha A+\beta A.$” only."} {:db/id 17592186124779 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0df5346d-2966-5621-a5f7-4d0c104072b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -7 \\ \frac{3}{4}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186412253} {:answer/id #uuid "3399bc79-2b67-5b83-87af-7604a8fccdc9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-12 \\ -7 \\ \frac{1}{5}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186412254} {:answer/id #uuid "477dde1b-8255-51b0-8585-d23e885143e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 7 \\ -\frac{3}{4}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186412255} {:answer/id #uuid "bad600d9-2cbf-50b7-ab3f-443e1558ed42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -5 \\ \frac{3}{4}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186412256} {:answer/id #uuid "e0cb3c90-da08-5155-bc03-351fcfe80179" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}12 \\ -7 \\ \frac{3}{4}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186412257}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186412253} :answer-field/id #uuid "82f02e4f-8fa1-5737-a974-c8725a5027aa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186412258}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6ab6a329-d125-54e3-98aa-c411b7b2d383" :question/math-academy-id "q-127045" :question/problem "Consider the straight line given by the following parametric equations:

$$
y=a(x-h)^{2}+k,
$$

where $a$ is the leading coefficient and $(h,k)$ is the vertex. 

- Since $h=-\frac{5}{6}$ and $k=-\frac{1}{2},$ the vertex is $(-\frac{5}{6},-\frac{1}{2}).$

- Since $a=1>0,$ the parabola opens upwards.

Because the parabola opens upwards, there is no maximum output, and the vertex corresponds to the minimum output.

Therefore, the range is $[-\frac{1}{2},\infty ).$ 

![](images/54/54e0b0ea5dd498a36fc854781dc5120ce1de9bee0c333eecc6d895ce09b72424.png)"} {:db/id 17592186124875 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0df9a543-b5df-589d-9923-b17fb9588714" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\frac{4}{3},\infty )" :db/id 17592186549338} {:answer/id #uuid "3d610a34-2b2c-5b7f-a6ee-1208ff230466" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\infty ,-\frac{4}{3}]" :db/id 17592186549439} {:answer/id #uuid "5d61e674-449f-5c1e-8470-6d7a912ecbd3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\infty ,\frac{1}{3}]" :db/id 17592186549503} {:answer/id #uuid "9f1dd293-3094-5184-81d3-8f43b189007b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\infty ,\frac{4}{3}]" :db/id 17592186549619} {:answer/id #uuid "f1f407d3-59e6-5e5d-8e6f-2e775ce3251f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[-\frac{4}{3},\infty )" :db/id 17592186549764}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186549619} :answer-field/id #uuid "8f8e4aed-0ad7-583b-bf1d-eb2a74efae0c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186121850}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7bfd7586-e0f5-50a2-a9b8-3d8eb173ed99" :question/math-academy-id "q-35155" :question/problem "What is the range of the function $f(x)=-\frac{1}{3}(x+2)(x-2)?$" :question/worked-solution "The given parabola is written in factored form,

$$
y=a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2}),
$$

with $a=-\frac{1}{3}<0.$ 

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the parabola opens downward. Consequently, there is no minimum output, and the vertex corresponds to the maximum output.

The two roots of the parabola are ${x}_{1}=-2$ and ${x}_{2}=2,$ and we can find the $x$-coordinate of the vertex by taking the average of the roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{-2+2}{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=0$ back into the function to find the $y$-value of the vertex:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}(x+2)(x-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(0+2)(0-2) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot (-2) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is $(0,\frac{4}{3}),$ and the range of the function is $(-\infty ,\frac{4}{3}].$

![](images/d9/d9c96e13ab078005333cdf02d8939c96d41fe6802b7f4caf0d4bab041cf8a314.png)"} {:db/id 17592186124908 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26e9f934-e03e-503b-a010-328e30e41619" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186321453} {:answer/id #uuid "479e45fc-1d7f-5d7e-8007-b0940b6f80a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186321710} {:answer/id #uuid "ccc42a8c-8c3c-5672-849f-ffbb11b0b342" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186322740} {:answer/id #uuid "d7707a59-0026-5ff4-b80a-b1f6053dd56b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "The set is linearly independent" :db/id 17592186322829} {:answer/id #uuid "f7599531-0562-5f9d-a7d3-40986e05a5e0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186323088}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186323088} :answer-field/id #uuid "2a4cc6a3-052d-57fe-8e32-3d8bcf6effd8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323258}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "3e020612-0797-57a0-b15e-fb17a4ce38c2" :question/math-academy-id "q-35752" :question/problem "Consider the set $\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ of polynomials from $\mathbb{R}[t],$ where

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2t-4{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=3t-6{t}^{2}.
$$

If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}$ from a non-zero solution of ${x}_{1}\cdot {p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}\cdot {p}_{2}(t)=0.$" :question/worked-solution "If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ not both zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=0.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the given expressions for ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t)$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(2t-4{t}^{2})+{x}_{2}(3t-6{t}^{2}) & =0 \\ (2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2})t+(-4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}){t}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$

and
$\mathbf{r}(t)=t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+{t}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.$" :question/worked-solution "The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]=\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t).

In addition, we've been given that

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+3y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}+3y}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\frac{2(t)}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{(t)^{2}+3({t}^{2})}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{{t}^{2}+3{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{2t}{4{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\mathbf{i}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =(\frac{1}{2t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\mathbf{i}+2t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\left(\frac{1}{2t}\right)\cdot 1+\left(\frac{3}{4{t}^{2}}\right)\cdot 2t \\  & =\frac{1}{2t}+\frac{3}{2t} \\  & =\frac{4}{2t} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(1))] & =\frac{2}{1}=2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124960 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bde96964-49e5-5f8c-9a85-bf83f3f624a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-17" :db/id 17592186122361} {:answer/id #uuid "c18873f1-6416-5e3f-84a8-30f0d1e34a57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186122362} {:answer/id #uuid "eb8b5412-a282-5231-a52a-c430c381a304" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-15" :db/id 17592186122363} {:answer/id #uuid "55bd4f06-001b-5b40-9449-067e29d3fd21" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186122364} {:answer/id #uuid "5c13ba27-5c90-535c-9ea9-9232444e86bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186122365}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186122361} :answer-field/id #uuid "30ce640c-974a-53b3-8a92-6e2b4d383ffe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186122360}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e234e1ce-e3a5-5460-9b85-a8876cb6e36c" :question/math-academy-id "q-36247" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+3xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨{t}^{2},t+1,-t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+3xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x+3yz,3xz,3xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=t+1,$ and $z=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2({t}^{2})+3(t+1)(-t),3({t}^{2})(-t),3({t}^{2})(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}-3{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2t,1,-1⟩ \\  & =(-{t}^{2}-3t)\cdot 2t+(-3{t}^{3})\cdot 1+(3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2})\cdot (-1) \\  & =-2{t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} \\  & =-8{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =-8{(1)}^{3}-9{(1)}^{2}=-17.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124961 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b632d6e-7a98-53fb-a62b-8c9001dbea44" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186122369} {:answer/id #uuid "019ba0e0-ece3-5798-adda-30d5f0d23288" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}⁡2" :db/id 17592186479360} {:answer/id #uuid "3c938f80-1a2e-5bdc-937f-bbe6aa683da7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\operatorname{cos}⁡8" :db/id 17592186479449} {:answer/id #uuid "5f8f5ab1-0a45-584c-b611-498bfb7e8229" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2" :db/id 17592186479497} {:answer/id #uuid "ccd3d589-8795-5da6-b2f2-1c064d2c6d7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\operatorname{cos}⁡2" :db/id 17592186479672}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186479497} :answer-field/id #uuid "bbe9c851-9ada-5f1b-ae5b-56517e51d11b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186122366}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8571bcaa-6cdf-5385-98c4-d1ed2624cfd7" :question/math-academy-id "q-36253" :question/problem "Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨2\sqrt{t},4t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2\sqrt{t}$ and $y=4t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)\cdot 4 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{1}-4\cdot 1)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}-4) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124962 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "91e3020e-b220-554e-a3f0-07e483342e90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4\sqrt{21}}{21}" :db/id 17592186122373} {:answer/id #uuid "a1e6986e-ec79-5752-9e0d-ea5960beab16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "14\sqrt{29}" :db/id 17592186122374} {:answer/id #uuid "a8340c19-e527-5c1b-953c-c260766408b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{14\sqrt{21}}{21}" :db/id 17592186122375} {:answer/id #uuid "db0760d0-b134-5ae3-af68-54c39c2f1781" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{10\sqrt{29}}{29}" :db/id 17592186122376} {:answer/id #uuid "0801896c-1c2b-510b-86df-c0542a7bf4e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{14\sqrt{29}}{29}" :db/id 17592186122377}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186122377} :answer-field/id #uuid "5dfb4078-c321-5580-bb20-9356ac667745" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186122372}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4ba373e3-c7d5-54ce-a51c-b2950c874b69" :question/math-academy-id "q-36273" :question/problem "Find the directional derivative of the function $f(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2}$ at the point $(0,1)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf{v}=5\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}.$" :question/worked-solution "The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}}=\sqrt{29} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{29}}(5i+2j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =2\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇\,f(0,1) & =2\,i+(2\cdot 1)\,j \\  & =2i+2j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(0,1) & =∇\,f(0,1)\cdot u \\  & =(2i+2j)\cdot (\frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}i+\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}}j) \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 5+2\cdot 2}{\sqrt{29}} \\  & =\frac{14\sqrt{29}}{29}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124965 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08ff85bb-8ce2-5025-a0a1-83fc98417ed7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-2\pi ,-2,-\pi ⟩" :db/id 17592186321217} {:answer/id #uuid "636513d9-9ad2-5bbe-b8b3-cd67a4bf8d3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2,2,1⟩" :db/id 17592186321920} {:answer/id #uuid "9f98fa5a-9408-52f3-8b7e-8f25e3ab2ecf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨-\pi ,-1,\pi ⟩" :db/id 17592186322407} {:answer/id #uuid "c672059e-d68f-556c-9a70-117d11270e16" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨\pi ,2,\pi ⟩" :db/id 17592186322686} {:answer/id #uuid "cdeb1fca-19f0-5446-8266-9a4f0c5b2778" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "⟨2\pi ,2,\pi ⟩" :db/id 17592186322752}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322752} :answer-field/id #uuid "cd3b7500-df79-56f9-843a-ede4ff70a4be" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323570}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9a412c3a-6b92-5f8b-8cf9-ec76f9ca97fa" :question/math-academy-id "q-36305" :question/problem "In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)={y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,1,2)?$" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.
