"85182b2a-10d4-5663-831b-41623c395cce" :question/math-academy-id "e-11374" :question/problem "![](images/48/48a7c7ea2614c0b46df169cf353183f5b862f5feabab97a050107fe227f1521a.png)

 

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 2z\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} \:\textrm{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$ for $y \leq 0,$ shown above." :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = 

\iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \:  \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi.
$$

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad

y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad 

z = \rho\cos\phi
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

![](images/cd/cd2f48915774902314c38f2b5e40baa646761ae14b560eab401d8841f61f5612.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 3, \: \pi \leq \theta \leq 2\pi, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z) = 2z\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho  \\  & =2{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}2{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{4}\,d\rho  \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =\pi }^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{5}{\rho }^{5}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(1-1)\cdot (2\pi -\pi )\cdot \frac{1}{5}(243-0) \\  & =0\cdot \pi \cdot \frac{243}{5} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186128854 :question/id #uuid "ff5e1f9e-d67d-5264-b556-2f7b3a946c3f" :question/math-academy-id "e-12391" :question/problem "By integrating first with respect to $z,$ then $x,$ and then $y,$ evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R z-xy  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

over the rectangular box $R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \:0 \leq x \leq 2, \: -1 \leq y \leq 1, \: 1 \leq z \leq 3 \right\}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express our triple integral as a repeated integral:

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} z-xy \: \textrm{d}V
= 
\int_{-1}^{1} \int_{0}^{2} \int_{1}^{3} z-xy \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}y
$$

Since we're integrating first with respect to $z,$ then $x,$ and then $y,$ we write $\textrm d V = \textrm d z\:\textrm d x\:\textrm d y.$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z,$ treating $x$ and $y$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}z-xy\,dz\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{1}^{3}z-xy\,dz]dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{2}-xyz]}_{z=1}^{z=3}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(9-1)-xy(3-1)\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}4-2xy\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}4-2xy\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2}4-2yx\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[4x-y{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}4(2-0)-y({2}^{2}-0)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}8-4y\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}8-4y\,dy & =[8y-2{y}^{2}]_{y=-1}^{y=1} \\  & =8(1-(-1))-2({1}^{2}-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =8\cdot 2-2(1-1) \\  & =16-0 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186128858 :question/id #uuid "72795f5f-0d15-52e1-bfd8-997ae8e20265" :question/math-academy-id "e-12404" :question/problem "Evaluate
$$
\displaystyle
\int_{0}^{1} \int_{y}^{1} \int_{0}^{y} 3e^{x^3} \: \textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y.
$$

*Hint: Change change the order of integration to $\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x.$*" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
\int_{a}^{b} \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)} 3e^{x^3} \:\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: y \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq y \right\}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
\int_{a}^{b} \int_{v_1(x)}^{v_2(x)} \int_{0}^{y} 3e^{x^3} \:\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](images/bd/bdd856ef8a7940a009b7ee27d6614fdb8c042e6655c2316ce4db0633bfd04e9f.png)

The region $D$ is type II region in the $xy$-plane:

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \quad y \leq x \leq 1 \right\}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}x \: \textrm{d}y$ to $\textrm{d}z \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $y = y(x),$ is

$$
x = y \qquad\Longrightarrow \qquad y = x
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
y = 0.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 0 \leq y \leq x \right\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/1e/1e28e1cef9743da80d6fd2d38840810b12239d8546254c4d4cca767568f76a53.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}{\int }_{0}^{y}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}[{\int }_{0}^{y}\text{d}z]\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}[z]_{0}^{y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}3y{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}[{\int }_{0}^{x}y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{e}^{{x}^{3}}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[{e}^{{x}^{3}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186128862 :question/id #uuid "0a99e46a-2104-5285-862b-96b98e7a2f85" :question/math-academy-id "e-12482" :question/problem "![](images/0c/0cfd94391c0090bc628e4203af3ff15ff7407c9ecc4cc4e7a6f6ac7a1cf36b25.png)

A triangular plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant enclosed by the lines $y=x$ and $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. The mass density at each point is proportional to its distance from the $x$-axis. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by
$$
I_x =  \iint\limits_D y^2\lambda(x,y)  \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by
$$
I_y =  \iint\limits_D x^2\lambda(x,y)  \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by
$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2)\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm dA = I_x + I_y.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation
$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq x \right\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/c1/c1301c17b1dbb8b48716d09ad6f0a7a105917ea7a1c0e942bbe087b12772f254.png)

From the description, the mass density function can be written as 
$$
\lambda(x,y) = k|y| = k y,
$$
where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. 

Since the density contains the unknown constant $k$, we first use the total mass $M$ to determine $k.$

We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle M & \displaystyle  = \underset{D}{\iint } \lambda  ( x , y ) \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} A \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{0}^{x} k y \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} y \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = k {\int }_{0}^{1} [ {\int }_{0}^{x} y \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} y ] \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = k {\int }_{0}^{1} {[ {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} {y}^{2} ]}_{0}^{x} \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = k {\int }_{0}^{1} {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} {x}^{2} \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{k}{2}} {\int }_{0}^{1} {x}^{2} \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{k}{2}} {[ {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} {x}^{3} ]}_{0}^{1} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{k}{2}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{k}{6}}\end{array}
$$

Therefore, $k = 6M$ and hence $\lambda(x,y) = ky = 6M y.$ Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {I}_{y} & \displaystyle  = \underset{D}{\iint } {x}^{2} \lambda  ( x , y ) \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} A \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 6 M {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{0}^{x} {x}^{2} \cdot  y \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} y \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 6 M {\int }_{0}^{1} [ {\int }_{0}^{x} {x}^{2} y \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} y ] \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 6 M {\int }_{0}^{1} {x}^{2} {[ {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} {y}^{2} ]}_{0}^{x} \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 6 M {\int }_{0}^{1} {x}^{2} ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} {x}^{2} ) \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 3 M {\int }_{0}^{1} {x}^{4} \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = 3 M {[ {\displaystyle \frac{1}{5}} {x}^{5} ]}_{0}^{1} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{3 M}{5}} {[ {x}^{5} ]}_{0}^{1} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{3 M}{5}} .\end{array}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186128863 :question/id #uuid "dbf6a3b7-abb9-5f62-83af-00169c673bc6" :question/math-academy-id "e-12483" :question/problem "![](images/12/12fb5f07885b074f983cab3a5fba0faff607d8aa34d7cd3abe4e94abf53dac25.png)

Consider the plate that occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the polar circles $r = 1$ and $r = 2$ and the polar rays $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda(x,y) = \dfrac{1}{x^2}.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda(r,\theta),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
I_x = \iint\limits_D \lambda(r,\theta) \cdot r^3\sin^2{\theta} \:\textrm{d}r\:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
I_y = \iint\limits_D \lambda(r,\theta) \cdot  r^3\cos^2{\theta} \:\textrm{d}r\:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D \lambda(r,\theta) \cdot  r^3 \:\textrm{d}r\:\textrm{d}\theta = I_x + I_y.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 1 \leq r \leq 2, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda(r,\theta) = \dfrac{1}{r^2 \cos^2{\theta}}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{r}^{2}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot {r}^{3}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{2}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{2}r\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4-1)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot \frac{\pi }{12} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186128872 :question/id #uuid "c6b6a911-843f-5c96-a792-ebd807b5d60e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12875" :question/problem "Find the value of $2 + \left(-4\right)^{-2} \div \left( 1.5 + \dfrac{2}{15} \right)^0.$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

Any number raised to the power of $0$ equals $1.$ So, we have 

$$
\left( 1.5 + \dfrac{2}{15} \right) ^0 = 1.
$$

Next, we evaluate the negative exponent and get

$$
\left(-4\right)^{-2}  = \dfrac{1}{(-4)^2} = \dfrac{1}{16}.
$$

Substituting all these values into the expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}2+{(-4)}^{-2}÷{(1.5+\frac{2}{15})}^{0} &= 2+\frac{1}{16}÷1 \\ &= 2+\frac{1}{16} \\ &= \frac{32}{16}+\frac{1}{16} \\ &= \frac{33}{16}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186128983 :question/id #uuid "5110af12-1d0a-5f7e-8a3b-626cc437c53e" :question/math-academy-id "e-6097" :question/problem "Evaluate the repeated integral $$
\displaystyle \int_{2}^{4}  \int_{0}^{2} \dfrac{x^3}{y^2} \, \textrm{d}x  \, \textrm{d}y.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:    

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{{x}^{3}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}(\frac{{2}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{0}^{4}}{4})\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{4}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =4{[-\frac{1}{y}]}_{2}^{4} \\  & =4(-\frac{1}{4}-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186128984 :question/id #uuid "bd93891e-1f9f-51af-a5c2-4eb5ca1178d9" :question/math-academy-id "e-6098" :question/problem "Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac y{x^2} \, \textrm d A,
$$ where 
$D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \:2 \leq x \leq 4,\: 0 \leq y \leq 3\right\}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:    

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[-\frac{y}{x}]}_{2}^{4}\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-\frac{y}{4}-\left(-\frac{y}{2}\right))\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{y}{4}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{y}{4}\,\text{d}y & ={[\frac{{y}^{2}}{8}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{{3}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{8} \\  & =\frac{9}{8}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186128990 :question/id #uuid "a5567cb9-1c16-56a6-b0e8-759edf693a41" :question/math-academy-id "e-6107" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{R} \left(x^2-y^2 +3\right)  \textrm d A,
$$  where $R= [-1,3] \times [2, 4].$" :question/worked-solution "Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\text{ }\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's evaluate each of the three integrals.

- The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-2){\int }_{-1}^{3}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-1}^{3} \\  & =2(\frac{27}{3}+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{56}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(3-(-1)){\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =4\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{3}{|}_{2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{4}^{3}-\frac{4}{3}{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{224}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The function under the third integral is a constant, so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}3\,\text{d}A=3\,\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot (2\cdot 4)=24.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3)\,\text{d}A=\frac{56}{3}-\frac{224}{3}+24=-32.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129008 :question/id #uuid "9b2415da-21b8-5a59-9b3f-2f30b624c36f" :question/math-academy-id "e-7194" :question/problem "Change the order of integration and evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle{\int_0^{1} \int_{\sqrt{x}}^{1 } 9\sqrt{y^3+1}\,\textrm{d}y\,\textrm{d}x}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/10/1045aaad8025b20309b92477b4a1cf98e138064210c6fbc960c64ec26c9951df.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad \sqrt{x} \leq y \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y = \sqrt{x} 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x=y^2.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \quad 0 \leq x \leq y^2 \big\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/40/40cbaaff270daddf4b60115cc272fbc8b165b83b8823d19de2c19802617ebdb4.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{x}}^{1}9\sqrt{{y}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}9\sqrt{{y}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{y}^{3}+1}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{y}^{3}+1}[x\,]_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\,dy \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}3{y}^{2}({y}^{3}+1)^{1/2}\,dy \\  & =3{[\frac{2}{3}({y}^{3}+1)^{3/2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[2({y}^{3}+1)^{3/2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =2(2)^{3/2}-2 \\  & =4\sqrt{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129011 :question/id #uuid "b4697448-d5f7-59ae-86a1-689ae00ebb73" :question/math-academy-id "e-7197" :question/problem "![](images/1d/1d180fd5de88ebc465df522879142e5a4c5446c758aaccde792092968078c254.png)

The region $D$ is enclosed by the curves $x=2y^3-2y$ and  $x=y^3-4y,$ and the $y$-axis, as shown in the picture. Evaluate the double integral $$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm{d}A.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The region $D$ can be partitioned into two type II regions $D_1$ and $D_2,$ as shown below. 

![](images/68/6812e8036df171e162bee49d2edcff6d4a742e7bb4f14247713bd2332c64ccc6.png)

 

As a result, we get

$$
D_1 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq y  \leq 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq y^3\!-\!4y \bigg\}
$$

and 

$$
D_2 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y  \leq 1, \quad 2y^3\!-\!2y \leq x \leq 0 \bigg\}.
$$

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{{D}_{1}}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{{D}_{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{3}-4y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{3}-2y}^{0}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}[x]_{0}^{{y}^{3}-4y}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{2{y}^{3}-2y}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}({y}^{3}-4y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}(2y-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}-2{y}^{2}]}_{-2}^{0}+{[{y}^{2}-\frac{{y}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129014 :question/id #uuid "9a9885cc-6a93-57ee-bfd0-b4285395e326" :question/math-academy-id "e-7263" :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle 
\iiint\limits_{R} y \cos{x} \sin{z} \: \textrm{d}V
$$

over the box $$
\displaystyle R = \bigg\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \: 0 \leq z \leq \pi \bigg\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express our triple integral as a repeated integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}V & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Since the domain of integration $R = \left[0,\pi/2\right]\times[0,1]\times\left[0,\pi\right]$ is a rectangular box, and the integrand can be expressed as $f(x)\cdot g(y)\cdot h(z),$ we can rewrite our repeated integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x\,{\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y\,{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating each integral separately, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x\,{\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y\,{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z & =[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]_{0}^{\pi /2}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡z]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(1-0)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-0)\cdot (1-(-1)) \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129015 :question/id #uuid "9de92581-00d5-5343-90be-3b5527bfab49" :question/math-academy-id "e-7283" :question/problem "Using the change of variables 

$$
u =3x-2y, \quad v=x+y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(3x-2y)^2 - y - x = 0$ and the line $x+y=4.$" :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

$$
\mathbf{T}:{\left[ \begin{array}{c}u \\ v\end{array} \right]} \to {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( u , v ) \\ y ( u , v )\end{array} \right]}
$$

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u = 3x-2y, \qquad v=x+y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

$$
\mathbf{T}^{-1}:{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x \\ y\end{array} \right]} \to {\left[ \begin{array}{c}u ( x , y ) \\ v ( x , y )\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $3x-2y = u$ and $x+y = v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-2y)^{2}-y-x=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x + y = v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y+x=4\,⟹\,v=4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v &={u}^{2} \\ v &=4\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}u &=\pm 2 \\ v &=4.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2, 4).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -2 \leq u \leq 2, \, u^2 \leq v \leq 4\big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/0a/0a3d0211dfbe18e5737b62e8b61cf9308af2735ef827d14bae7b5dbfffaa4faa.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\begin{vmatrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = (5)^{-1} = \dfrac 15.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[v]_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[4u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(8-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{16}{3}\right) \\  & =\frac{32}{15}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129016 :question/id #uuid "d3ae6c85-14bd-57ad-b8cc-1cebb53683b7" :question/math-academy-id "e-7346" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
\displaystyle \int_{0}^{\pi/8} \int_0^{\sin2\theta} r \, \textrm d r\,\textrm d \theta.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{[{r}^{2}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{\sin }^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the double-angle formula

$$
\cos{2x} = 1-2\sin^2 x.
$$

Substituting $x=2\theta$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\sin^22\theta = \dfrac12\left(1-\cos4\theta\right).
$$

 

Finally, we can finish our integral by integrating with respect to $\theta,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{\sin }^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\theta -\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right))-(0-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{2}{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{32}(\pi -2)\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129018 :question/id #uuid "f31dd085-70fa-5eed-adf9-89fb0e6654e1" :question/math-academy-id "e-7348" :question/problem "Integrate the function $f(x, y) = 15xy^2$ over the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $x \geq 0,y \geq 0.$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D\mathbin{:}$

![](images/05/051cfbbf3fd37f01ff7e4442fccdc5ec4ce506e3c452b68bfa2ed5ae6e5cf6b9.png)

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \:0\leq \theta \leq  \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}15x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}15r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\sin }^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\sin }^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\sin }^{2}⁡\theta \,{[{r}^{5}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\sin }^{2}⁡\theta ({2}^{5}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\sin }^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{[{\sin }^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =32({\sin }^{3}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-{\sin }^{3}⁡(0)) \\  & =32(1-0) \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129024 :question/id #uuid "7dcea6be-fd16-5312-b50c-157bafcc2d65" :question/math-academy-id "e-8189" :question/problem "Find the volume of the solid $R,$ given by

$$
R = \Big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 2, \: 0 \leq z \leq \sqrt{2y}, \: 0 \leq x \leq yz \Big\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that we have a three-dimensional type II region.

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2y}}{\int }_{0}^{yz}\,dx\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2y}}[x]_{x=0}^{x=yz}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2y}}yz\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}y{[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{2y}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{y}{2}{(\sqrt{2y})}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(8-1)-0 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129025 :question/id #uuid "b0ad2f24-6f0c-5d66-9312-5e41840b4fe5" :question/math-academy-id "e-8190" :question/problem "![](images/04/043adf0ef683c24fbf4680145411d86fa94b52016bee44ac8f08ca7c5ca9f1b7.png)

 

Find the volume of the solid region above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the top one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/75/75a76a2dbc34c889335e66623e12b686eb9a255ee0d67f9be0e3792f2650360c.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type I region

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (x,y) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 4-x-y \big\},
$$

where

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/e1/e19ffe6a0555851c2b05526272beb21dbcdc082a23a2e11809c661666efdf133.png)

Hence, the type I representation of $R$ is

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 4-x-y \big\}.
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={∭}_{R}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-x-y}dz\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}[z]_{z=0}^{z=4-x-y}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-x-y)-0\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}4-x-y\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[(4-x)y-\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((4-x)(2)-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2})-0\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6-2x\,dx \\  & =[6x-{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(6(1)-{1}^{2})-0 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129026 :question/id #uuid "7883263b-110b-558f-83b2-0f6ec28be2c5" :question/math-academy-id "e-8191" :question/problem "Find the volume of the solid region enclosed by the surface $y=xz,$ the plane $y=2,$ and the planes $x=0,$ $x=1,$ $z=0,$ $z=1.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that our solid can be written as a type III region.

For each point $( x , z )$ in the rectangular base region
$$
0 \le  x \le  1 ,  0 \le  z \le  1 ,
$$
the variable $y$ runs from the surface
$$
y=xz
$$
up to the plane
$$
y=2.
$$

So we can write:
$$
R = \left\{(x,y,z) \:: \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: xz \leq y \leq 2 \right\}
$$

Therefore, the volume of $R$ is given by the following triple integral:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle V & \displaystyle  = \underset{R}{\iiint } \text{d} V \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{x z}^{2} \hspace{0.222em} \mathrm{d} y \hspace{0.222em} \mathrm{d} z \hspace{0.222em} \mathrm{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{0}^{1} [ y {]}_{y = x z}^{y = 2} \hspace{0.222em} \mathrm{d} z \hspace{0.222em} \mathrm{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{0}^{1} {\int }_{0}^{1} 2 - x z \hspace{0.222em} \mathrm{d} z \hspace{0.222em} \mathrm{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{0}^{1} {[ 2 z - {\displaystyle \frac{x {z}^{2}}{2}} ]}_{z = 0}^{z = 1} \hspace{0.222em} \mathrm{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{0}^{1} [ 2 ( 1 - 0 ) - {\displaystyle \frac{x ( {1}^{2} - 0 )}{2}} ] \hspace{0.222em} \mathrm{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{0}^{1} 2 - {\displaystyle \frac{x}{2}} \hspace{0.222em} \mathrm{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {[ 2 x - {\displaystyle \frac{ {x}^{2}}{4}} ]}_{x = 0}^{x = 1} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = ( 2 - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{4}} ) - 0 \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{7}{4}}\end{array}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129027 :question/id #uuid "27249c57-7f17-5e3e-9a21-0518320f5076" :question/math-academy-id "e-8192" :question/problem "![](images/73/73e2bd9a47c9d16f93d5240db3c4babc36f9fbe703ac9e0af449acaa7528f804.png)

A triangular plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the lines $x=1,y=0$ and $y=x,$ as shown above. The plate's mass density function $\lambda$ is given by $\lambda(x,y) = xy^2.$ Find the total mass of the triangular plate." :question/worked-solution "The mass of the triangular plate occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda(x,y) = xy^2$ is given by

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle M & \displaystyle  = \underset{D}{\iint } x {y}^{2} \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} A .\end{array}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type I region. So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\iint \limits_{D} xy^2\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{0}^1 \int_{0}^{x} xy^2\,\mathrm{d}y \, \mathrm{d}x
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle M & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{0}^{1} x [ {\int }_{0}^{x} {y}^{2} \hspace{0.167em} \text{d} y ] \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{0}^{1} x {[ {\displaystyle \frac{ {y}^{3}}{3}} ]}_{0}^{x} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\int }_{0}^{1} x ( {\displaystyle \frac{ {x}^{3}}{3}} - 0 ) \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} {\int }_{0}^{1} {x}^{4} \text{d} x\end{array}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} {\int }_{0}^{1} {x}^{4} \text{d} x & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} {[ {\displaystyle \frac{ {x}^{5}}{5}} ]}_{0}^{1} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{1}{3}} ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{5}} - 0 ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{1}{15}}\end{array}
$$

Therefore, the total mass of the plate is $\dfrac{1}{15}.$"} {:db/id 17592186129029 :question/id #uuid "92b9b5ea-1153-580a-a03a-94338f30fe3e" :question/math-academy-id "e-8195" :question/problem "![](images/f0/f0db928874dba8d872cde46d1467686010f3484765b2d7e39807b5a32a131b09.png)

Find the total charge $Q$ of a copper plate that occupies the region $D$ shown above, and has charge density 

$$
\rho (x,y) = \dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}  .
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the region $D$ represents one-quarter of the disk of radius $3$ centered at 
$\left(0,0\right).$

The total charge $Q$ of an object occupying the region $D$ with charge density $\rho (x,y) =  \dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}$ is given by

$$
Q = \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{4x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}  \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \rho(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ \rho(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

The following equations connect Cartesian and polar coordinates:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \\ y &=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta\end{aligned}\right.
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the curve $x^2+y^2=9$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =9 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =9 \\ {r}^{2}({\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta ) & =9 \\ {r}^{2} & =9 \\ r & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: \pi \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{4x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\sqrt{{r}^{2}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{\sin }^{2}⁡\theta }}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [{\int }_{0}^{3}r\,\text{d}r]\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (\frac{9}{2}-0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =18{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =18[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =18[-1-0] \\  & =-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total charge of the quarter-disk is $Q = - 18.$"} {:db/id 17592186129030 :question/id #uuid "c317696a-899d-5af5-9bf4-2d38862f5877" :question/math-academy-id "e-8542" :question/problem "![](images/de/de882e240d0a6ca824e77397fe9c6b51eb94d36c2e5e3524422ef0a0f28103de.png)

A triangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the $y$-axis and the lines $y=0$ and $y=2-x,$ as shown above. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by
$$
I_x =  \iint\limits_D y^2\lambda(x,y)  \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by
$$
I_y =  \iint\limits_D x^2\lambda(x,y)  \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by
$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2)\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm dA = I_x + I_y.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq 2-x \right\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/68/68904cbee1839a61f4d65c5ff03066d8f28b8a5e070f6ddb00c82c29cfd93fcd.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 
$$
\mathcal{A} =  \dfrac12 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 2.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:
$$
\lambda(x,y) = \dfrac{M}{\mathcal{A}} = \dfrac{M}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {I}_{x} & \displaystyle  = \underset{D}{\iint } {y}^{2} \lambda  ( x , y ) \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} A \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{M}{2}} {\int }_{0}^{2} {\int }_{0}^{2 - x} {y}^{2} \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} y \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{M}{2}} {\int }_{0}^{2} [ {\int }_{0}^{2 - x} {y}^{2} \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} y ] \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{M}{2}} {\int }_{0}^{2} {[ {\displaystyle \frac{ {y}^{3}}{3}} ]}_{y = 0}^{y = 2 - x} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{M}{6}} {\int }_{0}^{2} ( 2 - x {)}^{3} \hspace{0.222em} \text{d} x \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{M}{6}} {[ - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{4}} ( 2 - x {)}^{4} ]}_{0}^{2} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = - {\displaystyle \frac{M}{24}} {[ ( 2 - x {)}^{4} ]}_{0}^{2} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = - {\displaystyle \frac{M}{24}} ( {0}^{4} - {2}^{4} ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = - {\displaystyle \frac{M}{24}} \cdot  ( - 16 ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{2 M}{3}} .\end{array}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129031 :question/id #uuid "bee275c6-cca6-515f-b737-597ecca278a6" :question/math-academy-id "e-8543" :question/problem "![](images/46/46d6a57700d1df7f2de9a46507821a8553876eb956be6ef87a455d5ca0fabafb.png)

A plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the curves $y=x^2$ and $y=1$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda(x,y) = 4xy,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
I_x =  \iint\limits_D y^2\lambda(x,y)  \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
I_y =  \iint\limits_D x^2\lambda(x,y)  \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2) \lambda(x,y)  \:\textrm{d}A = I_x + I_y.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: x^2 \leq y \leq 1 \right\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/88/8846da0fe3b1e8369a9277bbaba1e082d040136a71105a5816af7b13d2788027.png)

Using the formula for $I_x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}{y}^{2}\cdot 4xy\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}4x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x{y}^{4}]_{y={x}^{2}}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x(1-{x}^{8})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x-{x}^{9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{10}}{10}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{10} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129045 :question/id #uuid "418e4c16-f718-53ec-af1d-bc871c175c1d" :question/math-academy-id "e-9600" :question/problem "Find the general solution to the difference equation $a_n + 100a_{n-2} =0$." :question/worked-solution "Let

$$
a_n=\lambda^n
$$

Then, we have

$$
a_{n-1} = \lambda^{n-1}, \qquad a_{n-2} = \lambda^{n-2}
$$

Substituting the above into our difference equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ^{n} + 100λ^{n - 2} &= 0 \\
λ^{n - 2}(λ^{2} + 100) &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ^{2} + 100 &= 0 \\
λ^{2} &= -100 \\
λ &= ± 10\textrm{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\lambda_1 = 10\textrm i
$$

and

$$
\lambda_2 = -10\textrm i
$$

Expressing our solutions in polar form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ_{1} &= 10(\cos \left(\frac{π}{2}\right) + \textrm{i}\sin \left(\frac{π}{2}\right)), \\
λ_{2} &= 10(\cos \left(\frac{π}{2}\right) - \textrm{i}\sin \left(\frac{π}{2}\right))
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using De Moivre's theorem, we can write the general solution to the difference equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= Cλ_{1}^{n} + Dλ_{2}^{n} \\
&= C[10(\cos \left(\frac{π}{2}\right) + \textrm{i}\sin \left(\frac{π}{2}\right))]^{n} + D[10(\cos \left(\frac{π}{2}\right) - \textrm{i}\sin \left(\frac{π}{2}\right))]^{n} \\
&= C[10^{n}(\cos \left(\frac{nπ}{2}\right) + \textrm{i}\sin \left(\frac{nπ}{2}\right))] + D[10^{n}(\cos \left(\frac{nπ}{2}\right) - \textrm{i}\sin \left(\frac{nπ}{2}\right))] \\
&= 10^{n}(A\cos \left(\frac{nπ}{2}\right) + B\sin \left(\frac{nπ}{2}\right))
\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
A = C+D, \qquad B = \textrm i(C-D)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129046 :question/id #uuid "9f13580e-2a41-52f0-9b69-d881c85683e0" :question/math-academy-id "e-9601" :question/problem "Consider the recurrence relation
$$
\displaystyle a_n = -6a_{n-1} - 12a_{n-2}, \quad a_0 =-1, \quad a_1=3+\sqrt{3}.
$$
Given that the solution takes the form
$$
\displaystyle a_n = \big(2\sqrt{3}\big)^n \left(A\cos\left(\dfrac{5n\pi}{6}\right) + B\sin\left(\dfrac{5n\pi}{6}\right) \right),
$$
find the value of $A + B$." :question/worked-solution "The general solution to the recurrence relation is

$$
a_n = \big(2\sqrt{3}\big)^n \left(A\cos\left(\dfrac{5n\pi}{6}\right) + B\sin\left(\dfrac{5n\pi}{6}\right) \right)
$$

We find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $a_0 = -1$ into the general solution gives
$$
\begin{aligned}(2\sqrt{3})^{0}(A\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{0\cdot 5\pi }{6}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{0\cdot 5\pi }{6}\right)) & =-1 \\ 1\cdot (A\cdot 1+B\cdot 0) & =-1 \\ A & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$
- Substituting $a_1=3+\sqrt{3}$ and $A=-1$ into the general solution gives
$$
\begin{aligned}(2\sqrt{3})^{1}(-1\cdot \operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{1\cdot 5\pi }{6}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{1\cdot 5\pi }{6}\right)) & =3+\sqrt{3} \\ 2\sqrt{3}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+B\cdot \frac{1}{2}) & =3+\sqrt{3} \\ 3+\sqrt{3}B & =3+\sqrt{3} \\ B & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
A + B = -1 + 1 = 0
$$

Finally, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_{n} &= (2\sqrt{3})^{n}(\sin \left(\frac{5nπ}{6}\right) - \cos \left(\frac{5nπ}{6}\right))
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129047 :question/id #uuid "bf1a806e-e676-5cd9-8d42-2995623b2941" :question/math-academy-id "e-9602" :question/problem "Solve the recurrence relation
$$
\displaystyle a_n =2a_{n-1} - 2a_{n-2}, \quad a_0=2, \quad a_1=5.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Moving all terms of our recurrence relation to the left-hand side, we obtain

$$
a_n - 2a_{n-1} + 2a_{n-2} = 0
$$

First, we find the roots of the characteristic equation:

$$
\lambda^2 - 2\lambda + 2 = 0
$$

This equation can be solved by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ^{2} - 2λ + 2 &= 0 \\
(λ^{2} - 2λ + 1) - 1 + 2 &= 0 \\
(λ - 1)^{2} + 1 &= 0 \\
(λ - 1)^{2} &= -1 \\
λ - 1 &= ± \textrm{i} \\
λ &= 1 ± \textrm{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\lambda_1 = 1 + \textrm{i}, \qquad \lambda_2 = 1 - \textrm{i}
$$

Expressing our solutions in polar form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
λ_{1} &= \sqrt{2}(\cos \left(\frac{π}{4}\right) + \textrm{i}\sin \left(\frac{π}{4}\right)), \\
λ_{2} &= \sqrt{2}(\cos \left(\frac{π}{4}\right) - \textrm{i}\sin \left(\frac{π}{4}\right))
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution to the recurrence relation is

$$
a_n = \big(\sqrt{2}\big)^n \left(A\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{4}\right) + B\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{4}\right)\right)
$$

We now find the constants $A$ and $B$ using the initial conditions:

- Substituting $a_0 = 2$ into the general solution gives
$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{2})^{0}(A\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{0\cdot \pi }{4}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{0\cdot \pi }{4}\right)) & =2 \\ 1\cdot (A\cdot 1+B\cdot 0) & =2 \\ A & =2.\end{aligned}
$$
- Substituting $a_1=5$ and $A=2$ into the general solution gives
$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{2})^{1}(2\cdot \operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{1\cdot \pi }{4}\right)+B\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{1\cdot \pi }{4}\right)) & =5 \\ \sqrt{2}\cdot (\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2}+B\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) & =5 \\ 2+B & =5 \\ B & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
a_n = \big(\sqrt{2}\big)^n \left(2\cos\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{4}\right) + 3\sin\left(\dfrac{n\pi}{4}\right)\right)
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129061 :question/id #uuid "6a2bc6d1-176a-5c20-9c74-b5432a247270" :question/math-academy-id "e-9740" :question/problem "A bank account pays $10 \%$ annual interest, compounded yearly. Find the equivalent annual interest rate when compounding monthly. Round your answer to the nearest tenth of a percent." :question/worked-solution "If the initial deposit is $P_0$, using the compound interest equation, the total amount on the account after $t$ years will be equal to

$$
P = P_0 \cdot \left(1+\dfrac{0.1}{1}\right)^t = P_0 \cdot (1.1)^t
$$

To determine the equivalent annual interest rate when compounding monthly, we transform the equation above as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= P_{0} \cdot (1.1)^{t} \\
&= P_{0} \cdot ((1.1)^{1/12})^{12t} \\
&\approx P_{0} \cdot (1.007974…)^{12t} \\
&= P_{0} \cdot (1 + 0.007974…)^{12t} \\
&= P_{0} \cdot (1 + \frac{12 \cdot 0.007974…}{12})^{12t} \\
&\approx P_{0} \cdot (1 + \frac{0.095689…}{12})^{12t}
\end{aligned}
$$

This represents the annual interest rate of

$$
{\color{blue}0.095\,689\,\ldots} \approx 9.6\%
$$

when compounding monthly (${\color{red}12}$ times per year)."} {:db/id 17592186129075 :question/id #uuid "205f4d6b-affa-530e-979b-a394e7a46bd3" :question/math-academy-id "e-9869" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x = 1+3t, \quad y = 2t^{3/2}, \quad t\in \left[0,1\right].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi x\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{t_1}^{t_2} x \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\,\textrm d t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $t_1=0$ to $t_2=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)=3 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3/2})=3{t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{{(3)}^{2}+{(3{t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{9+9t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{9(1+t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\cdot 3\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u = 1+t.$ Then, $1+3t=3u-2$ and $\textrm{d}u = \textrm d t.$ We also need to compute new limits, given below.



<div class="source-table-scroll"><table class="source-table" data-rules="all" data-table-align="center" data-frame="true">
<tbody><tr data-next-row="true">
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>$t$</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$0$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$1$</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8">$u$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$1$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$2$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table></div>


Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =6\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(1+3t)\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(3u-2)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}(3{u}^{3/2}-2{u}^{1/2})\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\pi \cdot {[\frac{6{u}^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{4{u}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =6\pi [(\frac{6({2}^{5/2})}{5}-\frac{4({2}^{3/2})}{3})-(\frac{6}{5}-\frac{4}{3})] \\  & =6\pi [(\frac{24\sqrt{2}}{5}-\frac{8\sqrt{2}}{3})-(\frac{6}{5}-\frac{4}{3})] \\  & =6\pi [\frac{32\sqrt{2}}{15}+\frac{2}{15}] \\  & =\frac{4\pi }{5}(16\sqrt{2}+1).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129401 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "82a340a7-1cb8-5713-a6c0-73e88d9a4f21" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186125907} {:answer/id #uuid "8ec2540e-833a-59ec-b158-e41320a2668e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186125908} {:answer/id #uuid "e03523a9-0302-57bf-a2c8-251c6a1e70fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186125909} {:answer/id #uuid "47320515-e4d1-52ac-8b21-d215511c4422" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186125910} {:answer/id #uuid "62c801a9-62f1-574f-bc1b-80ea2e7a8932" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186125911}] :answer-field/id #uuid "fa3745de-a8d8-5125-8613-9346955c5eb7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186125906}] :question/id #uuid "2af8994b-c9e2-5d59-9c51-e7eeafbf6a0d" :question/math-academy-id "q-100300" :question/problem "What is $$

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?" :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{\sin }^{2}⁡2t+{\sin }^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡2t=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4{\sin }^{2}⁡2t+{\sin }^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{4(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+{\sin }^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{16{\sin }^{2}⁡t{\cos }^{2}⁡t+{\sin }^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{{\sin }^{2}⁡t(16{\cos }^{2}⁡t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{{\sin }^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{16{\cos }^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot |\operatorname{sin}⁡t|\cdot \sqrt{16{\cos }^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{16{\cos }^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129489 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c38703c5-45dc-5793-893f-51ebd1bb3422" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3π}{4}" :db/id 17592186126435} {:answer/id #uuid "d397cbc0-4e07-5c45-8dd4-852495431b53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9π}{5}" :db/id 17592186126436} {:answer/id #uuid "d9805686-3f2d-5075-841f-d4f6c06d0a02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6π}{5}" :db/id 17592186126437} {:answer/id #uuid "e3ada45f-083a-58f4-9181-cea8a0d45c2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{12π}{5}" :db/id 17592186126438} {:answer/id #uuid "3c32b447-7838-5154-afcf-456d96af856b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3π}{5}" :db/id 17592186126439}] :answer-field/id #uuid "70570f6a-0123-5e2d-97df-d5a17cdaa0ef" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186126434}] :question/id #uuid "1424de6d-6c16-544a-91e8-426cab364f19" :question/math-academy-id "q-138946" :question/problem "Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-{t}^{3})=3-3{t}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})=6t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(3-3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{(6t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9-18{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}+36{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9({t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\cdot 3\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\sqrt{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot |{t}^{2}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi \cdot {[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =18\pi [(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3})-(\frac{0}{5}+\frac{0}{3})] \\  & =18\pi \cdot \frac{8}{15} \\  & =\frac{48\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129515 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e6ca8e4-3abb-5ecc-8a9f-2f961bcc8621" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2({e}^{2}-3)" :db/id 17592186275754} {:answer/id #uuid "68eeb45f-07c6-5215-a78f-8cb259c032a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2}-1" :db/id 17592186276420} {:answer/id #uuid "8a9f54c2-adbf-5b87-8306-1c8b43e09d39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186276732} {:answer/id #uuid "e0b7672e-9f7f-55fd-be19-526fc9fd907b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{e}^{2}" :db/id 17592186277442} {:answer/id #uuid "f75ec5f1-3773-576e-a82d-dd222ccc2a42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{e}^{2}-2" :db/id 17592186277638}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186277638} :answer-field/id #uuid "6c87638f-dc8d-582e-8040-334b48acda2b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277916}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "9ce80f42-293e-5e66-a70f-dd95799ecbec" :question/math-academy-id "q-161374" :question/problem "By integrating first with respect to $z,$ then $x,$ and then $y,$ evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}(x-y){e}^{z}\,dV
$$

over the rectangular box $R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 0,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡2\le z\le 2}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we express our triple integral as a repeated integral:

$$
{∭}_{R}(x-y){e}^{z}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{2}(x-y){e}^{z}\,dz\,dx\,dy
$$

Since we're integrating first with respect to $z,$ then $x,$ and then $y,$ we write $\text{d}V=\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z,$ treating $x$ and $y$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{2}(x-y){e}^{z}\,dz\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{2}(x-y){e}^{z}\,dz]dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}[(x-y){e}^{z}]_{z=\operatorname{ln}⁡2}^{z=2}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-y)({e}^{2}-2)\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-y)({e}^{2}-2)\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(x-y)({e}^{2}-2)\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[({e}^{2}-2){\int }_{0}^{1}(x-y)\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({e}^{2}-2){[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({e}^{2}-2)[\frac{1}{2}(1-0)-(1-0)y]dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({e}^{2}-2)(\frac{1}{2}-y)dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}({e}^{2}-2)(\frac{1}{2}-y)dy & =({e}^{2}-2){\int }_{-1}^{0}\frac{1}{2}-y\,dy \\  & =({e}^{2}-2){[\frac{1}{2}y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=-1}^{y=0} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-2}{2}(0-(-1)+1) \\  & ={e}^{2}-2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129529 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "562d0704-f8bb-56d1-ad51-2efebd134efa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e-1" :db/id 17592186279380} {:answer/id #uuid "65d6262f-31f6-5c6a-a73b-e3a7b55728a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186279520} {:answer/id #uuid "d301c278-fecb-50eb-a7b0-cf15bf32c993" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}-1" :db/id 17592186280453} {:answer/id #uuid "d5144876-7c4f-5ef7-b912-312e36e6a5a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186280471} {:answer/id #uuid "f7eac3ef-b262-53cc-9f03-528d3cd26d5e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186280764}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280471} :answer-field/id #uuid "35b87413-958f-55b3-b6a9-0b06c650f7b3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280929}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "c00cd44a-d34c-5f6e-aacf-b4ef475837d1" :question/math-academy-id "q-162253" :question/problem "Evaluate
$$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{z}}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.
$$

*Hint: First change the order of integration to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.$*" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find the limits of integration such that our integral can be expressed as 

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the domain of integration $R$ can be written as a type III region as follows:

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,\sqrt{z}\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le {e}^{z/x}\}
$$

Since all repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $y,$ the $y$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x
$$

 

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane shown below.

![](images/e8/e83c249a6abf9710a201462e16c646a11411dbcdbca46f34e9beb8d2db7a654b.png)

The region $D$ is type II region in the $xz$-plane:

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,\sqrt{z}\le x\le 1\}.
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $D$ as a type I region.

Notice that the top boundary of the region $D,$ written in the form $z=z(x),$ is

$$
x=\sqrt{z}\,⟹\,z={x}^{2}
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region $D$ is

$$
z=0.
$$

Then, the type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le {x}^{2}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/7e/7e684766b85a214d1f1dd7845979052c532e11ecce74d0284b8fc379b5669957.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{z}}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}[y]_{0}^{{e}^{z/x}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{e}^{z/x}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{e}^{z/x}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x{e}^{z/x}]_{z=0}^{z={x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x{e}^{x}-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[(x-1){e}^{x}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(0-\frac{1}{2})-(-1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129531 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c5c064b-08ea-5bfd-ab69-59d08747b4f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186278982} {:answer/id #uuid "36add068-fc21-5310-b6d6-2c342cf02faa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279070} {:answer/id #uuid "402db993-f88f-5fbe-94b2-191a8a4097a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279160} {:answer/id #uuid "a97f6f5d-dae7-50c8-b1bc-6c5e4d06a4bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280096} {:answer/id #uuid "bf6093ca-d163-58ee-a9e0-b840646a5e22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280274}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280274} :answer-field/id #uuid "8415b494-bfb5-5759-9d5d-906937712b89" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281071}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d5a597a5-f786-5891-91b3-c78b73413f55" :question/math-academy-id "q-162905" :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{1}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{3} \\  & =\frac{5M}{3}.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $\frac{5M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186129532 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a0a8b33a-6039-541e-b58e-1f0a29efa688" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}" :db/id 17592186126690} {:answer/id #uuid "bdc5d6a1-85df-58ec-8f12-88aeac9bf8ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{3}" :db/id 17592186126691} {:answer/id #uuid "f26bff63-e8ea-527f-8e55-bced519e9384" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "M" :db/id 17592186126692} {:answer/id #uuid "18fe4b91-2465-5f90-aa80-4b1a75799c68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{2}" :db/id 17592186126693} {:answer/id #uuid "27fbd22f-ff3d-5928-ab73-3c683a066225" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3M}{2}" :db/id 17592186126694}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186126690} :answer-field/id #uuid "dabbdf32-9b8d-5ae1-a71a-6f12fe91d019" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186126689}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f0af98bb-12cf-5c0f-a924-a0fe039adf99" :question/math-academy-id "q-162906" :question/problem "![](images/64/64cadaa8b079c80659d661be55709e572c05b185a6b6fdb60e24801a9d1e84a5.png)

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le 3-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/bc/bcf045b47856148dc5f7c05a2800804fb34aad2d0755983375c20c35bb00f0e4.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot 2=3.

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y/2}^{3-y}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{y/2}^{3-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{2}(3-y-\frac{1}{2}y)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[{y}^{3}-\frac{3}{8}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}[(8-6)-0] \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129533 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e5b79f0-fe1f-5968-a6d9-ee148fae971f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "87.5\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186278874} {:answer/id #uuid "4e3f6e9e-364f-5a41-b13a-37d28222531f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "30\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279301} {:answer/id #uuid "721017c5-8b67-597e-9158-5d6c86e5e6b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "97.5\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279628} {:answer/id #uuid "89ce2a87-a695-5f87-a1c3-117382df04e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "102.5\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279820} {:answer/id #uuid "a013ac40-9905-5921-9ec1-6a069c738d7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "95\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280015}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279628} :answer-field/id #uuid "7b28007f-9cca-5200-a487-d957cfccad04" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281057}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e40dca43-d21c-5ed7-bbc5-5f37b500695b" :question/math-academy-id "q-162922" :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(6-xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2}6{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}y+6{y}^{2}-x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[2{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}y+6x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}16-4y+12{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[16y-2{y}^{2}+4{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =48-18+108-\frac{81}{2}-0 \\  & =97.5.\end{aligned}
