$$"} {:db/id 17592186134132 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "77457099-bf92-5a80-b30d-5158400cc17a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{60}" :db/id 17592186371989} {:answer/id #uuid "114e3ccc-e21f-52db-b19d-3f3897328e86" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{25}" :db/id 17592186371990} {:answer/id #uuid "57a39c82-1760-5e0d-ab2f-00a266a5b5cf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186371991} {:answer/id #uuid "52460aa2-bb42-52a1-ba47-8cd7c05b7e29" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{32}" :db/id 17592186371992} {:answer/id #uuid "0670939e-8e1b-5069-8ab1-36c39e6a1734" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186371993}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186371989} :answer-field/id #uuid "1918f620-1ef5-50a5-bd08-efba031c5de5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186371988}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ab9a09b7-00f2-517e-bc29-69739ea5a8ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-161928" :question/problem "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(t-{t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(2{t}^{2}-2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [0,1).$
Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral

$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y=t-{t}^{3},\,z=2{t}^{2}-2t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(t-{t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+({t}^{2}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-{t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}-2t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k} \\  & =(2t-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(1-3{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(4t-2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =((t-{t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+({t}^{2}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k})\cdot ((2t-1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(1-3{t}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(4t-2)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}) \\  & =(t-{t}^{3})\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (1-3{t}^{2})+({t}^{2}-t)\cdot (4t-2) \\  & =t-4{t}^{2}+5{t}^{3}-2{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\mathbf{F}(r(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.278em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t-4{t}^{2}+5{t}^{3}-2{t}^{4})\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-\frac{4{t}^{3}}{3}+\frac{5{t}^{3}}{4}-\frac{2{t}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{4}{3}+\frac{5}{4}-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134133 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "91e141a3-db78-5e44-a461-551fe7a0bece" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{60}" :db/id 17592186130955} {:answer/id #uuid "ad54536a-b558-5c60-b187-fd8fa41d6e02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186130956} {:answer/id #uuid "e0ca6443-99c2-586e-b058-eaae89edfbc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{6}" :db/id 17592186130957} {:answer/id #uuid "2e445657-7a49-56a3-a596-aad6a22d87db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{100}" :db/id 17592186130958} {:answer/id #uuid "5e35f75a-b843-5afb-af33-d8260e24ea04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "100" :db/id 17592186130959}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186130955} :answer-field/id #uuid "3d428aec-71bd-5e76-8cd2-9b96389f1f6c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186130954}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4bba2c4b-bfab-581e-aa67-d4d398fc018f" :question/math-academy-id "q-162238" :question/problem "Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=(y-x)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}$ along the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf{r}(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+({t}^{3}-t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\operatorname{sin}(2\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "The circulation $Γ$ measures the total work done by a force $F$ in moving a particle along a *closed* curve $C.$
It is given by the formula

$$
Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y={t}^{3}-t,\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y-x)\,i \\  & =({t}^{3}-t-{t}^{2}+t)\,i \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)\,)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\,({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\,i\,)\cdot (\,(2t-1)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j+2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)\,k\,) \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)+0\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t) \\  & =2{t}^{4}-{t}^{3}-2{t}^{3}+{t}^{2} \\  & =2{t}^{4}-3{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Γ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\,2{t}^{4}-3{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}\,)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{2{t}^{5}}{5}-\frac{3{t}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{2}{5}-\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{3})-(0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{60}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134134 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00d95993-6fce-50a6-9da0-c38e0b9621ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186130961} {:answer/id #uuid "5b48ccdf-94f7-5b30-b9e9-c2b9d97a02fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186130965} {:answer/id #uuid "6eea3a9c-148b-5bbc-b698-c42d3d976666" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\pi " :db/id 17592186521016} {:answer/id #uuid "81f2f5fe-c2fa-5a14-a755-d561c640ccb1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi " :db/id 17592186521062} {:answer/id #uuid "9ce79bec-631d-5e6e-9ada-b94ec4a0d8f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\pi " :db/id 17592186521119}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186521062} :answer-field/id #uuid "cfbd2886-ea55-5ec0-b21b-dda63331dd6e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186130960}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "008f670b-b77a-5939-9c4f-8602d138cc7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-162377" :question/problem "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $\mathbf{r}(t)=\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{cos}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\operatorname{sin}(\pi t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in [-1,1).$
Given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{S}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t),\,y=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t),\,z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t).
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =x\,i+y\,k \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t))\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k)\cdot (\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\,j+\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)-0\cdot \pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)\cdot \pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t) \\  & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {\cos }^{2}⁡(\pi t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\pi {\cos }^{2}⁡(\pi t))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi t)+\frac{\pi }{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi t)))\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{{\sin }^{2}⁡(\pi t)}{2}+\frac{\pi t}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi t)}{4}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =0+\frac{\pi }{2}+0-(0-\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134140 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "305d1aaf-bbea-5c5f-a549-96aeb913edda" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186279014} {:answer/id #uuid "7052a4ed-9911-5fd7-bc04-95f5aa7e4565" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186279610} {:answer/id #uuid "774d71e4-5b4e-524f-b577-edc0dd3ee10b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186279657} {:answer/id #uuid "ca898aae-6598-59af-88de-b8842924f741" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186280367} {:answer/id #uuid "cd52ceb4-0135-536f-8588-e294bafcb89b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186280401}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280401} :answer-field/id #uuid "f6048b0a-8782-5f08-a33d-6088d1e77789" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281271}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b54a2292-f496-593a-8f3d-c0762d77f082" :question/math-academy-id "q-162606" :question/problem "Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=0,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ $y=1,$ $z=0,$ $z=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $\mathbf{F}={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\operatorname{sin}z\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+(x+y)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k},$ find the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across $S.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S}={∭}_{R}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $\mathbf{F},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{F} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}z)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}z)+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+y) \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}z+0+0 \\  & =2x\operatorname{cos}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{S} & ={∭}_{R}2x\operatorname{cos}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2x\operatorname{cos}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}y\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2x\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}z\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}z \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot [\operatorname{sin}z]_{z=0}^{z=\pi /2} \\  & =({2}^{2}-{0}^{2})\cdot 1\cdot (\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-\operatorname{sin}0) \\  & =4\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134193 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "44b6551a-3fd7-5fc8-b776-155d7f42341e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186321689} {:answer/id #uuid "481e33e3-c704-521d-be35-4336e9e7bafb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186321714} {:answer/id #uuid "4f512c51-d026-5336-9280-75aeb2ef260f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186321768} {:answer/id #uuid "8076af1e-0cff-5bf9-b91a-db9180b146bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186322159} {:answer/id #uuid "ab0447bf-78d4-5413-b5da-eaeda4aa826d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186322490}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186321689} :answer-field/id #uuid "be362aea-3f36-5fc4-9815-88138f880b78" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323541}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1b47314b-c252-595b-b8b8-d7b952718a63" :question/math-academy-id "q-37863" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dA,\,
$$ where $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le x}.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over the type I region $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le x}.$ 

So, we can express the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{0}^{x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134194 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "77d41ea4-f371-5e3c-a73f-9bb40eedaa54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi +1)" :db/id 17592186322086} {:answer/id #uuid "79cba168-b634-5cf6-87c8-7f03a009eabd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}⁡({\pi }^{5})+1" :db/id 17592186322102} {:answer/id #uuid "9e815f84-08d1-50d2-8c7e-3525d7eabe22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{32{\pi }^{6}}{3}" :db/id 17592186322396} {:answer/id #uuid "f8546e31-6b95-5665-9f52-993a1da0e3da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16{\pi }^{5}}{5}" :db/id 17592186323100} {:answer/id #uuid "fa59a30b-42ad-5c73-91a9-0efa5f1f736b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{35{\pi }^{5}}{5}" :db/id 17592186323120}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322396} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf0e1739-c91f-534f-a466-f07c42c462b9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323574}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e6bdaaf3-f25a-586a-927c-1d92815a4ea7" :question/math-academy-id "q-37864" :question/problem "$$

$$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{x}^{5}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{x}^{5}[{\int }_{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{x}^{5}[y]_{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}^{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{x}^{5}((1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{x}^{5}\,dx\end{aligned}

$$"} {:db/id 17592186134196 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1435c15c-cee2-5d63-99e5-950ff63fbcbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186321311} {:answer/id #uuid "36470a66-3fc0-52e3-8595-d34b998f8b45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186321561} {:answer/id #uuid "43603675-9305-525e-a36a-4ac8b0c1f71a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186321678} {:answer/id #uuid "517e72de-c47e-5705-a920-d0a098c5aa68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186321788} {:answer/id #uuid "cbe849ce-750d-523c-9c5c-cdf9f8962247" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186322730}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322730} :answer-field/id #uuid "1cd2908f-886b-5e6a-b664-20111c79418b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323225}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8f095d13-dd7c-5406-aa62-9362d833b9d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-37995" :question/problem "Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}\,dx\,dy.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}[x]_{0}^{{y}^{2}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}({y}^{2}-0)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{\pi /2}}{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}

$$"} {:db/id 17592186134201 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "133eafdf-8b1b-5f1e-970a-ff8b46c6c703" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186324142} {:answer/id #uuid "4c334839-5b30-57fb-987f-491ba05009bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{4}" :db/id 17592186324595} {:answer/id #uuid "6f51e605-f913-5a44-9e67-faf1f088436f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186324886} {:answer/id #uuid "e31ec296-1126-5c08-9cea-da8982c72d20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186325967} {:answer/id #uuid "fe1135b3-8015-51a5-93d8-9fb4ab3c77bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{6}" :db/id 17592186326212}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186326212} :answer-field/id #uuid "9db5292a-83c4-57af-ab9d-6fd9b12906d1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326504}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "687f42ad-4d31-5616-a543-616339685f35" :question/math-academy-id "q-39205" :question/problem "If $u=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,,$ $v=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\,,$ and $u\cdot u=15,$ then $$
\displaystyle \frac{u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}u)}{u\cdot (\frac{3}{4}v)}=
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the fact that the dot product is linear.

To quickly compute the numerator $u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}u),$ we multiply $u\cdot u$ by $\frac{1}{2}.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}u) & =\frac{1}{2}(u\cdot u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 15 \\  & =\frac{15}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To quickly compute the denominator $u\cdot (\frac{3}{4}v),$ we compute $u\cdot v$ first and then multiply the result by $\frac{3}{4}.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot (\frac{3}{4}v) & =\frac{3}{4}(u\cdot v) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}({u}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}+{u}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}+{u}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}+{u}_{4}\cdot {v}_{4}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}((-1)\cdot (-3)+(-3)\cdot (-1)+(-2)\cdot (-2)+1\cdot 2) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(3+3+4+2) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot 12 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{u\cdot (\frac{1}{2}u)}{u\cdot (\frac{3}{4}v)} & =\frac{\left(\frac{15}{2}\right)}{9}=\frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134212 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5b6f0d80-4352-5158-8f93-1840b1e6324a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{55}{4}" :db/id 17592186324725} {:answer/id #uuid "64abec96-fecf-52bf-b665-465ae20f4135" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{27}{4}" :db/id 17592186324804} {:answer/id #uuid "95deb8cb-eec5-56d6-b7c7-f205853e1f6b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{35}{4}" :db/id 17592186325249} {:answer/id #uuid "9f9661da-4c00-5003-8d44-16815092e8eb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{89}{4}" :db/id 17592186325327} {:answer/id #uuid "b603e0fd-9b34-5f6e-b31b-3b2140f17ad6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{109}{4}" :db/id 17592186325535}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325535} :answer-field/id #uuid "ca3dfc2b-fd60-5b79-a0ca-b2bb5282bb22" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326587}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f7cef591-bf6c-502e-a297-4a0f671dac2e" :question/math-academy-id "q-39340" :question/problem "Evaluate $$
{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}
$$ given that $\mathbf{F}(x,y)={x}^{2}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ and $C$ is the path $\mathbf{r}(t)=3t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(2+t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in [0,1].$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}={\int }_{a}^{b}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have 

$$
x=3t,\,y=2+t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) & ={x}^{2}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(x+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =(3t)^{2}(2+t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =9{t}^{2}(2+t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =(18{t}^{2}+9{t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+t)\mathbf{j} \\  & =3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =((18{t}^{2}+9{t}^{3})\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+(3t+1)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (3\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \\  & =54{t}^{2}+27{t}^{3}+3t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r})\cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}54{t}^{2}+27{t}^{3}+3t+1\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}t \\  & ={[18{t}^{3}+\frac{27}{4}{t}^{4}+\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(18+\frac{27}{4}+\frac{3}{2}+1)-0 \\  & =\frac{109}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134234 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "138cac23-370e-5839-a092-017a89719e39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{7}{2} \\ 3 \\ -\frac{5}{2}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186417842} {:answer/id #uuid "274b7a59-8d6d-5f0d-a5bb-67d68e47b623" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}50 \\ 5 \\ 75\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186417845} {:answer/id #uuid "322e7a13-5d76-5091-9b4c-c0404f19e1ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 7 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186417847} {:answer/id #uuid "5a72aa28-97b8-5365-be9f-89839b7d4d8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186417851} {:answer/id #uuid "9859e5a1-f120-56a8-a412-5c766fcc01c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{7} \\ -\frac{5}{7} \\ \frac{15}{7}\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186417859}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186417851} :answer-field/id #uuid "84ea1ef5-c4c4-50df-8964-7eae36e54128" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186417867}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3a5d3d6c-a506-54c8-bf1d-2c93ad742095" :question/math-academy-id "q-39718" :question/problem "Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}-10 \\ -15 \\ 28\end{bmatrix},\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -3 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-2(\frac{3}{5}{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{6}{5}{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{6}{5}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{5}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{5}{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\right\}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot 6+(-15)\cdot 3+28\cdot 5}{{6}^{2}+{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-60-45+140}{36+9+25}b \\  & =\frac{35}{70}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{5}{2}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134268 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3dfa63d1-2a3c-5f98-ac88-3e5a9c4a677a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186324472} {:answer/id #uuid "50f72eff-980c-5d6b-bc19-dfa625820604" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186324636} {:answer/id #uuid "6699b8d5-c375-5917-8a45-ab199058df5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186324827} {:answer/id #uuid "9313c2e6-4978-5466-83ec-9afb5f029598" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186325220} {:answer/id #uuid "dbdb866a-5a0b-5141-8de8-88e091ddbf5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186325887}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325220} :answer-field/id #uuid "51388a81-fbd8-54d3-b307-b0098d6fa5e9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326357}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "02ff2794-de30-53c1-a133-ec1abbd3f0b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-40208" :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}2y\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le z\sqrt{3}\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axes, the line $y=2$ and the line $z=y$ in the first quadrant." :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z\sqrt{3}}2y\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z\sqrt{3}}2y\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}2y[x]_{x=0}^{x=z\sqrt{3}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2yz\sqrt{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](images/63/63a8768b2769fad339ba7667357812d2dda0ea856e846ad666a100f8bc1336e9.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2yz\sqrt{3}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}2yz\sqrt{3}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{3}[{\int }_{0}^{y}2z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{3}[{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{3}({y}^{2}-0)\,dy \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{16}{4}-0) \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134269 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9d97ca78-347a-502a-821b-6597b74d8dcf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186131654} {:answer/id #uuid "a47409bb-80da-5d21-bdd0-a7a9eb56e892" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}" :db/id 17592186131655} {:answer/id #uuid "32f83252-c914-58ec-9f1a-010c8c11df29" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186131656} {:answer/id #uuid "46373f4f-36ae-5bcb-8d56-e944ad9e67b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}" :db/id 17592186131657} {:answer/id #uuid "5a016800-771f-5899-bf47-fcbbd10697e2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186131658}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186131657} :answer-field/id #uuid "399e5cd9-589e-5b64-85f8-862324894700" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186131653}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "3e4b7092-101b-57be-87cd-a4a4c83a4d75" :question/math-academy-id "q-40215" :question/problem "Consider the vector $x$ and the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,\,x=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ given that the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is orthogonal." :question/worked-solution "Since the set $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2}\}$ is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x.
$$

So, we first find the orthogonal projections of $x$ onto $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1}\}$ and $\text{Span}\{{a}_{2}\}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{1}}{{a}_{1}\cdot {a}_{1}}{a}_{1}=\frac{4\cdot 1+1\cdot 0+2\cdot (-1)}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{a}_{1}=(1)\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ {\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x & =\frac{x\cdot {a}_{2}}{{a}_{2}\cdot {a}_{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{4\cdot 1+1\cdot 1+2\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{a}_{2}=\frac{7}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & ={\text{proj}}_{{a}_{1}}x+{\text{proj}}_{{a}_{2}}x \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{7}{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\left(3\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+7\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\right) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{10}{3} \\ \frac{7}{3} \\ \frac{4}{3}\end{bmatrix}=\hat{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the distance between $x$ and the subspace $S$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d(x,\hat{x}) & =‖x-\hat{x}‖ \\  & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\hat{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\hat{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\hat{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(4-\frac{10}{3})}^{2}+{(1-\frac{7}{3})}^{2}+{(2-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4}{9}+\frac{16}{9}+\frac{4}{9}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134271 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0595a4cc-deef-5094-b7bb-0720af556d3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186324021} {:answer/id #uuid "0627ead6-dc46-5d98-9b02-2ae980c8cc02" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{40}{3}" :db/id 17592186324027} {:answer/id #uuid "744f2c72-b380-5613-b966-e2ebaaa6e905" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186324941} {:answer/id #uuid "e0f8ae22-34af-5a81-8c18-1660be796a8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186325940} {:answer/id #uuid "fd819532-c21c-5b83-bdbf-bee884e297fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{52}{3}" :db/id 17592186326207}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186326207} :answer-field/id #uuid "4e483ff7-7ea2-525e-997c-5cecea2ffc57" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326347}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e1a1cf7f-cf9c-51a1-babc-d27035fc1ca5" :question/math-academy-id "q-40219" :question/problem "![](images/bc/bc1b0ea463b0f753a2c65784fa5d46203cde8f457116c481301bf3f20ce82f54.png)

Evaluate the triple integral 
$$
\displaystyle {∭}_{R}4y\,dV
$$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/9b/9bb9311cbaf796f76c4b8b7cb7ed81abec48abc445b894f838f940fbd92e534b.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 4-y-z},
$$

where

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 1}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](images/82/82f237dc5fb7d8b8ed34b7a1c16527ab338923a33462f0bd7dafbe54bc5e5158.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 4-y-z}.
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4y\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}4y\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}4y\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}4y\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}4y[x]_{x=0}^{x=4-y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}4y(4-y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(16y-4{y}^{2}-4yz)\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(16y-4{y}^{2}-4yz)\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(16y-4{y}^{2}-4yz)\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[16yz-4{y}^{2}z-2y{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(14y-4{y}^{2})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(14y-4{y}^{2})\,dy & ={[7{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =(28-\frac{32}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{52}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134277 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c13ee6c3-92c9-5a3d-b1c3-cc0e6dc9c11d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{96}{35}" :db/id 17592186131702} {:answer/id #uuid "dd83dc0f-ae75-597e-9bf5-97ca5882c46e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{24}{5}" :db/id 17592186131703} {:answer/id #uuid "23b2b615-b99c-50e0-a324-227c7235fe42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{104}{35}" :db/id 17592186131704} {:answer/id #uuid "442792c7-4dbd-5bc7-83a1-8c1fbcc8e6af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{62}{7}" :db/id 17592186131705} {:answer/id #uuid "6d3b94ad-f1e1-5a06-b9fd-7ea4ca4724ce" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{54}{7}" :db/id 17592186131706}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186131702} :answer-field/id #uuid "ae85dffa-91e2-5047-afe6-7098bbee9ba4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186131701}] :question/id #uuid "b920de5e-825e-5dcf-9aac-175e4a51e8a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-40258" :question/problem "Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x, y) = 3x$ along the curve $C$ parametrized by $$
\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨\frac{4{t}^{3/2}}{3},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}-t⟩\hspace{0.167em}
$$ for $t ∈ [0, 1]$." :question/worked-solution "For a scalar line integral, substitute the parametrization and multiply by speed. Here $r'(t)=\langle2\sqrt t,t-1\rangle$, so $\|r'(t)\|=\sqrt{4t+(t-1)^2}=t+1$ on $[0,1]$. Also $3x=4t^{3/2}$. Thus $$\int_C3x\,ds=4\int_0^1(t^{5/2}+t^{3/2})\,dt=4\left(\frac27+\frac25\right)=\frac{96}{35}.$$"} {:db/id 17592186134287 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26371e7c-d4aa-5cd0-a363-95439d905659" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186324279} {:answer/id #uuid "4d153674-baf0-565f-a0eb-dec9cc52f8a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186324608} {:answer/id #uuid "9a3d06d0-0635-568c-b9ca-dac6fef15963" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/id 17592186325283} {:answer/id #uuid "9b0a8c83-7180-5d2f-946a-f9b34a2d351d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186325291} {:answer/id #uuid "d4882293-69d6-5858-b2d4-78dc60ebf4d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186325820}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325283} :answer-field/id #uuid "a6c48fd4-9172-51c8-a0ec-c24aea7453e6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326519}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e6d26c08-ceec-5b48-a4a3-f3df87eec565" :question/math-academy-id "q-40403" :question/problem "Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2xyz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A
$$

given that the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \sqrt{4-2z},\,0\le z\le 2\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2xyz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}xz[{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}z\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type II region in the $xz$-plane.
Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to $x$ and then with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{3}z\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2z}}{x}^{3}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}z[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2z}}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}z{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{4-2z}}\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4}(4-2z)^{2}z\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}4z-4{z}^{2}+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={[2{z}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{z}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=2} \\  & =(8-\frac{32}{3}+4)-0 \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134291 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a51fd2d-571a-5a85-a07e-8a55c2f36207" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186324063} {:answer/id #uuid "0d3248ed-3d05-5adc-92c1-792f1a0ebd67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186324092} {:answer/id #uuid "742826f9-f5f3-501e-b5c7-9c646d471014" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{5}" :db/id 17592186324938} {:answer/id #uuid "8e2a6f8d-bce1-5b6d-87e3-5fb6cf8db2b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{6}{7}" :db/id 17592186325179} {:answer/id #uuid "f9e529c4-9682-5822-a2e8-498f2ddddcf0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186326168}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325179} :answer-field/id #uuid "44022b5c-a08a-5837-be96-44fecb3838ac" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326336}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "da6fd76e-d975-5906-a711-4e6478775eef" :question/math-academy-id "q-40446" :question/problem "Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type III region given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,{x}^{2}\le z\le 2{x}^{2},\,0\le y\le 2xz\}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2xz}2x\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2xz}2x\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{2xz}2x\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2{x}^{2}}2x[y]_{y=0}^{y=2xz}dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2{x}^{2}}2x(2xz)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2{x}^{2}}4{x}^{2}z\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2{x}^{2}}4{x}^{2}z\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2{x}^{2}}4{x}^{2}z\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{x}^{2}[{z}^{2}]_{z={x}^{2}}^{z=2{x}^{2}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{x}^{2}((2{x}^{2})^{2}-({x}^{2})^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{6}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{6}\,dx & ={[\frac{6{x}^{7}}{7}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =\frac{6}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134333 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2563641c-3674-599a-bc9b-6a7ff8dc6db8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186324278} {:answer/id #uuid "3380e44e-eb6f-5319-9afd-04efe1186590" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186324383} {:answer/id #uuid "4a8960b7-70fe-5198-ad4d-9a451b90165c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186324576} {:answer/id #uuid "d91bf06c-7c91-517f-8dda-93fec52181f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186325860} {:answer/id #uuid "f579c837-0e7b-5922-9481-0a119644e5dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186326131}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186325860} :answer-field/id #uuid "a6ad0704-99f4-509f-bb7d-ffd14144c5c5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326518}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "871a1be1-8f4a-5616-a788-c400e98cd9b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-40943" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ b \\ c\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}a \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+2b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}6 & -8 & 2 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 \\ 2 & -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}6 & -8 & 2 & 0 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 & -2\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 6 & -8 & 2 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 & 6\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-4(\frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3})+2{x}_{3}=-2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2+{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+2b+c=1+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+0=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134340 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0dd96ba1-2b4a-52b0-ae56-d48afc1ad438" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-4\sqrt{3},4\sqrt{3})" :db/id 17592186324095} {:answer/id #uuid "2ed05277-6e18-5e15-8940-2ac1cc7e711a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-4\sqrt{3},4\sqrt{2})" :db/id 17592186324343} {:answer/id #uuid "45a4f7ba-02b2-575e-9878-19dffb79d143" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-4,4\sqrt{3})" :db/id 17592186324534} {:answer/id #uuid "5ba9dd42-5731-5299-842c-9b4b8a43aecc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-4,4\sqrt{2})" :db/id 17592186324727} {:answer/id #uuid "eedf37c4-e836-577f-8644-c79747d63f14" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-4\sqrt{3},4)" :db/id 17592186326080}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186326080} :answer-field/id #uuid "c09b660e-acc3-5ec3-9d23-f8cb222700d1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326568}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d7c864f9-8a06-59dd-91e8-789300497ddc" :question/math-academy-id "q-41263" :question/problem "![](images/34/34b473c8e212297d8cb434fe0a2dd9872cfa2fda924ac3a4d528bc1318af8c5f.png)

The polar curve $r=8$ and the ray $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{6}$ intersect at the point $P,$ as shown above. What are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(r,\theta )=(8,\frac{5\pi }{6}).$ We can convert the polar coordinates of $P$ to Cartesian coordinates, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =8\cdot \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\  & =-4\sqrt{3} \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{5\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =8\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-4\sqrt{3},4).$"} {:db/id 17592186134367 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7924d408-b0a6-57f4-9535-29236f3d016b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\pi }^{2}-1" :db/id 17592186415810} {:answer/id #uuid "950ad376-e54c-57af-bfa1-45e819b52db4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi ({\pi }^{2}+2)" :db/id 17592186415816} {:answer/id #uuid "ab82bc31-acab-5197-b9ab-1bdf4558c405" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi ({\pi }^{2}-2)" :db/id 17592186415820} {:answer/id #uuid "c5551b46-21d7-59b0-b72c-4198c2a76d8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\pi }^{2}-1" :db/id 17592186415830} {:answer/id #uuid "d84a9c83-a85a-5496-be1f-846504032a6f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\pi }^{2}+1" :db/id 17592186415834}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415816} :answer-field/id #uuid "b60e1b91-b85b-56e9-90f2-353a69264f24" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415853}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "4381a978-8315-576b-b33a-7ce6b2ca6e4b" :question/math-academy-id "q-41810" :question/problem "Use Green's theorem to evaluate $$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r},
$$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{cos}y,{x}^{2}-2y⟩$ and $C$ is the boundary of the square $0\le x\le \pi ,0\le y\le \pi ,$ traversed counterclockwise." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/4f/4f75ee554c61dc799273c2c731d608766d27987937d0058df6ee1e0290d8b060.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+({x}^{2}-2y)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}-2y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le \pi ,0\le y\le \pi \}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+({x}^{2}-2y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{[2xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡y]}_{0}^{\pi }\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\pi x+2)\,dx \\  & ={[\pi {x}^{2}+2x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & ={\pi }^{3}+2\pi  \\  & =\pi ({\pi }^{2}+2).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134371 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "83a235db-fe30-5523-a6f2-1e7015a51178" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\pi \hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}" :db/id 17592186132266} {:answer/id #uuid "a24521cf-55f3-5015-939b-a0cc82725ed9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}" :db/id 17592186132267} {:answer/id #uuid "199823a5-e425-55bd-ac92-cb08df6ff59b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-\pi \hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}" :db/id 17592186132268} {:answer/id #uuid "26bbb2ee-97a5-5ba6-a39c-bf211651dd8e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\pi \hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}+\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}" :db/id 17592186132269} {:answer/id #uuid "6955754e-91e9-5e29-a742-fb32e4672dc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{0}" :db/id 17592186132270}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186132269} :answer-field/id #uuid "b6d59174-8d79-514e-8de5-8030757c35f4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186132265}] :question/id #uuid "edc90e26-2ff6-5c4d-97cc-a6c6e64cf17e" :question/math-academy-id "q-41899" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=x\operatorname{cos}yz\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+y\operatorname{ln}xz\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{k}$. Evaluate $\mathrm{∇}\times \mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1, \frac{π}{2}, 1)$." :question/worked-solution "The source asks for curl. For $\mathbf F=\langle x\cos(yz),0,y\ln(xz)\rangle$, where $xz>0$,
$$\nabla\times\mathbf F=\left\langle\ln(xz),-xy\sin(yz)-\frac yx,xz\sin(yz)\right\rangle.$$
At $(1,\pi/2,1)$ this becomes $\langle0,-\pi,1\rangle$."} {:db/id 17592186134375 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03eefc0e-dc5f-50f8-8aa8-37fedc5b6795" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{2}-3y)\text{ }dy\,dx" :db/id 17592186415777} {:answer/id #uuid "4dfb517d-314f-5d0e-adde-8ffca8af7876" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}y(2x-3)\text{ }dy\,dx" :db/id 17592186415796} {:answer/id #uuid "d8a94d74-4321-5c41-9daa-93ace7652c67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}x(3y+2)\text{ }dy\,dx" :db/id 17592186415835} {:answer/id #uuid "e3efbf16-6539-5ad4-bd13-0040d7d457e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}x(2y-3)\text{ }dy\,dx" :db/id 17592186415838} {:answer/id #uuid "eb384a4b-9a06-5ed5-bfb1-8be217c6cefa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(3y-2)\text{ }dy\,dx" :db/id 17592186415839}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415838} :answer-field/id #uuid "9db11add-d8be-5410-9153-1e6c3098e557" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415851}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1939a88a-677c-5293-8524-d0ecfaa79350" :question/math-academy-id "q-42085" :question/problem "Consider the square $C$ in the plane with vertices $(-1,0),(2,0),(2,3)$ and $(-1,3),$ traversed counterclockwise, and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ Express $$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r},
$$  where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨3xy,{x}^{2}y⟩,$ as a repeated integral." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/6f/6f831b2b707e63e8eb34ff5f6c1c45d0267f51001de2560834d212506b48ee41.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}3xy\,dx+{x}^{2}y\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=3xy$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 3\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}3xy\,dx+{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-3x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}x(2y-3)\text{ }dy\,dx\end{aligned}

for $t\in [0,\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =3\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.222em}\mathbf{i}+4\operatorname{cos}2t\hspace{0.222em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathrm{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}2t\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}2t\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}t{\operatorname{cos}}^{2}t\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}t \\  & =-12{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & =12{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}u \\  & =4{{u}^{3}|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =8\end{aligned}

Here, we have the following information:

- there are $n=7$ rolls

- the probability of getting a $2$ or $3$ on any roll of the die is

$$
p=\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X∼B(7,\frac{1}{3}).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the mean is given by

$$
\text{E}[X]=np,
$$

where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the mean number of times we get a $2$ or a $3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =np \\  & =7\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/2}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/2}}{4}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\left\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/2}}{2}, & x<0 \\ 1-\frac{{e}^{-x/2}}{2}, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134556 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ccd4eedd-785c-50cc-b42b-d0c55d4dc7fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186133375} {:answer/id #uuid "09ad71cc-daf3-58b7-84a2-09b46abc76fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186133376} {:answer/id #uuid "0eb7a6d3-821c-5832-b9c1-72309e5f24de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186133377} {:answer/id #uuid "53a6eac6-21c2-55fa-83d0-f2462264f741" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32" :db/id 17592186133378} {:answer/id #uuid "53fcafd6-845c-5bbc-8f67-a9ab04063640" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "64" :db/id 17592186133379}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186133376} :answer-field/id #uuid "eea0d8dc-6a12-5e38-917e-ecb844858392" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186133374}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e9f4765c-0e5e-5d52-b8b4-0d6e50464ddb" :question/math-academy-id "q-97441" :question/problem "Let $V=C[0,2]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,2],$ equipped with the inner product

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t-3t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)}{4}){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\pi )}{4}]-\frac{1}{2}[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}{4}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}

- Statement $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=0$ is true, while statement $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=2\pi $ is false. This is as a result of the above calculations.
