"ba048324-ec24-5cc4-9fc3-2455f8f53e00" :question/math-academy-id "q-95400" :question/problem "Consider the change of variables given by the matrix equation

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix},
$$

and the curve $C,$ defined as

$$
C:\,2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}-2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-26.
$$

 

Given that the change of variables above reduces $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}$ to its canonical (diagonal) form $6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2},$ what type of a quadratic curve is defined by $C?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we note the following:

$$
C:\,\underbrace{2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}}_{Q(x)}+4\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}-2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-26
$$

Let's write the given change of variables explicitly:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} &=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2},\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We know that the given change of variables reduces $Q(x)$ to its canonical form. Therefore, performing the change of variables on $C,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+5{x}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}-2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2} & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+4\sqrt{5}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2})-2\sqrt{5}(\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{y}_{2}) & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{2} & =-26\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the variable ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{2} & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+({y}_{2}^{2}-10{y}_{2}+25)-25 & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{({y}_{2}-5)}^{2}-25 & =-26 \\ 6{y}_{1}^{2}+{({y}_{2}-5)}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, performing the change of variables

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{z}_{1} &={y}_{1}, \\ {z}_{2} &={y}_{2}-5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{z}_{1}^{2}+{z}_{2}^{2} & =-1 \\ \frac{{z}_{1}^{2}}{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\right)^{2}}+{z}_{2}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

This defines an empty set, also called an imaginary ellipse. Notice that the left-hand side is non-negative for all ${z}_{1}$ and ${z}_{2},$ while the right-hand side is negative."} {:db/id 17592186172653 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f79c33c-3cd0-568c-bb05-a2c622afa98b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\,i+2\,j" :db/id 17592186414189} {:answer/id #uuid "6d9f2696-3096-581e-be2a-958e487b42b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8\,j" :db/id 17592186414196} {:answer/id #uuid "7e5b72a4-dae1-5b76-9b55-33e0ea99b81d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,i-2\,j" :db/id 17592186414199} {:answer/id #uuid "93205ff0-67cf-54ef-8742-39a6959494ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\,i+4\,j" :db/id 17592186414202} {:answer/id #uuid "c19a7ca8-149b-5715-af08-bbca65fbcc05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8\,i-8\,j" :db/id 17592186414208}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414196} :answer-field/id #uuid "18cb798f-48e6-5767-b1da-f2a745b148f0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414217}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8ffff090-3020-5818-a531-b90587e7f062" :question/math-academy-id "q-97566" :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along a counterclockwise circular path centered at $O$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity of $4\,\text{rad/s}.$ Given that the particle is located at $(2,0)$ when $t=0,$ find the velocity of the particle at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ seconds." :question/worked-solution "The position function of a particle moving in a circular path of radius $R$ in the $xy$-plane with a constant angular velocity $\omega $ is given by

$$
r(t)=R(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,j),
$$

where it is assumed that the circle is centered at $O,$ and the particle is at the position $(R,0)$ when $t=0.$

In our case, we have $R=2$ and $\omega =4\text{ rad/s},$ so we get that the position function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2(\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

We find the velocity vector by differentiating the position vector. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =(2(\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j))^{′} \\  & =-8\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,i+8\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the velocity vector at $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =-8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\,i+8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\,j \\  & =-8\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi \,i+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \,j \\  & =-8\,j\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172654 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "87e74c10-6010-5050-b7c0-c210e0b4ea3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6i - 6j" :db/id 17592186171550} {:answer/id #uuid "8824dff0-6218-523e-89ff-b9077023524b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-12\sqrt{3}i - 12j" :db/id 17592186171551} {:answer/id #uuid "9e9b3d2f-dc72-58e6-8e97-ac067586b54e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6\sqrt{3}i + \sqrt{3}j" :db/id 17592186171552} {:answer/id #uuid "3b650509-030d-5225-9e1c-80dea26a5af7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6i" :db/id 17592186171553} {:answer/id #uuid "42b5db76-f8bd-593a-bb98-2597e94188ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6i - $$
r(t)=a(\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\,j),
$$

where it is assumed that the circle is centered at $O,$ and the particle is at the position $(a,0)$ when $t=0.$

In our case, we have $a=3$ and $\omega =2\text{ rad/s},$ so we get that the position function is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =3(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

We find the velocity and acceleration vectors by differentiating. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =(3(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j))^{′} \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j \\ a(t) & =(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j)^{′} \\  & =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i-12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the acceleration vector at $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) & =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})\,i-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})\,j \\  & =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,i-12\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\,j \\  & =-\frac{12}{2}\,i-\frac{12\sqrt{3}}{2}\,j \\  & =-6\,i-6\sqrt{3}\,j\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186173110 :tutorial/content "Consider two samples of sizes $n_1=60$ and $n_2=90$ from two large populations where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the samples are independent and the numbers of individuals having the characteristic in the two samples are $x_1=24$ and $x_2=18$, respectively, we wish to carry out a hypothesis test at the $1\%$ significance level to determine whether there is sufficient evidence that the proportion $p_1$ of individuals having the characteristic in the first population is larger than the corresponding proportion $p_2$ in the second population.

Since $n_1=60$, $n_2=90$, $x_1=24$, $x_2=18$, we have that

- $$
\displaystyle \widehat{\,p}_1 = \dfrac{x_1}{n_1} = \dfrac{24}{60} = \dfrac{2}{5},
$$
- $$
\displaystyle \widehat{\,p}_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{n_2} = \dfrac{18}{90} = \dfrac{1}{5}
$$

and

- $n_1 \widehat{\,p}_1 = 60 \cdot \dfrac{2}{5} = 24 > 5$,
- $$
\displaystyle n_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1) = 60 \cdot \left(1-\dfrac{2}{5}\right) = 36 > 5,
$$
- $n_2 \widehat{\,p}_2 = 90 \cdot \dfrac{1}{5} = 18 > 5$,
- $$
\displaystyle n_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2) = 90 \cdot \left(1-\dfrac{1}{5}\right) = 72 > 5.
$$

As a result, we may use a normal approximation:

$$
\dfrac {(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)} {\sqrt{\overline{p}(1-\overline{p}) \left(\dfrac{1}{n_1}+\dfrac{1}{n_2} \right)} \phantom{\mid}} \sim N(0,1)
$$

where

- $$
\displaystyle \overline{p}=\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}=\dfrac{n_1\widehat{\,p}_1+n_2\widehat{\,p}_2}{n_1+n_2}
$$ is the pooled sample proportion,
- $\!\widehat{\,p}_1, \widehat{\,p}_2$ are the sample proportions,
- $p_1, p_2$ are the population proportions,
- $n_1, n_2$ are the sample sizes,
- $x_1, x_2$ are the numbers of elements in samples possessing the given characteristics.

In our example, the null and alternative hypotheses are the following:

- $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ is the null hypothesis (the population proportions are equal)
- $H_1: p_1 > p_2$ is the alternative (one-tailed) hypothesis (the first population proportion is larger)

First, we compute the pooled sample proportion:

$$
\overline{p}=\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2} = \dfrac{24+18}{60+90} = \dfrac{7}{25}
$$

Assuming the null hypothesis, i.e., $p_1-p_2=0$, we compute the test statistic:

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle z & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{( {\hat{\hspace{0.167em} p}}_{1} - {\hat{\hspace{0.167em} p}}_{2} ) - ( {p}_{1} - {p}_{2} )}{\sqrt{\overline{p} ( 1 - \overline{p} ) ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{ {n}_{1}}} + {\displaystyle \frac{1}{ {n}_{2}}} )} \phantom{|}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{( {\displaystyle \frac{2}{5}} - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{5}} ) - ( 0 )}{\sqrt{ {\displaystyle \frac{7}{25}} ( 1 - {\displaystyle \frac{7}{25}} ) ( {\displaystyle \frac{1}{60}} + {\displaystyle \frac{1}{90}} )} \phantom{|}}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  \approx  2.673\end{array}}
$$

Next, we determine the critical region corresponding to our significance level.

The table above shows the $z$-scores $z_p$ such that

$$
P(Z > z_p) = p
$$

for some particular values of $p$, where $Z\sim N(0,1)$.

So, we reject the null hypothesis $H_0$. As a result, we conclude that there is *sufficient* evidence that, at the $1\%$ level of significance, we have $p_1 \gt p_2$." :tutorial/id #uuid "b5963c87-2241-5a9b-829f-7987da6356c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10580 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186173118 :tutorial/content "Let $X_1$, $X_2$, and $X_3$ be three numbers independently chosen from $N(1,2^2)$. What is the approximate probability that the *minimum* of the three variables is at most $0$?

Suppose that $X_1, X_2, \ldots X_n$ is an I.I.D random sample from a probability distribution. The order statistics, denoted $X_{(r)}$, are defined by ranking the values from smallest to largest. Specifically:

- $X_{(1)} = \min\left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\}$
- $X_{(2)} =$ the second smallest of $\left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\}$
- $X_{(3)} =$ the third smallest of $\left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\}$
- $\quad\vdots$
- $X_{(n)} = \max\left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\}$

For continuous probability distributions, we may assume that

$X_{(1)} < X_{(2)} < X_{(3)} < \cdots < X_{(n)}$
since the probability that any order statistics are the same equals zero.

We wish to find

$$
P\left(X_{(1)} \le 0\right)
$$

To do this, we will first compute the complementary probability and then subtract it from $1{:}$

$$
P\left(X_{(1)} \leq 0\right) = 1 - P\left(X_{(1)} > 0\right)
$$

The event $X_{(1)} > 0$ means that all three numbers $X_1, X_2, X_3$ must be greater than $0$. One such configuration is shown below.

![](images/97/970d7d45c23ff3eaf4e8ac24a14daf583aa0c20c57687c2e2ad4ab9b9582f813.png)

Since the numbers are chosen independently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X_{(1)} > 0) &= P(X_{1} > 0, X_{2} > 0, X_{3} > 0) \\
&= P(X_{1} > 0) \cdot P(X_{2} > 0) \cdot P(X_{3} > 0)
\end{aligned}
$$

Each $X_i \sim N(1,2^2)$, so, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X_{i} > 0) &= P(Z > \frac{0 - 1}{2}) \\
&= P(Z > - 0.5)
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability that $X_i > 0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X_{i} > 0) &= P(Z > - 0.5) \\
&= 1 - P(Z \le - 0.5) \\
&= 1 - Φ(-0.5) \\
&= 1 - 0.3085 \\
&= 0.6915
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the probability that all three numbers are greater than $0$ is

$$
P\left(X_{(1)} > 0 \right) = 0.6915 \cdot 0.6915 \cdot 0.6915 \approx 0.3307
$$

Finally, the desired probability is

$$
P\left(X_{(1)} \leq 0 \right) = 1 - P\left(X_{(1)} > 0\right) \approx 1 - 0.3307 = 0.6693
$$

Thus, the probability that the minimum of $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$ is at most $0$ is $0.6693$." :tutorial/id #uuid "63fd0d31-d5dc-53fb-b276-21a22183aef9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10703 :tutorial/title "Calculating Probabilities Associated With Minimums"} {:db/id 17592186173119 :tutorial/content "Consider two samples of sizes $n_x=16$ and $n_y=18$ from independent normal populations $X$ and $Y$ with equal population variance, where the sample means are

$$
\overline{x}=15.2
$$

and

$$
\overline{y}=13.5
$$

and the sample standard deviations are $s_x=1.75$ and $s_y=2.25$.

We wish to carry out a hypothesis test at the $2.5\%$ significance level to determine whether there is sufficient evidence that the population mean $\mu_x$ of $X$ is larger than the population mean $\mu_y$ of $Y$.

To solve a problem like this, we proceed as follows.

We are told that the populations are normally distributed and their variances are equal, but we do not know the population variance $\sigma^2$.

In cases like this, the random variable

$$
\dfrac{\overline{X} - \overline{Y}- (\mu_x - \mu_y)}{S_p \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n_x} + \dfrac{1}{n_y}}}
$$

follows a student's $t$-distribution $T_\nu$ with

$$
\nu=n_x+n_y-2
$$

degrees of freedom, where

- $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$ are the sample means,
- $\mu_x$ and $\mu_y$ are the population means,
- $n_x$ and $n_y$ are the sample sizes,
- $S_x^2$ and $S_y^2$ are the sample variance, and
- $S_p^2 = \dfrac{(n_x-1)S_x^2+(n_y-1)S_y^2}{n_x+n_y-2}$ is the pooled estimate of the variance.

In our example, the null and alternative hypotheses are the following:

- $H_0: \mu_x = \mu_y$ is the null hypothesis
- $H_1: \mu_x \gt \mu_y$ is the alternative (one-tailed) hypothesis

First, let's compute the number of degrees of freedom and the pooled estimate of the variance for our samples:

$$
\begin{aligned}
ν &= 16 + 18 - 2 = 32 \\
S_{p}^{2} &= ((16 - 1)(1.75)^{2} + (18 - 1)(2.25)^{2})/(16 + 18 - 2) = \frac{33}{8}
\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming the null hypothesis, i.e.,

$$
\mu_x-\mu_y=0
$$

we compute the test statistic:

$$
\begin{aligned}
t &= (x^(―) - y^(―) - (μ_{x} - μ_{y}))/(S_{p}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{x}} + \frac{1}{n_{y}}}) \\
&= (15.2 - 13.5 - (0))/(\sqrt{\frac{33}{8}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{1}{16} + \frac{1}{18}}) \\
&\approx 2.436
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the critical region corresponding to our significance level.

Given a random variable $T$ that has a student's $t$-distribution $T_k$ with $k$ degrees of freedom, the table below shows the $t$-scores $t_{k,p}$ such that

$$
P(T > t_{k,p}) = p
$$

for some particular values of $k$ and $p$.

As a result, we conclude that there is *sufficient* evidence that, at the $2.5\%$ level of significance, we have $\mu_x \gt \mu_y$." :tutorial/id #uuid "3d6c8cc0-c865-5755-b168-60ee83f39b21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10764 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186173126 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to carry out the following hypothesis test:

- $H_0: p_1 = p_2$
- $H_1: p_1 > p_2$

As we just saw, the variance of the difference between the two sampling distributions is

$$
\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}
$$

Now, under the null hypothesis, the two proportions are equal. Thus, assuming that $H_0$ is true, we can set

$$
p_1 = p_2 = p
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var} [\widehat{p}_{1} - \widehat{p}_{2}] &= (p(1 - p))/(n_{1}) + (p(1 - p))/(n_{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var} [\widehat{p}_{1} - \widehat{p}_{2}] &= p(1 - p)(\frac{1}{n_{1}} + \frac{1}{n_{2}})
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the two proportions are equal under the null hypothesis, we can use a **pooled estimate** $\overline{p}$ of the shared proportion $p$ to form a point estimate.

$$
\overline{p} = \dfrac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2} = \dfrac{n_1\widehat{\,p}_1+n_2\widehat{\,p}_2}{n_1+n_2}
$$

where $x_1$ and $x_2$ give the number of sample elements from the first and second samples, respectively, with the characteristic.

Thus, our estimate for the variance is

$$
\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] =\overline{p}(1-\overline{p})\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}\right)
$$

This is similar to the pooled variance estimate we saw in a previous lesson.

As a result, we can use the following normal approximation:

$$
\dfrac {(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)} {\sqrt{\overline{p}(1-\overline{p}) \left(\dfrac{1}{n_1}+\dfrac{1}{n_2} \right)} \phantom{\mid}} \sim N(0,1)
$$

Note the following:

- A pooled variance estimate is preferable to an unpooled estimate when the null hypothesis assumes $p_1 = p_2$. It can be shown that the standard error of the pooled estimate is lower than the unpooled one, making our hypothesis test more reliable.
- On the other hand, suppose we have the following null hypothesis:
$H_0: p_1 - p_2 = k \neq 0$.
In this case, the variances cannot be assumed equal, and we must use an unpooled estimate for the variance, i.e.,
$$
\displaystyle \textrm{Var}[\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}.
$$

In this lesson, we'll only consider null hypotheses of the form $p_1 = p_2$." :tutorial/id #uuid "388c4ec8-6df7-5308-9eba-d8575c965a0f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10795 :tutorial/title "Pooled vs. Unpooled Estimates of Proportion"} {:db/id 17592186173137 :tutorial/content "Let's use our knowledge of the uniqueness property of moment-generating functions to prove some general results.

- **Sums of Bernoulli Random Variables**: Suppose $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\sim \textrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ are independent. Then
$Y = X_1+X_2+ \cdots + X_n \sim B(n,p)$.
To prove this, let $M_{X_i}(t)$ be the moment-generating function of $X_i$ for $i=1,2,\ldots, n$. Then, we have
$M_{X_i}(t) = 1 - p + pe^t$.
By the multiplicative property of moment-generating functions, we have that
$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{Y}(t) & ={M}_{{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}}(t) \\  & ={M}_{{X}_{1}}(t)\cdot {M}_{{X}_{2}}(t)\cdot \hspace{0.222em}⋯\hspace{0.222em}\cdot {M}_{{X}_{n}}(t) \\  & =(1-p+p{e}^{t})\cdot (1-p+p{e}^{t})\cdot \hspace{0.222em}⋯\hspace{0.222em}\cdot (1-p+p{e}^{t}) \\  & =(1-p+p{e}^{t})^{n},\end{aligned}
$$
which is the moment-generating function of a binomial random variable with distribution $B(n, p)$. Now, since any given distribution is characterized by its moment-generating function (meaning that no other distribution can have the same moment-generating function), we conclude that
$Y\sim B(n,p)$.
- **Sums of Binomial Random Variables**: Suppose $X_1\sim B(n_1,p)$ and $X_2\sim B(n_2,p)$ are independent. Then
$Y = X_1+X_2\sim B(n_1+n_2, p)$.
To prove this, let $M_{X_1}(t)$ and $M_{X_2}(t)$ be the moment-generating functions of $X_1$ and $X_2$ respectively. Then, we have
$$
\displaystyle M_{X_1}(t) = (pe^t+q)^{n_1}, \qquad M_{X_2}(t) = (pe^t+q)^{n_2}.
$$
By the multiplicative property of moment-generating functions, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{Y}(t) & ={M}_{{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}}(t) \\  & ={M}_{{X}_{1}}(t)\cdot {M}_{{X}_{2}}(t) \\  & =(p{e}^{t}+q)^{{n}_{1}}\cdot (p{e}^{t}+q)^{{n}_{2}} \\  & =(p{e}^{t}+q)^{{n}_{1}+{n}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
This is the moment-generating function of a binomial random variable with distribution $B(n_1+n_2, p)$. Therefore, by the uniqueness property, we conclude
$Y\sim B(n_1+n_2, p)$.
- **Sums of Poisson Random Variables**: If $X_1\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1)$ and $X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_2)$ are independent, then
$Y = X_1+X_2\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$.
To prove this, let $M_{X_1}(t)$ and $M_{X_2}(t)$ be the moment-generating functions of $X_1$ and $X_2$ respectively. Then, we have
$$
\displaystyle M_{X_1}(t) = e^{\lambda_1(e^t-1)}, \qquad M_{X_2}(t) = e^{\lambda_2(e^t-1)}.
$$
By the multiplicative property of moment-generating functions, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{Y}(t) & ={M}_{{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}}(t) \\  & ={M}_{{X}_{1}}(t)\cdot {M}_{{X}_{2}}(t) \\  & ={e}^{{\lambda }_{1}({e}^{t}-1)}\cdot {e}^{{\lambda }_{2}({e}^{t}-1)} \\  & ={e}^{{\lambda }_{1}({e}^{t}-1)+{\lambda }_{2}({e}^{t}-1)} \\  & ={e}^{({\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2})({e}^{t}-1)}\end{aligned}
$$
This is the moment-generating function of a Poisson random variable with distribution $\textrm{Po}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$. Therefore, by the uniqueness property, we conclude
$Y\sim \textrm{Po}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$.

- **Sums of Normal Random Variables**: Suppose $X_1\sim N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)$ and $X_2\sim N(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)$ are independent. Then
$Y = X_1+X_2\sim N(\mu_1+\mu_2, \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$.
To prove this, let $M_{X_1}(t)$ and $M_{X_2}(t)$ be the moment-generating functions of $X_1$ and $X_2$ respectively. Then, we have
$$
\displaystyle M_{X_1}(t) = \exp\left(\mu_1 t + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2_1 t^2\right), \qquad M_{X_2}(t) = \exp\left(\mu_2 t + \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2_2 t^2\right),
$$
where $\exp(x) = e^x$ is the exponential function.By the multiplicative property of moment-generating functions and by the properties of the exponential function, we have that
$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{Y}(t) & ={M}_{{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}}(t) \\  & ={M}_{{X}_{1}}(t)\cdot {M}_{{X}_{2}}(t) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}({\mu }_{1}t+\frac{1}{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}{t}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{exp}({\mu }_{2}t+\frac{1}{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}({\mu }_{1}t+\frac{1}{2}{\sigma }_{1}^{2}{t}^{2}+{\mu }_{2}t+\frac{1}{2}{\sigma }_{2}^{2}{t}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}(({\mu }_{1}+{\mu }_{2})t+\frac{1}{2}({\sigma }_{1}^{2}+{\sigma }_{2}^{2}){t}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
This is the moment-generating function of a normal random variable with distribution $N(\mu_1+\mu_2, \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$. Therefore, by the uniqueness property, we conclude
$Y\sim N(\mu_1+\mu_2, \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$.

- **Sums of Chi-Square Random Variables**:
Suppose $X_1\sim \chi^2(k_1)$ and $X_2\sim \chi^2(k_2)$ are independent. Then
$Y = X_1+X_2\sim \chi^2(k_1+k_2)$.
To prove this, let $M_{X_1}(t)$ and $M_{X_2}(t)$ be the moment-generating functions of $X_1$ and $X_2$ respectively. Then, we have
$$
\displaystyle M_{X_1}(t) = (1-2t)^{-k_1/2}, \qquad M_{X_2}(t) = (1-2t)^{-k_2/2}.
$$
By the multiplicative property of moment-generating functions, we have that
$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{Y}(t) & ={M}_{{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}}(t) \\  & ={M}_{{X}_{1}}(t)\cdot {M}_{{X}_{2}}(t) \\  & =(1-2t)^{-{k}_{1}/2}\cdot (1-2t)^{-{k}_{2}/2} \\  & =(1-2t)^{-({k}_{1}+{k}_{2})/2}.\end{aligned}
$$
This is the moment-generating function of a chi-square random variable with distribution $\chi^2(k_1+k_2)$. Therefore, by the uniqueness property, we conclude
$Y\sim \chi^2(k_1+k_2)$." :tutorial/id #uuid "78e2b173-dfe3-56d9-901c-b2d4882ae192" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10928 :tutorial/title "Proving Some Well-Known Results"} {:db/id 17592186173162 :tutorial/content "Consider the unit circle configured in the usual way in the coordinate plane. Suppose a particle $P$ is initially at the point $(1,0)$ and moves counterclockwise along the unit circle with a fixed **angular velocity** of $\dfrac\pi3$ **radians per second.** 

The first three seconds of the particle's motion are illustrated below.

![](images/00/009b83d5d0e48c6983950a48523838cc569b3a92511dc9362630316b1d88f86b.png)

    

Since the angular velocity is constant, we refer to this as **uniform circular motion**. This fixed angular velocity is denoted $\omega,$ and we write

$$
\omega = \dfrac\pi 3\,\textrm{rad/s}.
$$

Now, let $\mathbf r(t)$ be the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$ Then, we have

$$
\mathbf {r}(t)= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \, \mathbf i + \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right) \,\mathbf j.
$$

It's worth building a picture of why this formula is true:

- We know that $\mathbf r(\theta) = \cos\theta\,\mathbf i + \sin\theta\,\mathbf j$ traces out a unit circle, starting at the point $(1,0).$

- We can see from the picture that $P$ will return to the starting position after $t=6$ seconds, so the angular frequency of the motion is

$$
\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot t)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi t}{3}\right)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi t}{3}\right)\,j\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $P$ indeed returns to its starting location when $t=6{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(6) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{6\pi }{3}\right)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{6\pi }{3}\right)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)\,j \\  & =r(0).\end{aligned}
$$

In general, if a particle moves counterclockwise along a circle of radius $R$ centered at $O$ with initial position $(R,0),$ then its position vector $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\mathbf {r}(t)= R\left(\cos\omega t \, \mathbf i + \sin\omega t \,\mathbf j\right)\!\,.
$$

Note that for clockwise motion, we have $\omega < 0.$

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "a0eebf3c-594c-5d34-868e-6c476f587498" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5092 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186173177 :tutorial/content "Consider the surface $S$ that's parametrized by the vector-valued function $\mathbf r (u,v),$ given by

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) =\big\langle \sqrt{2}\cos u, \:  v, \: \sqrt{2}\sin u + 2 \big\rangle, \qquad 
0\leq  u \leq \dfrac{\pi}2, \quad -2\leq v \leq 2.
$$

 

How can we determine the tangent plane to this surface at the point $P$ where $u=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $v=-1?$

First, notice the following: 

- By fixing $v=-1,$ we get the parametric curve ${\color{blue}C_u}$ with vector function $\mathbf{r}\left(u,-1\right)$ that depends only on the parameter $u.$

- By fixing $u=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ we get the parametric curve ${\color{red}C_v}$ with vector function $\mathbf{r}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},v\right)$ that depends only on the parameter $v.$

The curves $C_u$ and $C_v$ are called **grid curves**. The domain of the parameter space $D$ and the grid curves $C_u$ and $C_v$ on the surface $S$ are shown below.

![](images/d9/d96a41f9d397419f53956426c2e659ffc207c72c7dface95566338e649efa177.png)

Now, we find the tangent vectors to $C_u$ and $C_v$ at our point $P\mathbin{:}$

- The tangent vector to $C_u$ is denoted $\mathbf{r}'_u,$ and is defined as

$$
\dfrac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial u} = \mathbf{r}'_u.
$$

- The tangent vector to $C_v$ is denoted $\mathbf{r}'_v,$ and is defined as

$$
\dfrac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial v}  = \mathbf{r}'_v.
$$

If $\mathbf{r}'_u$ and $\mathbf{r}'_v$ are nonparallel, then these two vectors can be used to define a unique tangent plane to the surface at the given point.

The corresponding partial derivatives evaluated at $P$ are calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {r}_{u}^{'}=⟨-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}u,\,0,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}u⟩ & \,⟹\, & {r}_{u}^{'}(\frac{\pi }{4},-1)=⟨-1,0,1⟩ \\  & {r}_{v}^{'}=⟨0,1,0⟩ & \,⟹\, & {r}_{v}^{'}(\frac{\pi }{4},-1)=⟨0,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the vectors are not parallel, they indeed define a unique plane. 

![](images/75/753a7abc66d9b101b8c1b86cb77da642f88d48dc8b12997ca39df0b61c9e27cc.png)

Furthermore, we can find a normal vector to the plane by computing the cross product. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{'}\times {r}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}=⟨-1,\,0,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "0cdedbf2-bb57-56a6-b983-c2463e402731" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5330 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186173203 :tutorial/content "Let's now build up a geometric understanding of what the arc length element $\textrm d s$ means. First, we'll consider the case of a parametric curve defined as

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle x(t),\, y(t)\rangle.
$$

Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\mathbf r.$

![](images/2b/2b302806eef01fd6e8160ee6e3183959537c0e9f5c6907238a2eea1d208d3da7.png)

Now consider a small change $\Delta t$ in the parameter $t.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\mathbf r + \Delta\mathbf r,$ where $\Delta \mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. 

![](images/0b/0b1eb1dcc7be637e4e6024b5a8e9e13a4ea5c3e7439be7a2e3083f5ec274ef71.png)

According to the diagram we have

$$
\Delta x = x(t+\Delta t) - x(t), \qquad \Delta y = y(t+\Delta t) - y(t),
$$

where $\Delta x$ and $\Delta y$ are the changes in $x$ and $y,$ respectively, corresponding to the change in $t.$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, these quantities can be approximated as

$$
\Delta x \approx \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\Delta t, \qquad \Delta y \approx \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\Delta t.
$$

The change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Therefore, by the Pythagorean theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & ={(Δx)}^{2}+{(Δy)}^{2} \\  & ≈{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2} \\  & ={\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}(Δt)^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}(Δt)^{2} \\  & =[{\left(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)}^{2}](Δt)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta s

\approx

\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2  + \left( \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\, \Delta t.
$$

If we imagine the limiting case where $\Delta t \to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\textrm d s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm d s

=

\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}\right)^2  + \left( \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}\right)^2}\, \textrm d t
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "65578a76-05f7-551a-acbd-956ae6831965" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5802 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of the Arc Length Element for a Parametric Curve"} {:db/id 17592186173204 :tutorial/content "Now, let's derive the formula for the arc length element $\textrm d s$ for a curve defined using plane polar coordinates. We will use a similar geometric approach.

Consider a curve $r= r(\theta)$ defined using polar coordinates. Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\mathbf r.$

![](images/7f/7fa77b8d4ad159967f917b438096f472cbd7f541495847e11b919a6843e6259b.png)

Now consider a small change $\Delta \theta$ in the parameter $\theta.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\mathbf r + \Delta\mathbf r,$ where $\Delta \mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. 

![](images/10/105112a2bb993a13282c5f36190ca99a46d80a22a4203f653f7f67060e486d48.png)

From here, we see that the vector $\Delta \mathbf r$ can be approximated as the vector addition of two components:

- a vector of length $\Delta r$ acting parallel to $\mathbf r,$ and

- a vector of length $r\Delta \theta$ acting perpendicular to $\mathbf r.$

![](images/08/080fa1112410328ba369e1c2e5d70fc2e5ddba97606a2fdeaa90d61e3e20d874.png)

Note that $\Delta r$ is simply the difference of the radial lengths between the points $P$ and $P'.$ The expression $r\Delta \theta$ comes from the formula for the arc length of a sector of a circle.

Now, the change in arc length $\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\Delta \mathbf r.$ Since our two components are perpendicular, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\  & ≈(Δr)^{2}+(rΔ\theta )^{2} \\  & =Δ{r}^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, we have

$$
\Delta r = r(\theta + \Delta\theta) - r(\theta) = \dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\Delta\theta.
$$

Substituting this into our expression for $(\Delta s)^2$ above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2} \\  & ={r}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}(Δ\theta )^{2} \\  & =[{r}^{2}+{\left(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }\right)}^{2}](Δ\theta )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta s = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\Delta\theta.
$$

If we imagine the limiting case where $\Delta \theta \to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\textrm d s\mathbin{:}$

$$
\textrm d s

=

\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\textrm d\theta
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b310dc84-9da7-5492-9639-145086fe7403" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5803 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of the Arc Length Element for a Polar Curve"} {:db/id 17592186173208 :tutorial/content "Green's theorem allows us to write line integrals as double integrals, and we've seen how Green's theorem simplifies circulation calculations. Even more, Green's theorem can also be used to simplify flux calculations!

To see how, we first recall that the flux of $\mathbf{F}(x,y) =  P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\mathbf j$ across $C$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s= \oint\limits_C P\, \textrm{d}y -Q\, \textrm{d}x
$$

where $C$ is closed and $\mathbf n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

Now, let's set $M= -Q$ and $N=P$. Then, by the circulation form of Green's theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x & ={∮}_{C}N\,\text{d}y+M\,\text{d}x \\  & ={∮}_{C}M\,\text{d}x+N\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂N}{∂x}-\frac{∂M}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}-\left(-\frac{∂Q}{∂y}\right))\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we've obtained the **Green's theorem in flux form**, which we restate below:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \iint\limits_D \left(\dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} +\dfrac{\partial  Q}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A
$$

Now, recall that the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F =  \dfrac{\partial P }{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q }{\partial y}.
$$

Therefore, we can also write Green's theorem in flux form as

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem in flux form allows us to convert a flux line integral into an equivalent double integral." :tutorial/id #uuid "7f3b4b70-8b58-53d1-bc8d-a42daddfab4d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5868 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186173247 :tutorial/content "We have the following critical region at the $5\%$ significance level.

![](images/33/33f033cf537d9c4af2b4654b15d6958bdfc8a03ad9e8777afd22f0314ae9b72b.png)

Also, we have the following sample data:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{x} & =40.2,\hspace{2em} & \overset{―}{y} & =39.9 \\ {n}_{x} & =14,\hspace{2em} & {n}_{y} & =16, \\ {\sigma }_{x} & =0.25,\hspace{2em} & {\sigma }_{y} & =0.3\end{aligned}
$$

Assuming the null hypothesis, i.e.,

$$
\mu_x=\mu_y
$$

we compute our test statistic as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
z &= (x^(―) - y^(―) - (μ_{x} - μ_{y}))/(\sqrt{\frac{σ_{x}^{2}}{n_{x}} + \frac{σ_{y}^{2}}{n_{y}}}) \\
&= (40.2 - 39.9 - (0))/(\sqrt{\frac{0.25^{2}}{14} + \frac{0.3^{2}}{16}}) \\
&\approx 2.987
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our test statistic ($2.987$) lies in the critical region, as shown below.

![](images/ab/abd4d3e613641b0029efffd8bbf65f2ee161066c032e9eeaf17d107e8817a42d.png)

Therefore, we conclude the following:

- If we assume $\mu_x=\mu_y$ (i.e., the null hypothesis is true), getting two samples where the means differ by $\overline{x}-\overline{y} = 0.3\,\textrm{mm}$ or more has a probability that is *smaller than* $0.05 = 5\%$, our significance level.
- Therefore, we have a statistically significant result and reject the null hypothesis.
- In conclusion, there is *sufficient* evidence that, at the $5\%$ level of significance, we have $\mu_x \gt \mu_y$.

Let's now look at a situation where we must consider the left tail of the critical region." :tutorial/id #uuid "d20fc878-86f7-5ed8-8fa0-2958b7674b2c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7003 :tutorial/title "Computing the Test Statistic"} {:db/id 17592186173252 :tutorial/content "Consider the surface integral of the function

$$
f(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2+z^2
$$

 
over the parametric surface $S,$ defined as

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle u, \: 2v, \: -u \big\rangle, \quad (u,v)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is the unit square in the $uv$-plane given by

$$
D = \{(u,v) \: | \: 0\leq u\leq 1,\: 0\leq v\leq 1\}.
$$

Let's compute the surface integral of $f$ over $S.$

For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the surface integral of $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S 
=
\iint\limits_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \left\|  \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v \right\|  \text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂u},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}-1⟩ \\ {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂y}{∂v},\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\hspace{0.222em}2,\hspace{0.222em}0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the fundamental vector product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'} & =\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\left\langle \begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{vmatrix},\hspace{0.222em}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}\right\rangle  \\  & =⟨2,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖ & =‖⟨2,\hspace{0.222em}0,\hspace{0.222em}2⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) & =({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\hspace{0.167em}{|}_{x=u\,y=2v\,z=-u} \\  & ={u}^{2}+(2v)^{2}+(-u)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}+{u}^{2} \\  & =2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\hspace{0.167em}\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(\mathbf{r}(u,v))‖{\mathbf{r}}_{u}^{'}\times {\mathbf{r}}_{v}^{'}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}(2{u}^{2}+4{v}^{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\hspace{0.167em}{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\hspace{0.222em}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+8\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v+8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =12\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot (1-0)\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =12\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5620ba9b-3795-5fdb-bc39-1699fb66c6b7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7623 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} {:db/id 17592186173259 :tutorial/content "Suppose that the velocity $\mathbf v,$ in meters per second, of a particle $P$ of mass $2\,\textrm{kg}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf v = \langle t,\: t^2 \rangle,
$$

where $t \gt 0$ is the time in seconds. 

Let's use Newton's second law to calculate the resultant force acting on this particle.

We start by calculating the acceleration vector by differentiating the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, the resultant force $\mathbf F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =2\cdot ⟨1,\,2t⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,4t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the resultant force acting on the particle at time $t.$ 

To calculate the force at a particular moment, say, $t = 3\,\textrm s,$ we substitute this value into the expression for $\mathbf F{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(3) &=⟨2,\,4(3)⟩=⟨2,\,12⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force acting on $P$ when $t=3\,\textrm s$ equals $\left\langle 2,\: 12 \right\rangle\!\,\textrm N.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1177bebb-22a2-5475-8ae5-b29b33718235" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7809 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"}]

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $50\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $105\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $\frac{1}{180}\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $15\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=105\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=105I=105\,\frac{dq}{dt}.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{(1/180)}=180q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=15\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=15\,\frac{dI}{dt}=15\,\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dq}{dt}\right)=15\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

$$
50\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=105\,\frac{dq}{dt}+180q+15\,\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}},
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}q}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+12q=\frac{10}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${q}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{d{q}_{c}}{dt}+12{q}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{q}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-3t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}_{p} & =\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{d{q}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{q}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+7(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\, &  \\ +12(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{10}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ (-21\alpha +3\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(3\alpha +21\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =\frac{10}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-21\alpha +3\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ 3\alpha +21\beta &=\frac{10}{3}\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{1}{45},$ $\beta =\frac{7}{45}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{q}_{p}(t)=\frac{1}{45}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{45}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
q(t)={q}_{c}(t)+{q}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{45}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{45}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Differentiating this expression for $q(t),$ we obtain the following expression for $I$ in amperes:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}(A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{45}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{45}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) \\  & =-4A{e}^{-4t}-3B{e}^{-3t}-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{15}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=-4A{e}^{-4t}-3B{e}^{-3t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function $$
\displaystyle {I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{15}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)
$$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{15}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{1}{15}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{7}{15}\right)}^{2}}≈0.47,
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

$$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{1}{15}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\frac{7}{15}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{\left(\frac{1}{15}\right)}^{2}+{\left(\frac{7}{15}\right)}^{2}}≈0.47,
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Since the integration of vector functions is done component-by-component, the properties of integrals of vector functions are immediately inherited from those of the integrals of real-valued functions. 

Suppose that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are vector-valued functions that are continuous on a closed interval $[a,b],$ and $\alpha$ is a scalar. 
Then, the *vector addition and scalar multiplication rules* are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}(f(t)+g(t))\text{d}t={\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\,+\,{\int }_{a}^{b}g(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{vector addition rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}\alpha \,f(t)\,\text{d}t=\alpha \,{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{scalar constant multiple rule}\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, if $\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle t, \: \cos t\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf g(t) = \left\langle -t^2, \: \sin t \right\rangle,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int [f(t)+2g(t)]\text{d}t & =\int f(t)\,\text{d}t+2\int g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t+2\int ⟨-{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩+⟨2\int -{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\,2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩+⟨-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{3},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{2}-4{t}^{3}}{6},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $C_1, \, C_2, \, C_3, \, C_4$ are arbitrary real constants and ${\mathbf C} = \langle C_1+C_3, C_2+C_4 \rangle$ is a constant vector.

Consider the curve $C$ that's defined parametrically by 
$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle t, \: t^3 +1 \right\rangle, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

The point $P$ corresponding to $t=1$ on the curve has coordinates $(1,2).$ We know that a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is given by $\mathbf f'(1),$ as shown below.

![](images/2b/2b4f4dad09042b761fe950c694c8cf645501106cd1d1d9c0f7a78967b224951c.png)

We compute $\mathbf f'(t)$ as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\mathbf{f}}^{\prime } ( t ) & \displaystyle  = \langle  {\displaystyle \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} t}} ( t ) , \hspace{0.222em} {\displaystyle \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d} t}} ( {t}^{3} ) \rangle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \langle  1 , 3 {t}^{2} \rangle  ,\end{array}
$$

Substituting $t=1$ into the above gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P:$

$$
\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle {\mathbf{f}}^{\prime } ( 1 ) & \displaystyle  = \langle  1 , \hspace{0.222em} 3 ( 1 {)}^{2} \rangle  \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \langle  1 , 3 \rangle  ,\end{array}
$$

As we'll see, it's more helpful to work with unit vectors. Notice that $\mathbf f'(1)$ is not a unit vector because

$$
\begin{array}{cc}\Vert  {\mathbf{f}}^{\prime } ( 1 ) \Vert  &  = \sqrt{{1}^{2} + {3}^{2}} \\  &  = \sqrt{10} .\end{array}
$$

The **curvature** of a curve measures how much the curve "bends" at a given point. It can also be thought of as a measure of how much the curve deviates from being a straight line. Curvature is denoted by the Greek letter $\kappa$ (pronounced "kappa"). 

If $\kappa=0$ at some point on a curve, then that curve looks like a straight line in some neighborhood of the point.

If the curve $\mathbf{r}(s)$ is parametrized by the arc length $s,$ then the curvature $\kappa$ is the magnitude of the change of direction of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T$ per unit of arc length. That is,

$$
\kappa(s) = \left\| \dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf T}{\textrm{d}s}  \right\|= \| \mathbf T'(s) \|.
$$

Note that $|| \mathbf v ||$ denotes the magnitude of the vector $\mathbf v.$

For example, suppose we are given the curve 

$$
\mathbf r(s)= \left\langle \sin\left(\dfrac s2\right), \: \dfrac{\sqrt{3}s}{2}, \: -\cos\left(\dfrac s2\right)\right\rangle
$$

 
which is parametrized by arc length $s.$ Let's find the curvature of  $\mathbf r(s)$  at the point where $s={\pi}.$

First, we find the unit tangent vector:

$$
\mathbf T(s) =\dfrac 12 \left\langle \cos\left( \dfrac s2\right), \: \sqrt{3}, \: \sin \left(\dfrac s2\right)\right\rangle
$$

 

Next, we differentiate $\mathbf{T}(s)$ and evaluate its absolute value at $s=\pi\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(s) & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\sqrt{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right))⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right),\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(\pi ) & =\frac{1}{4}⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right),\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the curvature by taking the magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =‖{T}^{′}(\pi )‖=\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{(0)}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

**Note:** To calculate $\kappa,$ the function $\mathbf{r}(s)$ should be at least twice differentiable with respect to $s.$

The center of the osculating circle for a curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at a point where $t=t_0$ is located at the tip of the vector 

$$
\mathbf r(t_0)+R(t_0) \mathbf N(t_0)
$$

where $\mathbf N(t)$ denotes the principal normal vector to the curve.

For example, the curve $C$ parameterized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \bigg\langle t+1, 2- \dfrac{t^2}{2} \bigg\rangle
$$

has the normal vector

$$
\mathbf{N}(t) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+t^2}} \langle -t, \: -1 \rangle ,
$$

and the radius of curvature at the point $P(1,2)$ where $t=0$ is $R(0)=1.$

So, the center of the osculating circle is at the tip of the vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)+R(0)N(0) & =⟨0+1,\,2-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}⟩+1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}}}⟨0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2⟩+⟨0,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the center of the osculating circle at the point where $t=0$ is located at $\left(1, 1 \right),$ as shown below.

![](images/d8/d8cd8407e6398b3409e7f575e152976669393914e2e5d7335121287276af6e41.png)

If a curve has a curvature of zero at some point, the radius of curvature at that point is defined to be infinite.

It follows from the definition that a straight line has zero curvature at all of its points. Conversely, if a curve has zero curvature at any point, it must be contained on a straight line.

Suppose now that we want to find the radius of curvature for the curve 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle t^2, \: 1 - t^2, \: 1+ t^2 \right\rangle
$$

at an arbitrary point where $t> 0.$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and its magnitude $\| \mathbf r'(t) \|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,-2t,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(-2t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the last step, we used the fact that $\sqrt{t^2}=t$ since $t>0.$

Next, we find the unit tangent and its derivative for $t>0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}t}\cdot ⟨2t,\,-2t,\,2t⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨1,-1,1⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(t) & =⟨0,0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}t}{0}=\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, despite its "parabolic" appearance, the given curve is contained on a straight line!

**Note:** Often, the unit tangent vector of a curve $\mathbf T(t)$ may look a bit complicated. In such cases, the following formula involving a cross product may be useful. It says that the radius of curvature of a twice-differentiable curve $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by 

$$
R(t)=  \dfrac{1}{\kappa(t)} =\frac{{{{\left\| {\mathbf r'\left( t \right)} \right\|}^3}}}{{\left\| {\mathbf r'\left( t \right) \times \mathbf r''\left( t \right)} \right\|}}.
$$

To demonstrate using Cramer's rule on a $3 \times 3$ system, consider the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+z &=9 \\ 2y+3z &=7 \\ -8x+y+6z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

First, let's rewrite the system to reveal the coefficients:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4x+2y+1z &=9 \\ 0x+2y+3z &=7 \\ -8x+1y+6z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start finding the determinant of the coefficients matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}D=\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ -8 & 1 & 6\end{vmatrix} & =4\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{vmatrix}+1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4(12-3)-2(0+24)+(0+16) \\  & =36-48+16 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find $D_x,$ $D_y,$ and $D_z.$

- To find $D_x,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *first* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x}=\begin{vmatrix}9 & 2 & 1 \\ 7 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 6\end{vmatrix} & =9\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 6\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{vmatrix}+1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}7 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =9(12-3)-2(42-0)+(7-0) \\  & =81-84+7 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

- To find $D_y,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *second* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{y}=\begin{vmatrix}4 & 9 & 1 \\ 0 & 7 & 3 \\ -8 & 0 & 6\end{vmatrix} & =4\cdot \begin{vmatrix}7 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{vmatrix}-9\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 3 \\ -8 & 6\end{vmatrix}+1\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -8 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4(42)-9(0+24)+(0+56) \\  & =168-216+56 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

- To find $D_z,$ we take the coefficients matrix, replace the *third* column by the right-hand side of the system, and calculate the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{z}=\begin{vmatrix}4 & 2 & 9 \\ 0 & 2 & 7 \\ -8 & 1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & =4\cdot \begin{vmatrix}2 & 7 \\ 1 & 0\end{vmatrix}-2\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -8 & 0\end{vmatrix}+9\cdot \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -8 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =4(-7)-2(0+56)+9(0+16) \\  & =-28-112+144 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to the system is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩ & =⟨\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},\frac{{D}_{y}}{D},\frac{{D}_{z}}{D}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4}{4},\frac{8}{4},\frac{4}{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute a probability involving a normally distributed variable $X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2),$ it is convenient to transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring: $$ Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma} $$ So, we have $$ P(X < x) = P \left( Z < \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \right) $$ where $Z \sim N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. For example, suppose we have a random variable $X \sim N(1,2^2)$ and we want to compute $P(X \leq 1.4)$ using the following $z$-table:
$z$$\, 0 \,$$\, 0.01 \,$$\, 0.02 \,$
$\, 0 \,$$\, 0.5 \,$$\, 0.504 \,$$\, 0.508 \,$
$\, 0.1 \,$$\, 0.5398 \,$$\, 0.5438 \,$$\, 0.5478 \,$
$\, 0.2 \,$$\, 0.5793 \,$$\, 0.5832 \,$$\, 0.5871 \,$
The $z$-table above shows the cumulative probabilities for a normal random variable $Z \sim N(0,1).$ In order to use the table to compute $P(X \leq 1.4),$ we must first transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring: $$ \begin{aligned}P(X\le 1.4) & =P(Z\le \frac{1.4-1}{2}) \\ & =P(Z\le 0.2)\end{aligned} $$ According to the table, we have $$ P(Z \leq 0.2) = 0.5793 . $$ Therefore, $$ P(X \leq 1.4) = 0.5793. $$

If a surface is parametrized by a differentiable vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \big\langle x(u,v), \: y(u,v), \: z(u,v) \big\rangle
$$

where $(u,v) \in D\subseteq \mathbb R^2,$ then the **fundamental vector product** of the surface is defined as

$$
\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v = 
\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂u} \\ \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂v}\end{vmatrix}.
$$

In particular, if the fundamental vector product of a surface is nonzero at a point $(x_0, y_0),$ then it defines a normal vector to the surface at this point.

To derive a formula for a conical frustum's volume, we first extend the frustum to form a complete cone.

![](images/dc/dccb56262085d93198e45754f7e4ae7e1c106ec21dfd41733aefe86151c37d41.png)

Our frustum is the object that remains when we remove the smaller cone (on top) from the larger cone.

To calculate the volume of the frustum, we subtract the volume of the smaller cone from the volume of the larger cone. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{L} &= V_{big} - V_{small} \\
&= \frac{1}{3}πR^{2}(h + h^{′}) - \frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h^{′} \\
&= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + R^{2}h^{′} - r^{2}h^{′}) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + h^{′}(R^{2} - r^{2}))
\end{aligned}
$$

Now consider the right triangle made by the complete cone, shown below.

![](images/2a/2a1f0ca0e176fee61a5978971aaae76d8cac39de418a3616dece128b83bb7673.png)

Notice that $\triangle OPT$ and $\triangle OQS$ are similar by the AA criterion. So, we have

$$
\dfrac{h'}{r} = \dfrac{h+h'}{R}
$$

which can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}
h^{′}R &= (h + h^{′})r \\
h^{′}R &= hr + h^{′}r \\
h^{′}R - h^{′}r &= hr \\
h^{′}(R - r) &= hr \\
h^{′} &= \frac{hr}{R - r}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of our frustum is

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_{L} &= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + h^{′}(R^{2} - r^{2})) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + \frac{hr}{R - r}(R^{2} - r^{2})) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + \frac{hr}{R - r}(R - r)(R + r)) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}π(R^{2}h + hr(R + r)) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}πh(R^{2} + rR + r^{2}) \\
&= \frac{1}{3}πh(R^{2} + r^{2} + Rr)
\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose we want to calculate the arc length of the curve $C$ given by the vector-valued function

$$
\mathbf r(t)= \left\langle \dfrac{t^3}{3}, \: \dfrac{t^2}{2}\right\rangle, \qquad    t \in [0,1].
$$

 

The length of this curve is given by

$$
L= \int_{0}^{1} \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm d t.
$$

To compute $\| \mathbf r'(t) \|,$ we take the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ and compute its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}\right),\hspace{0.222em}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2},\hspace{0.222em}t⟩, \\ ‖{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{({t}^{2})^{2}+{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of the curve $C$ is given by the integral

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{4}+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{2}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{t}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}|t|\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this integral using substitution. Let $u = t^2+1,$ then $\textrm d u = 2 t\,\textrm d t.$ Therefore, our integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t\cdot \sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{[{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2\sqrt{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that if the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ is parametrized by a general parameter $t,$ then the curvature of $\mathbf{r}$ is given by

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|},
$$

where $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf r'(t)}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|}$ is the unit tangent vector to the curve. 

Here, $\mathbf r'(t)$ is a vector function and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|$ is a scalar function.
So, we differentiate $\mathbf T(t)$ by using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(T) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}\left(\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\right) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{′}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}\left(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\right)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂t}({r}^{′}(t)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂t}\left(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\right)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{″}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the cross product of a vector with itself equals $\mathbf{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\times {T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\times (\frac{∂}{∂t}\left(\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\right)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)+\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}\cdot {r}^{″}(t)) \\  & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,({r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the magnitude of both sides and use the fact that $\mathbf T$ is a unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖T(t)\times {T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ ‖T(t)‖\cdot ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ 1\cdot ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\,‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The **principal normal vector** to a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is a unit vector that 

- is perpendicular to the unit tangent vector, and

- points in the direction that the curve is bending.

In general, if the unit tangent vector is given by $\mathbf T(t),$ then the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|},
$$

where it is assumed that $\|\mathbf T'(t)\|\neq 0.$

To demonstrate, suppose that the curve $C$ is parametrized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle 2\cos t, \: 2\sin t \right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0, \pi].
$$

We will compute the principal normal vector at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

First, using the formula for the unit tangent, $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf f'(t)}{||\mathbf f'(t)||},$ we find that the general unit tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf T(t)= \left\langle {-\sin t}, \cos t\right\rangle.
$$

Now, when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ we have the point $P(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).$ The unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and the principal normal vector $\mathbf{N}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ at this point are shown below:

![](images/d0/d0a30a44bb825a8a12ca54153b6223b9bf0c2b754245b21650a5664db5e1647e.png)

To calculate the principal normal vector, we start by calculating the derivative of the unit tangent function. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general principal normal vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{||{T}^{′}(t)||} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{{\cos }^{2}⁡t+{\sin }^{2}⁡t}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $\mathbf N\left(\dfrac\pi 4\right),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}N\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, it's easy to check that $\mathbf T'(t)$ and $\mathbf N'(t)$ are perpendicular for all $t$ by computing the dot product and showing that we get zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\cdot N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf r (t)$ is given by $\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] .$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d t} [f(\mathbf r (t))] = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $\nabla f(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-z)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x,-2y,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x = \sin t, y=\cos t,$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $\nabla f(\mathbf r(t)){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}t,-2\operatorname{cos}t,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}t,-\operatorname{sin}t,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}t,-2\operatorname{cos}t,-1⟩\cdot ⟨\operatorname{cos}t,-\operatorname{sin}t,1⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}t\cdot \operatorname{cos}t-2\operatorname{cos}t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}t)-1\cdot 1 \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t+2\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t-1 \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)$ at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right))] & =4\operatorname{sin}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{cos}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)-1 \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,2⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$

The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{3}-yz$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨1,1,1⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1)-f(0,0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,1,1⟩-⟨0,0,0⟩) \\ 0-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ 0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨3{x}^{2},-z,-y⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨3{c}_{1}^{2},-{c}_{3},-{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ 0 & =⟨3{c}_{1}^{2},-{c}_{3},-{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ 0 & =3{c}_{1}^{2}-{c}_{3}-{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-0}{1} \\ x & =y=z\end{aligned}

Let's examine each of our statements in turn.

- Statement “For any $A\in S,$ we have $1\cdot A=A.$” is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A=({a}_{ij})\in S,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, we have

$$
1\cdot {a}_{ij}={a}_{ij},
$$

and hence,

$$
1\cdot A=A.
$$

- Statements “For any $A\in S$ and $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we have $(\alpha +\beta )A=\alpha A+\beta A.$” is true. Indeed, for any $2\times 2$ matrix $A=({a}_{ij})\in S,$ the entries are just real numbers. Thus, for any $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we obtain that

$$
(\alpha +\beta ){a}_{ij}=\alpha {a}_{ij}+\beta {a}_{ij},
$$

and hence,

$$
(\alpha +\beta )A=\alpha A+\beta A.
$$

- Statement “There is a matrix $A\in S$ such that $\frac{1}{2}(2A)\ne A.$” is false. For a matrix in $A\in S,$ we have that

$$
\frac{1}{2}(2A)=(\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2)A=1\cdot A=A
$$

since the scalar multiplication of matrices is associative.

Therefore, the correct answer is “For any $A\in S,$ we have $1\cdot A=A.$”; “For any $A\in S$ and $\alpha ,\beta \in R,$ we have $(\alpha +\beta )A=\alpha A+\beta A.$” only.

with $a=-\frac{1}{3}<0.$

$$

$$

If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ not both zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=0.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the given expressions for ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t)$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(2t-4{t}^{2})+{x}_{2}(3t-6{t}^{2}) & =0 \\ (2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2})t+(-4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}){t}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 3 & 0 \\ -4 & -6 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot column is the $1$st one. Hence, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the $1$st equation, we get

$$
2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix},\hspace{2em}{x}_{2}\in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Finally, for any ${x}_{2}\ne 0,$ we obtain 

$$
\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{(-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2})}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}y-1 & x\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}y-1 &=0 \\ x &=0\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=0 \\ y &=1.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,1).$ Since the point $(0,1)$ does not belong to the interior of $D,$ we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize each part of the boundary:

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(1,0)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨t,0⟩,\,t\in (0,1).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(t,0) \\  & =(t)(0)-(t) \\  & =-t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the derivative of $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have critical points on the open interval $t\in (0,1).$

- The line connecting $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
r=⟨0,t⟩,\,t\in (0,2).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(0,t) \\  & =(0)(t)-(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $F(t)$ is constant. So, $F(t)$ does not have local extremum points on the open interval $t\in (0,2).$

- The line connecting $(1,0)$ and $(0,2)$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0⟩+t(⟨0,2⟩-⟨1,0⟩) \\  & =⟨1,0⟩+t⟨-1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨1-t,2t⟩,\,t\in (0,1).\end{aligned}
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(1-t,2t) \\  & =(1-t)(2t)-(1-t) \\  & =-2{t}^{2}+3t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,1),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (-2{t}^{2}+3t-1)^{′} & =0 \\ -4t+3 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives one solution. Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain one candidate point, $(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{2}).$

Also, we have to include the corner points of the region as candidates for extrema. So, in total we obtain four candidates:

$$
(0,0),\,(1,0),\,(0,2),\,(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{2})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{8}$ |

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}16{x}_{1}+12{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 8{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -12{x}_{1}-9{x}_{2} &=0\end{aligned}\right.

Let $\delta >0.$ A *neighborhood* of a point ${x}_{0}$ is the set of points whose distance from ${x}_{0}$ is less than $\delta .$ 

$$
\{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta \}
$$

In two-dimensional space, a neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ is the open disc $|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta ,$ as shown below.

![](images/50/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

Furthermore, we have the following definitions:

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

Now, the set $A$ consists of all points that lie on or inside the ellipse $$
\displaystyle \frac{{x}^{2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\le 1.
$$ A sketch of this region is shown below:

![](images/04/0485539c238417b1b93904f9a0e889198c64ff29a4629636094d33048d0bdd32.png)

Let's add the points $P(0.5,0.5)$ and $Q(-1,\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})$ and some neighborhoods of these points to our diagram.

![](images/04/0485539c238417b1b93904f9a0e889198c64ff29a4629636094d33048d0bdd32.png)

Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The coordinates of $Q(-1,\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})$ satisfy the equation $\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=1.$ Hence, $P$ lies in the set $∂A,$ the boundary of $A.$

- Statement II is true. The coordinates of $P(0.5,0.5)$  satisfy the inequality $$
\displaystyle \frac{{x}^{2}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\le 1.
$$ Hence, $P$ lies in the set $A.$

- Statement III is false. Every open neighborhood of $Q$ contains points that belong to $A$ and points that do not belong to $A.$ The point $Q$ is a boundary point for the given set.

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I and II only.'

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))]=\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
\mathrm{∇}f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+x\operatorname{cos}y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.
$$

First, we substitute $x=\frac{t}{2}$ and $y=t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) & =\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{t}{2}\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf{r}(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))] & =\mathrm{∇}f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot {\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\frac{t}{2}\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j})\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}t\cdot \frac{1}{2}+\frac{t}{2}\operatorname{cos}t\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}t+t\operatorname{cos}t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we obtain

$$

$$

$$

Suppose we want to find the equation of the **tangent line** to the ellipse 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} =1
